Dying Hadrian adopts Antoninus Pius — the torch of good rule passed hand to hand in history's strangest accident of power.
The shipowner-preacher Marcion splits the church over which books count as scripture — heresy as the question the faith needed to answer.
Ptolemy's great star catalog maps the heavens for a thousand years — gloriously, usefully wrong, and the start of how science works.
Ptolemy publishes the Geography that will guide mapmakers for a thousand years — every map a promise, his the longest-kept.
The freed slave Hermas writes his visions of a shepherd angel — Rome's first bestseller of faith, almost a book of the Bible.
The philosopher-emperor Marcus Aurelius takes the throne — a good man with absolute power who never stopped trying to deserve it.
Plague comes home with the legions from the East and kills millions — empires fear barbarians, but they should fear microbes.
Merchants claiming to be Rome's envoys arrive at the Han court by sea — two empires meeting face to face at last.
The physician Galen becomes Rome's medical voice — one man's curiosity stretched across fifteen centuries of medicine.
Trapped legions pray on the Danube and a sudden storm saves Marcus Aurelius's army — the rain came when men needed it most.
Christians are tortured in Lyon's arena and the slave girl Blandina will not break — a slave stronger than the empire.
Marcus Aurelius writes his private thoughts in Greek on the frontier — the most honest book ever written by a king, never meant for us.
Marcus Aurelius dies on the Danube and Commodus ends the golden age — a father's love undoing what five adoptions built.
Taoist healers lead a peasant revolt that bleeds the Han white — faith and hunger make a fearsome army.
The warlord Dong Zhuo burns Luoyang and China slides into chaos — one man's ambition, and a civilization falls apart.
Commodus fights in the arena, thinking himself Hercules — when the man at the top loses his mind, the whole pyramid wobbles.
Commodus is murdered in his bath and the guard auctions the throne — the empire already dead, just still walking around.
Septimius Severus marches on Rome and founds a soldier-emperor dynasty — the sword becomes the vote.
At Lyon, Romans fight Romans in the bloodiest civil battle — sixty thousand dead for one man's throne.
Rabbi Judah the Prince gathers the oral law into the Mishnah — generations of debate made permanent, Judaism saved in books.
Young Antony gives away everything and walks into the Egyptian desert — seeking solitude with heaven, founding a movement instead.
Fire ships destroy Cao Cao's fleet at Red Cliffs — one night of fire splits China three ways and births a thousand years of stories.
Caracalla makes every free man in the empire a Roman citizen — the empire finally admitting it is the world itself.
Caracalla invades Parthia, then is murdered by his own guard on the road — the distance between triumph and a ditch is one blade.
Caracalla's baths open — marble halls where senators and slaves bathe together; hot water for everyone.
Fourteen-year-old Elagabalus brings his desert sun-god to Rome — for four strange years, the sun ruled the empire.
Elagabalus is killed and thrown in the Tiber — the palace eats the strange ones, and the grown-ups are back in charge.
Ardashir overthrows the Parthians and crowns a new Persian empire — Rome's old enemy with a new and fiercer face.
Wei, Shu, and Wu divide China — a hundred years of war, and the stories left behind worth more than the prize.
Soldiers murder Severus Alexander and fifty years of chaos begin — twenty-six claimants, the empire split and bleeding.
Shapur I takes Persia's throne — Rome will learn to fear him, and his victories are still carved in the cliffs.
Philip the Arab takes power — a boy from the Syrian desert wearing the purple; the empire belongs to no single people now.
Philip celebrates a thousand years of Rome with games — banners and cheering over cracks that run to the foundation.
A new plague empties cities and Bishop Cyprian tells Christians to nurse the dying — sometimes the best argument for a faith is a hand on a forehead.
Decius orders the first empire-wide persecution — thousands choose prison and death with a quiet certainty that frightened Rome.
Bishop Cyprian's letters hold the African church together through plague and persecution — a pen stitching the church whole.
The oldest known church building stands on the Euphrates — a house, a font, a painting, and people who believed.
Valerian targets Christian leaders; Pope Sixtus dies preaching — two years later the persecutor himself is in Persian chains.
Postumus breaks away and Gaul rules itself for fourteen years — the scandal was that it worked fine without Rome.
Shapur captures Valerian — the first Roman emperor taken alive; the empire that conquered the world could not protect its own head.
Gothic raiders burn Athens — if the school of the world could burn, the lesson ran, anything could.
Antony retreats deeper into the desert as monks begin to follow — the loneliest movement in history, thousands of hermits alone together.
Warrior queen Zenobia seizes the Roman East — for three years a woman rules from Egypt to Anatolia, and the desert carries her name.
Aurelian retakes the East and Zenobia walks in golden chains through Rome — unbroken, even in chains.
Aurelian makes the Unconquered Sun's birthday — December 25 — an imperial holiday; history had other plans for that date.
Rome builds a twelve-mile wall around itself — every stone an admission that the capital now fears attack.
Sima Yan's Jin reunites the Three Kingdoms — a real cheering, a false peace; some reunions are just the pause between storms.
The Balkan soldier Diocletian ends fifty years of chaos — not with poetry, with administration; Rome exhales.
Diocletian takes the East, Maximian the West — one empire, two thrones, and the beginning of the parting.
The Tetrarchy divides Rome among four emperors — orderly, rational, doomed; men don't share power the way maps share borders.
Constantius recovers Britain from the usurper Allectus — but the island had learned it could stand alone.
Diocletian's treaty fixes Rome's eastern border for forty years — in the history of Rome and Persia, that counts as a miracle.
King Tiridates converts and Armenia becomes the first Christian nation — a small mountain kingdom beating Rome to it by twelve years.
Diocletian fixes maximum prices across the empire — the merchants laughed, hid their goods, and the market ignored him.
Diocletian orders churches destroyed and scriptures burned — the worst persecution Rome ever managed, and it failed completely.
Diocletian abdicates and grows cabbages — the only emperor to walk away from absolute power, and mean it.
Soldiers at York proclaim Constantine emperor — history's hinge was a shield-bang in a drafty northern fortress.
Constantine sees the cross in the sky and wins at the Milvian Bridge — the persecuted faith becomes the emperor's faith in one battle.
The Edict of Milan grants Christians freedom of worship — after three hundred years of blood, a parchment says enough.
Constantine gathers bishops at Arles to settle the church's first great quarrel — the faith, now free, can finally argue about itself.
Northern invaders sack Luoyang and China's court flees south — four centuries of division begin in the ashes.
Chandragupta I founds the Gupta dynasty — golden ages never announce themselves; historians name them later.
Pachomius gathers monks into a ruled community — the first monastery, a city of God in the desert that shapes a thousand years.
Constantine declares Sunday a day of rest — the weekend's ancient grandfather, decreed by an emperor hedging between gods.
Constantine defeats Licinius and becomes sole emperor — one man, one empire, one God; the Christian empire begins.
Three hundred bishops define the creed at Nicaea — the church speaks with one voice, hammered out word by word.
Constantine's mother Helena journeys to Jerusalem and raises churches on holy ground — the mother of pilgrimage.
Constantine founds his new Rome on the Bosporus — the world's center moves east and never moves back.
King Ezana converts and crosses replace the old gods on Aksum's coins — sixteen hundred years of unbroken faith begin.
Bishop Eusebius completes the first history of the church — without him we'd know almost nothing of the first three hundred years.
Samudragupta's armies roll across India — the warrior-poet whose conquests sheltered a golden age that outlived them.
Rome's Christians first celebrate Christ's birth on December 25 — light born in darkness, in the deepest week of winter.
The first Christian emperor is baptized on his deathbed — power and baptism are hard to hold in the same hand.
Shapur II persecutes Persia's Christians for forty years — faith under fire hardens into something that outlasts empires.
Bishop Nicholas of Myra dies, leaving the legend of secret gifts — kindness is the most durable miracle.
Ulfilas invents a Gothic alphabet and translates the scriptures — a whole people given the book in their own mouth.
A restless boy is born at Thagaste — history's giants start as nobody's children; he will become the voice of Western Christianity.
Young Julian crushes the Alamanni at Strasbourg — a victorious general in the sun, and the last hope of the old gods.
Amma Syncletica's sayings guide the women of the desert — history remembers the Fathers; the Mothers cut just as deep.
The last pagan emperor tries to turn the empire back to the old gods — eighteen months of courage against the tide.
Julian falls to a Persian spear and the pagan revival dies with him — the old gods lose their last champion.
A quake lifts Crete and a tsunami drowns Alexandria's shore — nature doesn't care about empires; the cities learn their smallness.
A monk carves the first cave at Dunhuang — one vision in stone that outlasts dynasties and births a thousand years of art.
Hun horsemen burst out of the east and the Goths flee — the storm that will break Rome's dam begins as a rumor, then thunder.
The king of Goguryeo welcomes Buddhist monks from China — a new faith for an old kingdom, temples on every mountain to come.
Valentinian bursts a blood vessel shouting at envoys and dies mid-rage — anger kills, sometimes the angry man first.
Fleeing the Huns, the Goths beg Rome for refuge — Rome cheats them, and mercy refused becomes vengeance at Adrianople.
The Goths annihilate Rome's eastern army and Emperor Valens dies — the empire's invincibility dies on that plain.
The Spanish general Theodosius takes the shattered East and rebuilds it — one tired general between Rome and the abyss, holding.
Theodosius declares Nicene Christianity the empire's religion — the persecuted become the established; now the church must survive winning.
The bishops confirm the creed at Constantinople — the faith fully defined, hammered out in council chambers by lamplight.
The pagan Altar of Victory leaves the Senate house — symbols are how worlds end: quietly, carried out a side door.
A tiny southern army routs the giant northern host at Fei River — China's finest underdog victory; the giant falls.
Monks bring the dharma to Baekje's court — the kingdom that will carry Buddhism across the sea to Japan.
The Tuoba found the Northern Wei in north China — conquerors learning to be Chinese; conquest goes both ways.
After years of wandering, Augustine is baptized by Ambrose — Western Christianity's greatest voice born in a font, not a cradle.
After the Thessalonica massacre, Ambrose makes Theodosius repent in public — the church can judge the crown; power kneels.
Christians tear down Alexandria's great Serapeum — triumph and tragedy in one act; something precious lost in the rubble.
The great Goguryeo king Gwanggaeto begins his conquests — his stone stele still sings; the stone outlasts the sword.
Theodosius bans the pagan Olympics and the flame goes out — the silence in the stadium was the sound of an age ending.
At the Frigidus, Theodosius crushes the last pagan revival — the old gods lose their last army and become memory.
The last emperor of united Rome dies and his sons split East and West — the most consequential inheritance in history.
Augustine writes his soul's story — the first true autobiography; one soul laid bare, and every human heart in it.
The monk Faxian leaves China on foot for India — fifteen years walking toward the Buddha's homeland, faith on foot across the roof of the world.
Kalidasa writes Shakuntala, India's great play of love and loss — the whole heart in seven acts of Sanskrit music.
Kumarajiva renders the sutras into singing Chinese at Chang'an — translation as resurrection, giving Indian wisdom a Chinese soul.
Honorius hides the western court behind Ravenna's marshes — empires don't fall all at once; they retreat, one marsh at a time.
Moved by a monk's protest, Honorius bans gladiatorial combat — a thousand years of arena blood ended by one man's conscience.
Mesrop Mashtots invents Armenian letters — the Bible speaks Armenian; an alphabet is armor, and a people with one is forever.
Jerome finishes the Latin Vulgate in Bethlehem — one man's Latin shaping a civilization's prayers for a thousand years.
Vandals, Suebi, and Alans pour across the frozen Rhine — four hundred years of frontier undone in one cold night.
The legions leave Britain — four hundred years of Rome ending with a letter; the stones remain, and the memory of vastness.
The great triple walls rise around Constantinople — a thousand years of holding; walls don't save civilizations, but good ones buy time.
Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome — the Eternal City fallen, the world reeling, and Augustine beginning his great answer.
At Carthage, Augustine defeats the Donatist schismatics — the church will be a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints.
With Rome fallen, Augustine begins his great defense of the faith — two cities, one that falls and one that cannot.
A Christian mob murders the philosopher Hypatia — Alexandria's golden age of learning ends in blood on a church floor.
Rome settles the Visigoths in Aquitaine — the first barbarian kingdom inside the empire; the Middle Ages begin with a treaty.
General Liu Yu takes the southern throne — the Southern Dynasties begin: brief, brilliant, doomed, beautiful.
The escaped slave Patrick returns to Ireland as a bishop — the island turns Christian by a former slave's stubborn love.
Persia's Christians declare independence from the western church — and carry the gospel farther east than Rome ever dreamed.
A new king founds the Maya city of Copan — while Rome falls, the Maya build; the world doesn't end everywhere at once.
Gaiseric leads the Vandals across to Africa — Roman Africa falls piece by piece; Rome's belly cut open, the empire starves.
As Vandals besiege Hippo, Augustine dies — the ancient world dims with him, and the medieval world begins in his books.
At Ephesus, Mary is proclaimed Mother of God — messy, political, human theology that shapes the prayers of billions.
The Ilopango volcano explodes, darkening Maya skies — nature doesn't negotiate; a mountain reshapes a civilization.
Rome raises its great church to Mary after Ephesus — faith becomes architecture, and architecture preaches longer than sermons.
Attila becomes sole king of the Huns — a plain man in plain clothes, and the terror of the world; the storm finds its rider.
Maya scribes mark the ending of a great calendar cycle in stone — time as a wheel, turning, celebrated like a coronation.
The first great collection of imperial law is published — sixteen books; law is how empires think out loud.
Gaiseric takes Carthage and the Vandals rule the western Mediterranean — without African grain, Rome starves.
Pope Leo takes the throne as barbarians close in — when emperors flee, the pope stays; the papacy's power is born.
The Huns ravage the Balkans and Constantinople pays gold for peace — humiliating, wise, and as lasting as the gold.
An inscription praises King Chandra beside Delhi's rustless iron pillar — sixteen hundred years bright; time cannot eat it.
Saxon warriors arrive in Britain as mercenaries and stay — England's making begins with an invitation that couldn't be un-sent.
Vatsyayana writes his guide to love and city life — the golden age's belief that pleasure, pursued with grace, is part of a good life.
Romans and Visigoths together stop the Huns at the Catalaunian Plains — the last great Roman victory in the West.
Chalcedon defines Christ's two natures — one definition, and half the Christian world answers no; the East begins to split.
Pope Leo meets Attila and the Hun turns back — sometimes words are the strongest walls Rome ever had.
Attila dies on his wedding night and his empire crumbles — the terror of two empires, ended by a nosebleed; death levels even scourges.
Gaiseric's Vandals strip Rome for two weeks — the word "vandalism" is born; the Western empire a ghost haunting its capital.
Skandagupta defeats the White Huns at India's gates — empires are saved by single stands in forgotten passes.
Pope Leo dies after saving Rome twice — when the state fails, the church remains; twenty-one years of standing firm.
Northern Wei carvers cut giant Buddhas into the Yungang cliffs — the Buddhas still smile while the carving empires are dust.
Rome's last great fleet against the Vandals ends in fire — one night that seals the Western empire's fate.
Vesuvius erupts again, burying villages south of Naples — some warnings are written in ash, and we keep building in the shadow.
Saint Simeon climbs his pillar and stays thirty years — seeking God by getting closer to the sky; he died up there.
Aryabhata is born — the baby who will say the earth itself spins; in 476 the West's lights go out, but India's stay on.
Northern Wei divides land among farmers — the state grows strong on grain; the farmers don't care who the emperor is, only that the field is theirs.
Benedict is born at Nursia — the boy who will write the Rule that seeds a thousand monasteries in Rome's wreckage.
King Peroz falls to the White Huns and Persia pays tribute — even great empires kneel sometimes; the steppe gives no mercy.
Workers raise the Daisen mound for Emperor Nintoku — Japan's largest tomb, a statement in earth: here lies power.
The great Marib dam waters Yemen's fields — seventeen hundred years of keeping its promise; in 490, the fields are green.
The pope declares priestly power above kings — church and state begin their thousand-year quarrel over two swords.
Emperor Xiaowen moves the Northern Wei court to Luoyang — a conqueror choosing culture over the sword, and the city shines.
Theodoric takes Italy and rules from Ravenna — a barbarian king governing like a Roman; for a generation, it works.
Emperor Xiaowen founds the Shaolin monastery — a quiet gift to a monk; the kung fu legend comes later.
Clovis is baptized at Reims — Catholic Europe's first great kingdom born in a font; France begins where he knelt.
Aryabhata publishes his astronomy — the earth spins, the year is 365 days; while the West stumbles, he does the math of heaven.
Polynesian voyagers cross the open Pacific to Hawaii — navigating by stars and memory; while empires fight over valleys, they claim an ocean.
The preacher Mazdak calls for shared wealth and Persia's poor rise — crushed, but the idea never dies.
The astronomer Varahamihira begins the works that will guide Indian stargazers for centuries — learning to read the sky.
At Vouillé the Franks break the Visigoths — one battle, a nation's birth; Gaul becomes Francia.
Qusai unites the Quraysh and takes charge of the Kaaba — Mecca becomes a city; the stage set, stone by stone.
Anastasius builds a forty-mile wall across Thrace — great cities need walls, and great empires need edges.
The Hun king Mihirakula's terror grips northern India — cruelty is loud, but India's endurance is louder.
Old soldier Justin becomes emperor with brilliant nephew Justinian waiting — the unlettered door, and the storm behind it.
The wild-eyed monk Bodhidharma brings Zen's seed to China — nine years facing a wall, and the most radical Buddhism takes root.
The last consul holds the last games — a thousand years of Rome's oldest office ending with a chariot race nobody knew was final.
King Dhu Nuwas massacres Najran's Christians — martyrdom backfires; Arabia unites against him and invasion follows.
Awaiting execution, Boethius writes the Consolation of Philosophy — the cell couldn't hold the thought; the Middle Ages' favorite book.
King Kaleb's fleet crosses the Red Sea to avenge Najran — Arabia learns that martyrs have armies.
A quake levels Antioch and hundreds of thousands die — great cities die blow by blow; this was the first mortal one.
Justinian takes power with Theodora beside him — the last Roman emperor in spirit; thirty-eight years of law, churches, and reconquest.
The martyr Ichadon's death wins Silla's court for Buddhism — the blood of the martyr, the seed of the church, even in Korea.
Benedict founds Monte Cassino — seventy-three chapters that become civilization's seed-bank through the dark centuries.
Justinian shuts Plato's Academy after nine centuries — the philosophers flee to Persia, but the ideas outlive the closing.
Young Belisarius checks the Persians at Dara — genius announces itself early; Justinian's great general is born.
Khosrow Anushirvan takes Persia's throne — justice and learning flourish; the name "the Just" earned, not given.
Chariot factions burn half of Constantinople; thirty thousand die — Theodora's courage saves the throne: purple makes a fine shroud.
Belisarius destroys the Vandal kingdom in a lightning campaign — a hundred years of rule ended in months; reconquest begins.
Justinian's great law book is published — Rome fell, but Rome's law never did; it just changed clothes and kept judging.
Belisarius lands in Sicily and twenty years of war for Italy begin — you can win the land and lose everything on it.
A veil of dust darkens the sun and crops fail worldwide — the worst year to be alive; a volcano sneezed, and the world starved.
Hagia Sophia's dome floats above Constantinople in gold and light — the most beautiful room ever built, and I was there when new.
Khosrow sacks Antioch and carries its people to Persia — the earthquake broke it; the Persians finished it; the queen became a village.
Plague reaches Egypt and will empty Constantinople — Justinian's dreams drown in mass graves; empires should fear fleas.
Ten thousand die a day in Constantinople; Justinian falls ill and lives — the plague takes half the world, the other half keeps going.
Rival missionaries carry Christianity up the Nile to Nubia — a thousand years of Christian kingdoms history forgets.
Justinian buys five years' peace with Persia for gold — humiliating, necessary; empires run on gold as much as glory.
The great Buddhist university of Nalanda grows under Gupta patronage — the mind of Asia gathered in one place.
Saint Ciaran founds Clonmacnoise — the monastery that lights Ireland's golden age; faith stubborn as Irish stone.
Totila recaptures Rome and Belisarius is recalled in disgrace — the empire's greatest general, discarded by an emperor's jealousy.
Justinian and Theodora glitter in gold on San Vitale's walls — art is the final court of appeal, and the verdict is splendor.
The empress Theodora dies of cancer — Justinian never recovers; the most powerful woman of the age, and the empire dims.

t: The City of the Gods Burns
x: Fire and revolt topple Teotihuacan — a hundred thousand people, then silence; the Aztecs will call the ruins where gods were born.
Quake and tidal wave destroy Beirut, the law schools' city — the classrooms rubble; the golden age ends in a single day.
Monks smuggle silkworm eggs from China — three thousand years of monopoly broken by smugglers in robes; espionage, sanctified.
A Korean king sends a Buddha statue to Japan — a golden gift and a question Japan tears itself apart over, then embraces.
The Fifth Council condemns the Three Chapters — East and West strain apart; councils called by emperors serve emperors.
Narses destroys the Goths; Italy is Roman again, but ruined — victory at this price is another word for loss.
The Nazca desert drawings reach their final form — a civilization's prayer in lines across the pampa, readable only from the sky.
Hagia Sophia's dome collapses in a quake and is rebuilt higher — resurrection in stone and gold; the church that wouldn't die.
Avar riders appear on the Danube — another age of migrations; the steppe keeps sending peoples west, each remaking Europe.
The desert's greatest odes hung in gold at the Kaaba — pre-Islamic Arabia's soul in poetry, ten years before Muhammad's birth.
Justinian and Khosrow sign fifty years' peace — the silk road flows; the rarest thing in four centuries of rivalry, worth celebrating.
Columba founds Iona — a windswept rock, a stubborn exiled monk, and the conversion of Scotland begins.
Justinian dies at eighty-three — his dreams outran his empire's strength; the last Roman, great in achievement and wreckage.
Alboin's Lombards pour into Italy — Justinian's reconquest undone in a generation; the peninsula splinters for centuries.
Abraha marches on Mecca with elephants; tradition says birds stopped him — the Year of the Elephant, and a boy born in it.
In the Year of the Elephant, Muhammad is born at Mecca — the most consequential birth of the millennium, and the world yawns.
Persian, Greek, and Indian doctors teach together at Gondeshapur — the world's first teaching hospital; healing without borders.
The fifty years' peace breaks and Rome and Persia bleed each other again — the war that will leave both hollow for the Arabs.
The ancient Marib dam bursts after seventeen hundred years — Yemen's green fields turn to dust; the desert takes back its own.
The north unites under Zhou — history's janitors clearing the stage; after two centuries of division, the road to reunion opens.
The kindly Tiberius tries to buy peace with gold — gold doesn't stop armies, but kindness in an emperor is rarer than victory.
Yang Jian takes the throne as Wendi — the Sui moves China toward reunion; brief, but laying the foundation the Tang will build on.
The Balkan general Maurice becomes emperor — twenty years of war, competent and unloved; the soldier holds the line.
Chilperic is murdered and queens Brunhild and Fredegund tear Francia apart — a forty-year feud poisoning a kingdom.
Leovigild crushes the Suebi and nearly all Spain is Visigothic — the first united Spain since Rome, barbarian but one.
King Reccared converts and Spain joins Catholic Europe — one faith, one kingdom; the Spanish Middle Ages begin at Toledo.
The great general Bahram Chobin rises against the Persian king — Persia's finest soldier destroyed by politics too honest to play.
Sui armies take the southern capital; four centuries of division end — the longest breakup in history, finally mended.
The monk Gregory becomes pope — governing ruined Rome like a father, and sending missionaries to England's shores.
With Roman help, Khosrow II regains Persia's throne — a restored king, a Roman friend, a peace; the last great war brewing underneath.
Empress Suiko ascends — Japan's first reigning empress; thirty-six years of steady hands guiding a nation's rebirth.
Maurice's armies push Slavs and Avars back across the Danube — winning, until his own soldiers' greed undoes him.
Muhammad marries the wealthy widow Khadija — fifteen quiet years; every prophet needs one person who believes first.
Gregory sends Augustine to Kent — forty frightened monks on a Kentish shore; England's conversion begins.
Augustine baptizes King Ethelbert at Canterbury — the English church is born; fourteen hundred years of archbishops begin.
Goguryeo repels Sui China's first great invasion — the small kingdom stands, and the great empire bleeds on Korean walls.
The great Turk khaganate divides east and west — the steppe's unity always fragile; divide, and be ruled.
A new dynasty raises Palenque toward its golden age — while Europe stumbles, the Maya build in the jungle light; in Palenque, morning.
The old Roman world ends and the medieval age begins — six hundred years of empires of faith; nothing ends, it only changes hands.
A traveler walks through freshly burned Teotihuacan, its great pyramids still standing over silent avenues, and keeps a child's whistle — the only voice left.
A caravan companion remembers young Muhammad's honesty on the trade roads, earning him the name "the trustworthy" before any revelation came.
Phocas seizes the throne by military coup; the narrator sees the transfer of power and feels Persia waking again across the frontier.
A newborn Pakal's first day in Palenque, with priests and carvers already preparing for the sixty-eight-year reign to come.
Prince Shotoku drafts Japan's first constitution of seventeen articles, turning the idea of harmony into the foundation of a state.
At Gregory the Great's deathbed, the narrator reflects on a church he organized so well it could survive the fall of everything else.

t: A Million Hands on the Canal
x: The Grand Canal's construction as a human sea of laborers — a wonder that will feed China for centuries, bought with the suffering of its builders.
Young Harsha builds India's last great Buddhist empire from a shattered throne, a ruler famous for giving away everything he owned.
Japan's first embassy to China arrives carrying a letter that addresses the Sui emperor as an equal — an island nation declaring itself.
Goguryeo strengthens its mountain fortresses as the Sui emperor masses an enormous invasion army across the border.
Heraclius overthrows Phocas and inherits an empire that Persia is devouring — a young general taking command in the middle of a storm.
General Eulji Mundeok annihilates a massive Sui invasion army at the Salsu River with a burst dam — one of history's great underdog victories.
Starving laborers and ruined soldiers rise against Emperor Yang — the Sui dynasty, builder of the Grand Canal, begins to crack under rebellion.
Persian armies capture Jerusalem and carry away the True Cross — a blow to Christendom that demands an answer.
Persecuted early Muslims flee across the Red Sea to Christian Abyssinia, where the Negus protects them from Mecca's hunters.
Heraclius watches his empire shrink province by province while quietly rebuilding an army from nothing — refusing to stop trying.
Li Yuan raises the banner of rebellion at Taiyuan and marches on the Sui — and the people fall in behind him, ending a dynasty.
The Tang dynasty is proclaimed at Chang'an — the narrator glimpses the golden age of poetry and empire about to dawn.
Tang clerks register every household and field — the unglamorous census work that lays the tax base for a golden age.
Muhammad's night journey to Jerusalem and through the heavens — an experience no one shared, that became the anchor of his followers' faith.
Under cover of night, men of Yathrib pledge to protect Muhammad — the secret oaths that open the road out of Mecca.
The flight from Mecca to Medina — hidden in a cave, crossing into a new city and a new calendar, Year One of Islam.
Muhammad writes the Charter of Medina, binding tribes and faiths into one community — the unglamorous legal plumbing of a new society.
Outnumbered three to one, the Muslims win at Badr — the battle that convinced Arabia that Muhammad's cause was divinely backed.
At Uhud, Muslim archers abandon their post for plunder and snatch defeat from victory — a lesson in discipline that became part of the faith.
Avars and Persians besiege Constantinople together, but the triple walls and Greek fire hold — the city survives its darkest hour.
Medina survives a ten-thousand-man siege behind a trench dug by its own defenders — the narrator carries earth alongside them.
Muhammad signs the "humiliating" ten-year truce at Hudaybiyyah — and peace wins more converts than war ever had.
Heraclius crushes Persia and restores the True Cross to Jerusalem — the triumphant reversal of fifteen years of defeat.
Muhammad enters Mecca peacefully with ten thousand followers, clears the idols from the Kaaba, and forgives the city that exiled him.
Tribes stream into Medina from across Arabia to pledge allegiance — a peninsula choosing its leader after watching him conquer without cruelty.
Muhammad's final sermon on the plain of Arafat — a declaration of human equality — weeks before his death in Medina.
Abu Bakr becomes the first caliph and holds the fragile Muslim community together through the wars of apostasy after Muhammad's death.
Khalid ibn al-Walid's lightning campaign smashes Persian armies across the desert — speed itself as a weapon of conquest.
Umar ibn al-Khattab builds the administrative machinery of the caliphate — ledgers, judges, and stipends — an empire run on justice and paperwork.
Damascus surrenders by treaty after a six-month siege — the ancient city passes to the caliphate without a sack.
In a dust storm at Yarmouk, the Byzantine army of the East is annihilated — Syria and Palestine pass to the Muslims in a single day.
At Qadisiyya, Muslim armies overcome Persia's war elephants and shatter the Sassanian field army — Iraq falls to the caliphate.
Umar enters Jerusalem on foot in a patched cloak and grants its people a covenant of protection — conquest without a sack.
Amr ibn al-As takes the Babylon fortress and begins the conquest of Egypt — the Nile's grain about to feed a new empire.
Alexandria surrenders by treaty — Greek and Roman Egypt ends with a signature, and its grain begins feeding the caliphate.
At Nahavand, the last Sassanian field army is destroyed — the "Victory of Victories" that leaves Persia open to the caliphate.
Xuanzang returns to Chang'an after sixteen years in India with 657 Buddhist scriptures — the treasure of a lifetime's pilgrimage.
Umar is assassinated by a Persian captive in the mosque — the caliphate mourns its lawgiver, who dies thinking of unity.
The Soga clan falls in a palace coup and Japan is remade on the Tang model — land reform, ranks, and codes: the Great Change.
Emperor Taizong writes the preface to Xuanzang's travel record, and imperial favor sends Buddhism soaring across China.
Harsha holds his final almsgiving at Prayag, giving away everything, and dies — his empire dying with him.
Queen Seondeok of Silla plays Tang China against her rival kingdoms — a woman ruler out-thinking warrior kings.
Taizong, the model Tang emperor, dies — and in the palace shadows his widow Wu Zetian is already preparing her climb to power.
The Khazar khanate rises between the Black and Caspian seas, growing rich taxing the trade roads between East and West.
Yazdegerd III, the last Sassanian shah, is murdered by a miller at Merv — four centuries of Persian empire ending in the dark.
Caliph Uthman orders a single standard text of the Qur'an, copied and sent to every province — one book for all time.
Wu Zetian becomes empress and begins her patient, unstoppable climb toward the throne itself.
Muawiya's fleet destroys the Byzantine navy off Lycia — the Mediterranean is no longer Rome's lake.
At the Battle of the Camel, Aisha's army fights Ali's — the first time Muslims wage war on Muslims, a wound that never heals.
At Siffin, the armies lower their spears for arbitration — and the attempt at peace hardens Islam's great schism instead.
Tang armies crush the Western Turks and plant garrisons at the Pamir Mountains — the dynasty at its greatest reach.
The Silla-Tang alliance crushes Baekje — Korea's three kingdoms begin their long road to becoming one.
Ali is assassinated in the Kufa mosque; Muawiya founds the Umayyad dynasty — the caliphate becomes a hereditary kingdom.
A Japanese rescue fleet is annihilated at Baekgang — Japan turns inward for centuries, abandoning foreign wars.
The Synod of Whitby chooses Roman over Celtic Christianity — a debate about tonsures and Easter dates that steers England's church for a millennium.
Xuanzang dies translating the scriptures he risked his life to bring home — his journey already becoming legend.
Ziyad ibn Abihi takes Kufa and rules Iraq with his famous speech of threats — order imposed by an iron hand.
Goguryeo falls to the Silla-Tang alliance — Korea stands nearly united for the first time in its history.
Muawiya launches the first Arab thrusts toward Constantinople — fleets sailing with confidence toward a fortress that has never fallen.
Uqba ibn Nafi founds Kairouan in the Maghreb — the staging ground from which the conquest of North Africa will march west.
The monk Yijing sails the sea route to India for scriptures — proving the dharma can travel by water as well as land.
Bede is born in Northumbria — the boy given to a monastery who will write England's history and its memory.
Greek fire incinerates the Arab fleet before Constantinople's sea walls — liquid flame burning on the water itself.
Arab armies and fleets settle into a four-year siege of Constantinople — and the city, which knows how to wait, simply outlasts them.
Jarir and al-Farazdaq begin their legendary verse-duels at the Umayyad court — poetry as public combat, wit as weapon.
Plague, Greek fire, and winter destroy the Arab siege — Constantinople holds, and the tide of conquest turns.
Asparukh leads the Bulgars across the Danube and founds Bulgaria — a steppe people planting a state that will stand a millennium.
Husayn and his companions are slaughtered at Karbala — the grief that gives birth to Shi'a Islam, mourned for thirteen centuries.
Byzantium signs a treaty recognizing Asparukh's Bulgaria — the steppe horsemen become a state with a seal.
The Kaaba burns during the siege of Mecca — the holiest shrine scarred while the caliphate tears itself apart in civil war.
Uqba ibn Nafi, who rode his horse into the Atlantic surf, is ambushed and killed at Tahuda — the conquest of the Maghreb stalls.
Abd al-Malik becomes caliph and sets out to make the empire speak Arabic — turning conquest into civilization.
Mukhtar raises the banner of revenge for Husayn in Kufa, hunting down Karbala's killers — vengeance that lights a fire never extinguished.
Justinian II buys peace with Abd al-Malik through tribute — gold traded for the time Byzantium needs to rebuild.
The Asuka Kiyomihara Code gives Japan its first written legal system — law as text, meant to outlive any ruler.
Wu Zetian declares herself emperor — the only woman to rule China in her own name, crowned by decades of patient power.
Abd al-Malik raises the Dome of the Rock over Jerusalem's Temple platform — Islam's first great monument, still standing.
Al-Hajjaj storms Mecca and kills the rival caliph Ibn al-Zubayr — the caliphate reunited, at the cost of blood in the holy city.
Al-Hajjaj takes Iraq and imposes his famous terrifying order — bandits gone, taxes collected, a province tamed by fear.
Justinian II is overthrown and mutilated — the Byzantine throne becomes a revolving door, though he will return.
Abd al-Malik mints purely Islamic coinage — no more emperors' faces, only the profession of faith in gold.
Hassan ibn al-Nu'man takes Carthage — seven centuries of Roman rule in Africa end, and the coast passes to the caliphate.
Qutayba ibn Muslim begins the campaigns beyond the Oxus — Islam's frontier about to leap into Transoxiana.
A poet in England begins the tale of Beowulf — the monster-slayer's epic, sung in a mead hall, outliving them all.
Li Bai is born — the "banished immortal" who will become China's greatest poet, drinking the moon into verse.
Japan completes the Taiho Code — its first full law code, a state built in the Tang mirror but distinctly its own.
The Berber queen al-Kahina is defeated after years of resistance — a brilliant general who sends her sons to safety before the end.
Al-Walid I becomes caliph and builds — mosques, roads, wells, hospitals — giving the conquered empire its roofs.
Craftsmen begin the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus — Roman columns under an Islamic dome, paradise in green and gold mosaic.
Musa ibn Nusayr secures Tangier — the strait to Spain lies open, fourteen miles of blue water from a new world.
Qutayba takes Bukhara — the caliphate's frontier leaps beyond the Oxus into the silk cities of Transoxiana.
The Japanese court settles at Nara, its first permanent capital — laid out like Chang'an, built to last centuries.
Tariq ibn Ziyad lands at Gibraltar and crushes the Visigoths at Guadalete — Spain begins its eight centuries under Islam.
Seventeen-year-old Muhammad ibn Qasim takes Sindh — Islam reaches the Indian subcontinent and never leaves.
The Kojiki is written — Japan's gods and emperors set down in the oldest chronicle, myths fixed in ink forever.
Xuanzong takes the throne and the High Tang begins — the golden age of Chinese poetry, all light and promise.
Qutayba ibn Muslim dies in a soldiers' revolt — the eastward drive stalls, momentum dying with the man.
Maslama's huge army rings Constantinople for the second great siege — Leo III waits behind triple walls with Greek fire.

t: The Winter That Saved an Empire
x: A brutal winter, Bulgar attacks, and Greek fire break the second siege — the Arab tide turns for good, and Europe is saved.
Japan completes the Nihon Shoki — its second chronicle, history arranged by the court to justify the present.

t: The Poet of Sorrow Is Born
x: Du Fu is born — the poet who will sing the Tang's glory and mourn its ruin, China's conscience in verse.
Saint Boniface fells Thor's sacred oak and builds a chapel from its wood — the pagans' god does not strike, and Germany converts.

t: The Water Clock of Yi Xing
x: The monk-astronomer Yi Xing builds a water-driven clockwork armillary sphere — the cosmos mechanized, a millennium before Europe's clocks.
Leo III orders the icons destroyed — Byzantium begins a century-long quarrel over whether God can be pictured.
Brahmagupta's numerals — and the daring zero — begin their journey west toward Baghdad, the most powerful idea in mathematics.
Hasan al-Basri dies in Basra — the Weeping Preacher whose sermons plant the seed of Sufism, Islam's mystic heart.
The imperial examinations widen under Xuanzong — a peasant's son can write his way into office; merit over blood.
Zhang Xu's wild cursive turns drunkenness into art — the Tang's freedom and joy flying off the brush.
The Byzantine heir marries a Khazar princess — steppe diplomacy enters the palace in a wedding procession.
Charles Martel stops the Umayyad advance at Tours-Poitiers — the Hammer holds the line, and Europe's fate turns on it.
Al-Farazdaq dies — the age of the desert verse-duels ends, and even his old rival Jarir weeps.
Bilge Khagan is murdered, but his memorial stones speak Old Turkic to the future — words that refuse to die.
Smallpox sweeps the Nara court, killing the Fujiwara brothers who ran the government — an invisible enemy decapitating a state.
The last Merovingian puppet dies and Charles Martel rules Francia with no king at all — the crown sitting empty, power undisguised.
Zayd ibn Ali rises in Kufa against the Umayyads and dies a martyr — another failed rising the Shi'a never forget.
Charles Martel dies and his sons Pepin and Carloman divide Francia — the Hammer's work carried on by his heirs.
Emperor Shomu decrees a colossal bronze Buddha for Nara — a sixteen-meter prayer to guard the realm after the plague years.
Al-Walid II is murdered and the third fitna begins — the Umayyad caliphate bleeding from a hundred cuts while black banners rise in the east.
Li Bai, Du Fu, and Gao Shi meet in a wine shop — the golden moment of Tang poetry over spilled wine.
The Uyghur Khaganate takes the steppe after the Turks fall — merchant-warriors ruling the grass sea from Ordu-Baliq.
Abu Muslim raises the Abbasid revolt in Khurasan — black banners against white, a revolution spreading like fire.
At the Zab, the Umayyads fall and the Abbasids take the caliphate — ninety years of rule ending in a river of blood.
Captured Chinese papermakers bring their craft west after Talas — paper mills rise in Samarkand and Baghdad, and knowledge becomes cheap.
The Great Buddha of Todai-ji is dedicated at Nara — the eye-opening ceremony wakes sixteen meters of bronze before the whole court.
Pepin grants central Italy to the Pope — the Papal States begin, a thousand years of the Pope as a territorial prince.
The frontier general An Lushan readies his veteran armies against the Tang throne — the golden age about to shatter.
An Lushan marches on Chang'an — the High Tang shatters in eight years of rebellion; the golden age ends in refugee columns.
Abd al-Rahman I, last of the Umayyads, lands in Spain and founds the emirate of Cordoba — exile becoming empire.
Sibawayh is born — the Persian scholar whose Book will fix Arabic grammar for thirteen centuries.
Al-Mansur founds Baghdad in a perfect circle — the City of Peace that will become the greatest city on earth.
Chenla builders raise brick temple towers along the Mekong — the first Khmer sacred architecture, before Angkor.
Alcuin teaches at York's great library-school — the light of the North, keeping learning alive for a continent.
Charlemagne becomes joint king of the Franks — the restless young king who will define the Middle Ages.
Carloman dies and Charlemagne rules Francia alone — the sole king unleashed on every frontier.
Gopala founds the Pala Empire — Bengal's Buddhist age of great monasteries and universities, the Elephant Kings.
Irene takes power as empress regent — clever, ruthless, devout, navigating generals and iconoclasts to rule alone.
Charlemagne executes thousands of Saxon prisoners at Verden — the north submits in terror, and the stain never washes off.
Harun al-Rashid takes the throne — the caliph of the Thousand and One Nights, ruling Baghdad at its zenith.
The Second Council of Nicaea restores the icons — whitewashed walls bloom again, and the painters come home.
Viking raiders strike Portland — the first recorded raid on England, three centuries of fire beginning on a Dorset beach.
Bai Juyi writes verses plain enough for a farmer — poetry tested on a peasant woman, for everyone.
Vikings sack Lindisfarne — the holy island desecrated, and the Viking Age begins in blood and fire.
Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day — the West has an emperor again, four centuries after Rome fell.
Jayavarman II declares himself god-king on Phnom Kulen — the devaraja ritual that begins Angkor's age.
Saicho and Kukai sail to Tang China and return with Tendai and Shingon — the founders of Japanese Buddhism.
Monks begin the Book of Kells — gold and knotwork on vellum, beauty made in the shadow of Viking axes.
Harun al-Rashid dies on campaign at Tus — his sons already maneuvering, the golden age about to tear itself apart.
Khan Krum routs the Byzantines at Pliska, kills Nikephoros I, and drinks from his silver-lined skull.
Al-Ma'mun wins the civil war and takes Baghdad — the scholar-caliph, whose reign will open the age of translation.
Al-Khwarizmi writes his algebra in Baghdad — the book and the man behind every equation and every algorithm.
Al-Kindi, the first philosopher of the Islamic world, writes in Baghdad — marrying Greek reason to revealed faith.
Al-Ma'mun's astronomers chart the heavens from the Baghdad observatory — measuring the earth, correcting Ptolemy.
Al-Ma'mun's men tunnel into the Great Pyramid — finding no gold, only empty chambers and four thousand years of awe.
Al-Mu'tasim's armies sack Amorium, the Byzantine emperor's home city — a wound the empire never forgot.
The Kyrgyz destroy the Uyghur Khaganate — the fallen steppe empire's people becoming scribes and merchants in the oases.
The Treaty of Verdun carves Charlemagne's empire into three — lines drawn in a day that become France, Germany, and a millennium of borders.
Emperor Wuzong suppresses Buddhism — temples closed, bells melted into coins; the monastic golden age ends in the melting pots.
Cordoba's librarians gather the books that will make it famous — hundreds of thousands of volumes, the light of the West.
Baghdad's craftsmen perfect the astrolabe — the heavens in a brass disc, humanity's first pocket computer.

t: The Boy Who Would Be Great
x: Alfred is born at Wantage — the youngest son nobody expected to be king, England's future "the Great."
The Slavs invite Rurik the Varangian to rule at Novgorod — the strangest founding of any nation, the first Russian state.
Cyril and Methodius bring the Glagolitic alphabet to Moravia — writing for the Slavic tongue, the root of a thousand years of literature.
Boris I baptizes Bulgaria — the steppe horsemen become a Christian kingdom with a written Slavic faith.
The Diamond Sutra rolls off a Chinese woodblock press — the world's oldest dated printed book, made for free distribution.
Alfred defeats Guthrum at Edington — the Danelaw is born, Wessex survives, and England exists because of this day.
Vikings besiege Paris for a year; Count Odo holds the walls — the city survives, and Odo becomes a hero and a king.
Alfred dies at Winchester — but his burhs, navy, laws, and schools hold England together after him.
Twelve monks found Cluny — a quiet reform of prayer that will become the most powerful monastic order in Europe.
Abd al-Rahman III proclaims the caliphate of Cordoba — the west has its own Commander of the Faithful, a light to rival Baghdad.
In Córdoba's golden age, al-Zahrawi compiles his thirty-volume medical encyclopedia, inventing some two hundred surgical instruments and founding surgery as a discipline.
At Takkolam, Rashtrakuta forces crush the Chola army and kill its king, overturning the balance of power in South India in a single battle.
Erik Bloodaxe is driven from York and killed at Stainmore, ending Viking rule in northern England and folding the Danelaw into a single English kingdom.

t: The City of a Thousand Churches
x: Ani becomes the Armenian capital, its red walls and countless churches rising on the trade frontier — a golden city that will be remembered long after its fall.
Constantine VII, the "purple-born" emperor, writes his great manuals of administration and ceremony — practical handbooks that preserve Byzantium's workings for a thousand years.
General Zhao Kuangyin is proclaimed emperor by his own troops at Chenqiao, founding the Song dynasty — one of China's great cultural ages, begun almost by accident.
Otto I is crowned emperor in Rome, reviving the western imperial title — the birth of the Holy Roman Empire, which will endure for eight centuries.
Court ladies of Heian Japan write the first flowering of native literature in kana — diaries, poems, and pillow books that become the foundation of Japanese letters.
Camel caravans cross the Sahara carrying slabs of salt south and gold dust north — the trans-Saharan trade that enriches empires on both sides of the desert.
The Fatimid general Jawhar conquers Egypt and founds al-Qahira — Cairo, the Victorious — with the mosque of al-Azhar that will make it a center of learning for a millennium.
Dinh Bo Linh defeats the twelve warlords, unifies the Red River delta, and proclaims the kingdom of Dai Co Viet — the founding act of Vietnamese independence.
Mieszko I's baptism turns Poland Christian, binding the realm to Latin Europe — a political conversion that shapes a thousand years of Polish identity.
The caliph's great hospitals and libraries keep Greek learning alive in Arabic — translators, physicians, and scholars running the world's memory while Europe sleeps.
Young Ferdowsi begins the thirty-year labor that will become the Shahnameh — sixty thousand verses preserving Persia's kings, heroes, and soul in poetry.
Song armies absorb the last southern kingdoms, reuniting China after fifty years of division — the foundation of the dynasty's golden age of commerce and culture.
In Bukhara, the child prodigy Ibn Sina — Avicenna — masters medicine and philosophy before his teens, beginning the journey toward the Canon that will teach Europe for five centuries.
Exiled from Iceland, Erik the Red sails west and names the icy land Greenland — a marketing lie that draws Norse settlers to farm the edge of the ice cap for four centuries.
At Tula, the Toltecs raise their colossal stone warriors and the priests of Quetzalcoatl rule — the golden-age city the later Aztecs will claim as their ancestors.
Blown off course, Bjarni Herjolfsson sights wooded shores west of Greenland — the first European glimpse of America — and sails home without landing.
Prince Vladimir baptizes Kiev in the Dnieper, choosing Orthodox Byzantium over Islam and Rome — the founding act of Russian Christianity, echoing in every onion dome since.
At Cahokia, the Mississippian people raise Monk's Mound — the largest earthwork in the Americas — heart of a city of twenty thousand, greater than London.
Venice's doge defeats the Adriatic pirates, and the Republic begins its ceremonial Marriage of the Sea — the founding gesture of a thousand-year maritime empire.
Olaf Tryggvason lands to convert Norway by persuasion and sword — the violent Christianization of the last Viking heartland.
Danish fleets return to raid England, and King Aethelred begins paying the Danegeld — silver tribute that only teaches the raiders England is worth conquering.
Millennial preachers warn the world will end in the year 1000 — crowds pray, kings tremble, and when the sun rises anyway, Christendom builds churches in relieved gratitude.
Leif Eriksson lands in Vinland — Europeans set foot on the American mainland five centuries before Columbus — and the short-lived colony enters the sagas as truth.
Aethelred orders the St Brice's Day massacre of Danes in England — a revenge killing that brings Sweyn Forkbeard's conquering armies down on the island.
The Treaty of Shanyuan ends the Song-Liao wars — China buys a century of peace with annual tribute of silk and silver, conceding the north it cannot retake.
A supernova blazes brighter than Venus for months — the brightest stellar event in recorded history, witnessed and recorded in China, Egypt, Japan, and Yemen.
The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim orders the Church of the Holy Sepulchre destroyed — a shock that echoes through Christendom and will help fuel the crusading call.
Ferdowsi completes the Shahnameh after thirty years — sixty thousand verses that preserve Persia's mythic history and save the Persian language itself.
The Soninke empire of Ghana grows rich on the gold trade at the Sahara's edge — gold dust weighed against salt in the markets of Koumbi Saleh.
At Clontarf, Brian Boru breaks Viking power in Ireland — and is killed in his tent after the victory, making the triumph a funeral in the same hour.
Cnut takes England's throne and rules a North Sea empire of England, Denmark, and Norway — a Viking king who governs wisely and demonstrates, tide and all, that even kings have limits.

t: The End of the First Empire
x: Basil II annexes Bulgaria after decades of war, climaxing in the blinding of fourteen thousand prisoners — the end of the First Bulgarian Empire and the peak of Byzantine power.
In the Levant's mountains, followers of al-Hakim preach a new faith holding the caliph divine — the birth of the Druze, who will keep their sealed books and mountain homes for a thousand years.
Under house arrest in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham writes his Book of Optics — proving with pinhole experiments that vision works by light entering the eye, founding optics as a science.
Basil II dies after a fifty-year reign, leaving Byzantium at its greatest extent in centuries — and with no strong heir, the long unraveling begins at the moment of the peak.
The Kalachakra — the Wheel of Time — takes root in Tibet, binding calendar, cosmos, and meditation into one teaching, drawn in sand mandalas and swept away.
Avicenna completes his Canon of Medicine — five books systematizing all known medicine — the textbook European universities will teach from for five hundred years.
Mahmud of Ghazni sacks the great temple of Somnath and carries its gold to Ghazna — the raid that earns him the name Idol-Breaker and wounds Hindu memory for a millennium.
Córdoba's caliphate collapses into the taifa kingdoms — small, glittering, quarrelsome courts where, amid the wreckage, poetry and philosophy bloom on rival patronage.
The abbey of Cluny begins its great third church — the largest in Christendom — the stone statement of the monastic empire that counsels kings and prays around the clock.
Cnut dies at forty, and his North Sea empire of England, Denmark, and Norway cracks apart among his sons — the Danish age in England ends with its builder.

t: Death of the Prince of Physicians
x: Avicenna dies at Hamadan — but his Canon and his philosophy outlive every king of his age, teaching European medicine for five centuries to come.
The craftsman Bi Sheng invents movable clay type — printing reinvented for mass pages — four centuries before Gutenberg, though China's thousands of characters keep the idea from catching fire.
Macbeth seizes Scotland's throne in battle and rules seventeen orderly, pious years — history's most slandered king, undone five centuries later by Shakespeare's need for a villain.
A Song military manual records the formula for gunpowder — the fire-drug, demonstrated as fireworks — the recipe that will eventually knock down every castle wall on earth.
Emperor Henry III deposes three rival popes at Sutri and installs his own — cleansing the papacy, which will repay the favor by turning on his son within a generation.
Omar Khayyam is born at Nishapur — astronomer who will reform the calendar five centuries early, and poet whose wine-dark quatrains will conquer the English language.
In Chaco Canyon, Pueblo builders raise the great crescent of Pueblo Bonito — six hundred rooms of stone, hub of a desert civilization of roads, turquoise, and ceremony.
Song astronomers at Kaifeng keep their nightly watch, thickening the star catalogues year by year — charting the heavens with bronze instruments and infinite patience.
A guest star blazes for weeks, visible by day — the supernova whose expanding wreckage is still glowing a thousand years later as the Crab Nebula.
Pope and Patriarch excommunicate each other in the Hagia Sophia — the Great Schism splits Christendom East and West over bread, a word, and pride, a wound never healed.
Malcolm kills Macbeth at Lumphanan — the real king dies sword in hand after seventeen good years, while Shakespeare's villain gets the ending the winners wrote.
The preacher Ibn Yasin founds the Almoravid movement in a desert ribat — stern warrior-monks who will sweep north to found Marrakesh and rule Spain's taifas.
Alp Arslan takes the Seljuk throne — the Heroic Lion whose Turkish horse-archers will push toward Byzantium and break it open at Manzikert.
Halley's Comet blazes over England in the spring of 1066 — sewn into the Bayeux Tapestry as an omen, believed by both sides, and fulfilled by autumn.
William lands at Pevensey, wins Hastings, and is crowned at Westminster — England gets a French king, and the Norman Yoke remakes the country for three centuries.
Wang Anshi launches his New Policies — state loans, fair taxes, granaries — the boldest reform gamble in Chinese history, undone by court faction before it can finish.
At Manzikert, Alp Arslan captures the Byzantine emperor and opens Anatolia to the Turks — one afternoon's battle that begins the end of Byzantine Asia.
Hildebrand becomes Pope Gregory VII and declares the Church free of kings — the Dictatus Papae, the revolution that will bring an emperor to his knees in the snow.
Kulothunga Chola I takes the throne at the empire's height — Chola ships ruling the eastern seas, Tamil merchants sailing to China, bronze gods dancing in temple firelight.
Almoravid armies take Koumbi Saleh, and the golden empire of Ghana begins its long fade — while in the south, the powers that will become Mali are already stirring.
Excommunicated, Henry IV kneels barefoot in the snow at Canossa before Gregory VII — the humbling of an emperor that gives history its phrase for ultimate submission.
Alexios Komnenos seizes the Byzantine throne and begins the long recovery — rebuilding army, coinage, and diplomacy, the restoration that saves the empire for another century.
Alfonso VI retakes Toledo, and Christian scholars flood in to translate its Arabic libraries — the pipeline through which Europe recovers Aristotle, Ptolemy, and Avicenna.
William's surveyors count every manor, plow, and pig in England — the Domesday Book, the most complete snapshot of any medieval country and the nakedest exercise of power ever bound.
William the Conqueror dies at Rouen — his death a farce of looted rooms and a bursting coffin — and his sons divide the empire he built and spend twenty years fighting over it.
At Bologna, law students band together and hire their own teachers — the university is born from below, a guild for learning, with no king or pope yet involved.
Hassan-i Sabbah seizes the mountain fortress of Alamut, and the Nizari Ismailis begin their long shadow war — scholar-assassins whose daggers reach further than armies.
The vizier Nizam al-Mulk is murdered, and within weeks the Seljuk empire begins fracturing — the division the crusaders will walk through seven years later.
At Clermont, Pope Urban II preaches the First Crusade — "God wills it" — and the roar of the crowd launches two centuries of holy war.
Peasant armies march east for the crusade and turn first on the Rhineland's Jewish communities — the crusade's first victims, murdered by Christians in Germany before the Turks destroy the column.
After an eight-month siege of starvation, crusaders storm Antioch through a traitor's gate — then, besieged in turn, break out behind the Holy Lance and march on Jerusalem.
Henry I seizes the throne and issues the Charter of Liberties — promises made for politics, written down, and remembered a century later at Runnymede.
Baldwin is crowned king in Bethlehem — the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem begins, a Frankish state in the Levant that will build great castles and last a century.
Crusaders take the great port of Acre — not a trophy but a lifeline, the window to the sea through which the crusader kingdom will survive for eighty years.
Henry I crushes his brother Robert at Tinchebray, reuniting England and Normandy — and keeps his brother caged in Cardiff Castle for twenty-eight years.
Louis VI takes the French throne and begins taming his robber-barons castle by castle — the fat fighting king who makes the French crown mean something beyond Paris.
Huizong holds the Song throne — a genius painter and calligrapher, a disaster as emperor — ruling the loveliest court on earth right up to the Jurchen catastrophe.
Suryavarman II seizes the Khmer throne and begins the building program that will raise Angkor Wat — the largest religious monument on earth, a usurper's apology in stone.
Bernard founds Clairvaux with twelve monks — the white monks of Citeaux, stripped to stone and silence, whose mother house will plant three hundred daughters across Europe.
Nine knights vow to guard the pilgrim roads — the Poor Knights of Christ, who will become the Templars, bankers to kings, until a king burns them for their gold.
Ilghazi annihilates the army of Antioch at the Field of Blood — the crusader states reel, and the Franks learn that overconfidence in the east is suicide.
The White Ship sinks off Barfleur with Henry I's heir and three hundred souls — England's succession drowns in the Channel, and nineteen years of civil war begin with one drunken race.
At Worms, pope and emperor compromise on the appointment of bishops — ending fifty years of Investiture war with a settlement that teaches bishops to serve two masters.
Ibn Tumart proclaims himself Mahdi in the Atlas Mountains — the Almohad spark, a stern reform movement that will topple the Almoravids and rule from Spain to Tunisia.
Jurchen Jin sack Kaifeng and drag two emperors north in chains — the Jingkang Shame, the fall of northern China and the flight of the Song across the Yangtze.
Gaozong proclaims the Southern Song at Hangzhou — the court in exile that becomes the richest, most cultured, most brilliant China there ever was, blooming on the memory of the lost north.
Roger II is crowned king of Sicily — Norman, Arab, and Greek in one trilingual court, proof that three faiths could share a throne room under a clever king.
Hildegard of Bingen begins writing her visions — abbess, composer, healer, and prophet, whose Scivias makes her the most famous woman in Germany, advising emperors and scolding popes.
Henry I dies, Stephen seizes the throne from Matilda, and nineteen years of civil war — the Anarchy — begin: castles sprouting, barons robbing, Christ and his saints asleep.
Fifteen-year-old Eleanor inherits Aquitaine — the richest prize in Europe — and marries the heir of France: the beginning of the most powerful woman of the Middle Ages.
Afonso Henriques wins at Ourique and is hailed Portugal's first king — legend says Christ appeared in the sky; the kingdom that followed lasted eight hundred years.
Abelard's teachings are condemned at Sens — the brilliant logician broken by Bernard, ending the Middle Ages' most famous love story in silence and separate cloisters.
Robert of Ketton translates the Qur'an into Latin at Toledo — the first time Europe reads Islam in its own tongue, beginning eight centuries of argument and occasional understanding.
Zengi takes Edessa, the first crusader state — the shock that launches the Second Crusade, all because one count left his city unguarded.
Bernard of Clairvaux preaches the Second Crusade at Vezelay — kings take the cross on the spot, a hundred thousand march east, and most of them die.
The Second Crusade breaks against Damascus's walls — four days of quarrel and thirst, then humiliating retreat — while a young Kurdish officer named Saladin watches and learns.
Suryavarman's builders raise Angkor Wat — five lotus towers, half a mile of carved galleries, the largest religious monument on earth, rising out of the jungle heat.
Eleanor's marriage to Louis is annulled; within eight weeks she weds Henry of Anjou — Aquitaine changes hands, and the most consequential divorce of the Middle Ages tilts the map of power.
Stephen and Henry make peace at Winchester — nineteen years of Anarchy settled with handshakes, peace through exhaustion, and the Plantagenets begin.
Henry II is crowned at twenty-one, ruling an empire from Scotland to the Pyrenees — the restless founder of the common law, whose greatness and impossibility arrive together.
Henry the Lion founds Munich on the Isar — monks, markets, and a salt toll bridge — the muddy market town that will become one of Europe's great cities.
Polynesian navigators settle the far Pacific — Hawaii, Rapa Nui — crossing thousands of miles of empty ocean by stars, swells, and memory, the greatest navigators in history.
On the Mongolian steppe, a chief's son named Temujin is born — the abandoned boy who will become Genghis Khan and redraw the map of the world.
The first stone of Notre-Dame de Paris is laid on the Ile de la Cité — the beginning of a hundred years of building, and of Gothic's great cathedral statement.
Lubeck's merchants band together for protection — the seed of the Hanseatic League, the trading empire with no king that will one day count two hundred cities.
Norman knights land in Ireland at Strongbow's side, hired by a deposed king — a mercenary contract on a Wexford beach that begins eight centuries of trouble.
Four knights murder Thomas Becket at Canterbury's altar on the king's angry words — the martyr's shrine rises as Henry does barefoot penance, and kings learn to watch their words.
Saladin ends the Fatimid caliphate with a changed Friday sermon — Egypt, its grain and gold, becomes the base from which he will face the crusaders.
Saladin takes Damascus, uniting Egypt and Syria — the Muslim counterweight to the crusaders grows, and the vise closes around the Frankish states.
The Seljuks ambush Manuel's army in the pass at Myriokephalon — Byzantium's last great eastern gamble fails, and Anatolia is never recovered.
Taira no Kiyomori rules Japan from behind the throne — the samurai age dawns in silk and ceremony, with the Minamoto sharpening their swords in the east.
Fifteen-year-old Philip II is crowned at Reims — the boy king who will take Normandy, win Bouvines, and make France, the Plantagenets' doom freshly anointed.
Minamoto and Taira sharpen their swords — the Genpei storm gathers, ronin crowding the inns, five years of clan war brewing like weather before a typhoon.
King Lalibela begins carving eleven churches from living rock at Roha — a new Jerusalem for Ethiopian Christians, faith expressed in negative space, cut down into the mountain.
At Dan-no-ura the Minamoto destroy the Taira fleet — and the boy emperor drowns in his grandmother's arms, ending the Genpei War and beginning Japan's warrior age.
Saladin destroys the crusader army at the Horns of Hattin — the True Cross captured, the king taken — and Jerusalem falls within months, ending eighty-eight years of the kingdom.
Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus take the cross and sail for the Holy Land — the crusade of kings, glorious in song, that wins every battle and loses the war.
Barbarossa drowns in the Saleph River — the Third Crusade's greatest army dissolves, and legend sets the emperor sleeping in his mountain, beard growing through the table.
After a two-year double siege, Richard retakes Acre — the crusaders' great prize — then massacres the prisoners when the ransom stalls, a stain the plain remembers.
Minamoto no Yoritomo becomes shogun at Kamakura — Japan's warrior government begins, emperors reigning while shoguns rule, for seven hundred years.
Richard and Saladin make peace at Jaffa — the coast stays Frankish, Jerusalem stays Muslim — the crusade of kings ending in a handshake between legends who never met.
Saladin dies at Damascus — his treasury holds one gold piece, his funeral is mourned by three faiths, and his empire divides among his kin before the body is cold.
Cahokia holds perhaps twenty thousand souls — the greatest city north of Mexico, mounds and plazas and sun-circles on the Mississippi — at a peak nobody knows won't last.
Crusaders take the cross, can't pay Venice for ships, and the blind doge turns their swords toward Christians — the crusade for Jerusalem becomes the road to Constantinople.

t: The Sack of the Queen of Cities
x: Crusaders storm Constantinople and loot it for three days — the Queen of Cities stripped, Byzantium shattered into pieces, the crusade destroying what it was called to save.
The ex-slave Qutb al-Din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate and begins the Qutb Minar — property become king, the first of history's strangest aristocracy.
Innocent III turns crusade against the Cathars of southern France — "Kill them all, God will know his own" — twenty years of war grinding the Languedoc under the northern heel.
Christian kings smash the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa — the Reconquista's turning point, after which Muslim Spain's fall becomes only a matter of time.
Thousands of children march for the Holy Land behind shepherd boys — most never come home; the sea doesn't part, and the innocent learn what the age does with innocence.
At Runnymede, barons force John to seal the Great Charter — sixty-three clauses hiding the sentences that become the foundation of liberty: no imprisonment without lawful judgment.
Crusaders take Damietta, refuse the sultan's offer of Jerusalem itself, march on Cairo instead — and the Nile rises and traps them; they surrender everything to get out alive.
Genghis Khan's armies shatter the Khwarezmian empire — Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv fall, cities vanish from the map, and the Mongol storm breaks over the world.
Genghis Khan founds Karakorum on the steppe — walls instead of tents, a polyglot capital of artisans, merchants, and priests where the empire's roads meet.
The last of Lalibela's eleven rock-hewn churches is finished — forty years of cutting complete, a holy city excavated from the mountain, still standing eight centuries on.
The exiled Sundiata Keita begins gathering the Malinke clans — the Lion King's rise, Mali's founding epic, starting not with battle but with chiefs bending the knee one by one.
Genghis Khan dies on campaign and is buried in secret — his empire splits among his sons into four khanates, the greatest land empire in history divided like an inheritance.
The excommunicated Frederick II sails east and wins Jerusalem back by treaty, not battle — crowning himself in the Holy Sepulchre, the crusade that worked through diplomacy.
Ferdinand III joins Castile and Leon for good — the Reconquista's engine assembled, one king pointed south, and within eighteen years only Granada will remain.
The Kamakura shogunate issues the Goseibai Shikimoku — fifty-one articles of warrior law, the operating system of feudal Japan for seven hundred years.
Sundiata crushes the sorcerer-king Soumaoro at Kirina — the Mali Empire is born, the lame boy become Mansa, ruler of the gold lands and the Niger trade.
Ferdinand III takes Córdoba — the Great Mosque becomes a cathedral, five centuries of Muslim rule ending in the city of the caliphs, the Reconquista made stone.
Batu's horsemen burn Ryazan — "none left to weep for the dead" — and the long Tartar night begins for Russia: two and a half centuries of the Mongol yoke.
The Mongols storm Kiev — the mother of Russian cities falls, the center of Rus' moves north, and the lands bow to the Golden Horde for two centuries.
Ogedei Khan dies, and the Mongol armies wheel away from Hungary's edge for the kurultai — Europe spared by a death five thousand miles away, the tide that never returns.
Alexander Nevsky defeats the Teutonic Knights on the frozen Lake Peipus — the eastward crusade dies on the ice, and Russia gets the hero who bowed to the Mongols and turned back the west.
Khwarezmian horsemen sack Jerusalem — the crusaders never hold it again; the crusading age's one prize, gone forever in a week of blood.
Friar John of Plano Carpini reaches Karakorum — Europe's first envoy to the Great Khan — and brings home the Khan's reply (submit or be destroyed) and the west's first real account of the Mongols.
Mamluk slave-soldiers seize Egypt — the Slave Kings, bought as boys and forged into the finest cavalry on earth, who will stop the Mongols and finish the crusaders.
Mongke Khan orders the empire counted — every household from China to Persia inventoried, the nomad empire's most ambitious bureaucracy, tax rolls that outlast the khans.
Robert de Sorbon founds his college for poor theology students in Paris — the seed of the Sorbonne, seven centuries of French intellect from one chaplain's charity.
Marco Polo is born in Venice — unremarked, a merchant's son in a canal house, with the whole of Asia waiting seventeen years down the road.
Tran dynasty armies drive the Mongols out of Dai Viet — the first of three repelled invasions; the empire that took Hungary could not take Vietnam.
The Mamluks crush the Mongols at Ain Jalut — the first pitched battle the Mongols ever lost, the high-water mark of their tide, broken by slave-soldiers at the Spring of Goliath.
Michael Palaiologos retakes Constantinople through an unguarded postern — Byzantium restored, diminished, beginning its long luminous two-hundred-year sunset.
Simon de Montfort summons knights and burgesses to Westminster — Parliament's first breath, commoners in the council of the realm, planted in a losing war by a desperate man.
Dante Alighieri is born in Florence — the moneylender's son who will write the Comedy, invent the Italian language, and turn a childhood glance at Beatrice into eternity.
The Mamluk sultan Baybars storms Antioch and destroys it utterly — the queen of the crusader east emptied and smoking, the states bleeding out castle by castle.
Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe and restores Ethiopia's Solomonic line — claiming descent from Sheba and Solomon, founding seven hundred years of continuous monarchy.
Marco Polo sets out with his father and uncle for Kublai Khan's court — three Venetians walking into the largest empire on earth, not to return for twenty-four years.
A typhoon shatters Kublai Khan's invasion fleet — the first kamikaze, the Divine Wind, saving Japan and becoming scripture: the gods protect these islands.
Marco Polo reaches Shangdu and enters Kublai Khan's service — paper money, burning black stones, post-horses — seventeen years of wonders, all written down for the book no one believes.
Kublai Khan completes the conquest of Song China — the last boy emperor drowned off the coast, the Yuan dynasty begins, Mongol khans on the Dragon Throne.
Stone walls rise on the Zimbabwe plateau — Great Zimbabwe, mortarless granite enclosures ruling the gold trade, eighteen thousand people in a city of stone.
A second, greater Mongol armada — four thousand ships — breaks on Japan's shores in a second typhoon; the kamikaze twice proven, and Kublai never tries again.
Edward I's great castles close around Wales — Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech, Beaumaris — conquest built in stone, the most beautiful subjugation ever raised.
The Kilwa sultanate mints its own gold coins — Swahili traders ruling the ocean's western shore, middlemen of the monsoon, one of the finest cities Ibn Battuta will ever see.
Kublai Khan rebuilds the Grand Canal — a thousand miles of waterway pumping southern rice to the northern capital, the Yuan's great artery, empires running on logistics.
Edward I expels the Jews from England — sixteen thousand people, property seized, the first complete expulsion in Europe, a shame that stands three and a half centuries.
The Mamluks take Acre and raze it — the last crusader stronghold falls, two hundred years of crusading ending not with a treaty but with a wrecking crew.
Kublai Khan dies at Dadu — the empire he built begins its slow, stately unraveling into four khanates, one in name, four in fact.
Prisoner in Genoa, Marco Polo dictates his travels to Rustichello — The Million, the book the scoffers call lies, that will sit annotated on Columbus's shelf two centuries later.
Boniface VIII opens the first Jubilee, and pilgrims flood Rome in numbers no one has ever seen, all of them hungry for forgiveness.
Under Kublai's heirs the Yuan rules all China — paper money, the Grand Canal, and cities of unmatched size — at the very crest of its power.
Florence exiles Dante Alighieri under sentence of burning, and the homeless poet begins the long road that will produce his great vision.

t: The King Summons the Three Estates
x: Philip IV gathers clergy, nobles, and townsmen into the first Estates-General — a king borrowing the people's voice to pay for his quarrels.
Flemish townsmen and farmers crush the French knighthood at Kortrijk and hang the dead knights' golden spurs as trophies — the common man's day.
French agents seize Pope Boniface VIII in his palace at Anagni; the humiliation breaks him, and he dies within weeks.
Alauddin Khalji storms Chittor, and the Rajput defenders choose the funeral fire over surrender — a fortress taken, a people unconquered.
Ghazan Khan, the Mongol ruler who made Islam the faith of his Persian realm, dies — conqueror turned believer.
Edward I's siege engines smash Stirling Castle, the last Scottish stronghold — and the Hammer mistakes a fallen fortress for a finished war.
Giotto fills the Scrovegni Chapel with frescoes that give saints real bodies, real grief, real weight — heaven learning to look human.
William Wallace is executed in London with full medieval cruelty — and England makes him the martyr Scotland will never let die.
Clement V, a Frenchman, becomes pope and never goes to Rome — the papacy's long captivity to France begins with a smile and a handshake.
