Robert the Bruce murders his rival in a church, then seizes Scotland's crown — a kingdom's freedom founded on a sacrilege the Scots accept.

t: The Hammer of the Scots Dies
x: Edward I dies on campaign against Scotland, and the weak Edward II inherits — the whole weight of an empire shifting in a single heartbeat.
Osman I's small frontier princedom quietly swallows Byzantine border forts one by one — the hairline crack nobody in Constantinople noticed.
Henry VII takes the imperial crown dreaming of restoring the empire's lost glory in Italy — one more generation chasing the old ghost.
Clement V settles the papal court in Avignon, beginning seventy years of exile — Rome abandoned, heaven's machinery relocated to France.
Venice expands its great Arsenal, the shipyard that assembles war galleys on a production line — organization as a weapon.

t: The Roads of Gold and Salt
x: Across the Sahara, salt trades weight for weight with gold, and Mali grows rich on the desert road — an empire built on thirst.
Catalan mercenaries lure the Frankish knights of Athens into a marsh at Halmyros and annihilate them in a single morning — hired swords changing history.
Bishops gather at Vienne to judge the age's scandals — the Templars dissolved, the Church's map of power redrawn under a watching king.
Mansa Musa takes Mali's throne, inheriting a gold empire — and already dreaming of the journey that will carry his name across the world.
Henry VII dies of fever on campaign in Tuscany — and Dante's dream of a united Italy is buried with him.
Robert the Bruce's spearmen shatter Edward II's great army at Bannockburn — Scotland wins its freedom in two days of mud and courage.
Endless rains drown the harvests and the Great Famine begins — no enemy, no war, just a closed sky and bread worth more than gold.
Swiss mountaineers crush Habsburg knights in the pass at Morgarten with rocks and halberds — the valleys' freedom born in an avalanche.
In the famine's worst year the starving dead outnumber any army's toll — Europe's quietest catastrophe, buried without trumpets.

t: A Bruce Crowned Across the Sea
x: Edward Bruce is crowned High King of Ireland, carrying Scotland's war across the sea — a brave, doomed gamble for Irish freedom.
After three years the rains relent and the famine breaks — Europe buries its dead, counts the terrible cost, and weeps over bread.
William of Ockham teaches that the simplest answer is usually right — a razor that cuts dogma too, and the Church will not forgive him.
Scots raiders rout a host of Yorkshire priests and levies at Myton — the White Battle, where war shows it doesn't spare holy men.
Scotland's lords write to the pope at Arbroath: they will never submit to England, under any king — a letter wielded like a weapon.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founds a new dynasty over Delhi, India's richest sultanate — another season turning in the city's long wheel of kings.
Peasant crusaders march south, then turn their crosses on Jews and priests — a holy dream curdling into a mob, put down in blood.
Dante dies in Ravenna, still exiled from Florence — his great vision of hell and heaven complete, the homeless poet at rest at last.
Charles IV takes the French crown and the direct Capetian line runs out — three hundred years ending not with a battle but with no more sons.
Marsilius of Padua writes that the people, not the pope, should rule the city — the whole order of things questioned in clean sentences.
Mansa Musa crosses the desert to Mecca with a caravan of gold so vast it crashes the price of gold in Cairo — Africa's king revealed to the world.
The Mexica raise Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco — a muddy beginning for the city that will rule an empire.
A young scholar leaves Tangier for Mecca and doesn't come home for thirty years — Ibn Battuta walks the whole known world and writes it down.
Isabella of France lands with an army and topples her husband Edward II — a queen deposing her king, cleanly and forever after imitated.
Orhan takes Bursa, giving the Ottoman Turks their first true capital — frontier raiders becoming a state with a throne-city.
Edward III is crowned at fourteen, with his mother and her lover ruling through him — a boy watching, learning, and counting the days.
Meister Eckhart dies — the mystic who preached that God lives in the soul's deepest ground, in plain German the Church couldn't silence.
Philip VI is crowned, first of the Valois — a new house on the old throne, while across the Channel Edward III studies his own claim.

t: Moscow Rises Under Ivan the Moneybag
x: Ivan Kalita gathers the Mongols' tribute and quietly buys Moscow's rise — no battles, just money, patience, and the Khan's favor.
French knights slaughter the Flemish rebels at Cassel, ending the peasants' rising — Kortrijk's triumph answered in blood.
Robert the Bruce dies; his embalmed heart is carried toward the Holy Land by his knight — the king's last crusade, fought by his heart alone.
The Serbs crush the Bulgarians at Velbazhd and Serbia becomes the Balkans' great power — while across the strait, the Turks take notes.
Edward III arrests his mother's lover Mortimer and seizes power — three years of watching ended in one night of action.
Edward III lures Flemish weavers to England, planting the looms that will clothe a nation — centuries of wealth, one immigrant shuttle at a time.
Ethiopia's Christian king Amda Seyon campaigns south, widening his mountain empire — holy war in Africa while Europe fights its own.
In Tunis a boy is born who will invent the science of how civilizations rise and fall — Ibn Khaldun, the historians' historian.
Kamakura falls and Emperor Go-Daigo briefly retakes the throne — a bright, brief restoration, doomed when the swords disagree.
English longbows mow down the Scots at Halidon Hill — Bannockburn's lesson reversed, and the border bleeds again.
The last strong Ilkhan dies and Persia's Mongol empire shatters — a hundred years of conquest dissolving like salt in rain.
Ashikaga Takauji seizes Kyoto, crushing the emperor's restoration and founding the shogunate that will rule Japan for two centuries.
Near Samarkand a lame boy is born who will make the world tremble — Timur, history's most unlikely vessel, already walking toward his destiny.
Gajah Mada vows to taste no spiced food until the whole archipelago bows to Majapahit — the Palapa Oath, an empire built on an empty stomach.
Two brothers raise Vijayanagara, a new Hindu capital defying Delhi's sultans — the city of victory rising from river boulders.
Philip VI seizes Aquitaine, Edward III claims the French throne — a century of war begins, and nobody understands what they've started.
Edward III burns his way through northern France, daring Philip to fight — smoke on every horizon, and a countryside taught to hate for a century.
English ships destroy the French fleet at Sluys — twenty thousand men and the sea itself, and England rules the Channel.
Petrarch is crowned poet laureate on the Capitol, Rome's first in a thousand years — the Renaissance beginning with a laurel wreath, not a painting.
Portuguese and Genoese sailors raid the Canaries — Europe reaches past the map's edge for plunder and comes back with a horizon.
Clement VI lives in Avignon like a king among kings — glittering, worldly, and yet the pope who will shield the Jews when the plague comes.
Edward III's unpaid debts sink the Bardi and Peruzzi, Florence's mightiest banks — kings borrow, bankers lend, kings don't pay.
English yeomen with longbows shred French chivalry at Crécy — the age of the knight ends, though the knights take a century to notice.
Stefan Dušan is crowned emperor of Serbs and Greeks at Skopje — Serbia's beautiful noon, nine years from its afternoon.
The young notary Cola di Rienzo seizes Rome and proclaims the republic reborn — one bright season of the ancient dream, then the nobles return.

t: The Plague Ships Dock at Messina
x: Plague galleys limp into Messina and the pestilence comes ashore — the Black Death reaches Europe, and a third of the world begins to die.
Fleeing plague-ravaged Florence, Boccaccio begins his hundred tales — laughter as defiance, stories as a wall against the dark.
In the plague year Charles IV founds Prague's university, the first in central Europe — planting learning while the world buries its dead.
King Ramathibodi founds Ayutthaya, the Siamese capital that will shine for four centuries — gold leaf and spires rising from the floodplain.
Inca warriors push beyond Cuzco under Cápac Yupanqui — the long climb to empire beginning, one next valley at a time.
Parliament tries to freeze wages after the plague — and fails, because you can't legislate the value of arms when half the workers are dead.
Starving peasants tie red cloths round their heads and rise against the Mongol Yuan — hunger, the oldest revolutionary, losing its patience.
King Gongmin moves to break the Mongols' grip on Korea — a small king with a long memory standing up to the greatest empire on earth.
An earthquake topples Gallipoli's walls and the Ottomans walk in — their first foothold in Europe, handed to them by the shaking earth.
The Black Prince burns a black road across southern France — war as economics, and the terrible part is that it works.
The Black Prince captures John II of France at Poitiers — a kingdom without its king, and England holding the head.
Charles IV's Golden Bull fixes how emperors are chosen — seven electors sealed in gold, and Germany's rules written for centuries.
The peasant-rebel Zhu Yuanzhang seizes Nanjing — twelve years from beggar's bowl to emperor's seal, and the Yuan already a ghost.
The Baltic merchant towns meet at Lübeck and swear to sail and trade together — the Hansa, a league of cities with no king, only contracts.
French peasants rise in the Jacquerie, burn castles, and are drowned in blood — the poor speak, the rich answer, and France will hear it again.
England and France sign the Treaty of Brétigny — a truce neither believes, nine years of quiet bought by exhaustion.
Parliament orders English, not French, spoken in debates and laws — three hundred years after Hastings, the people's tongue takes power.
The Ottomans take Adrianople, planting their flag deep in Europe — Constantinople now an island in a Turkish sea, down to a city and a prayer.

t: Lake Poyang: The Great River Battle
x: Two rebel fleets clash on Lake Poyang in one of history's greatest naval battles — the Ming dynasty decided on a burning lake before it had a name.

t: Charles the Wise Takes the Throne
x: Charles V is crowned — the canny king who will win France back without great battles, outlasting where others bled.

t: A King of Cyprus Sacks Alexandria
x: Peter I of Cyprus storms Alexandria in a last flash of crusading fire — magnificent, pointless, and already history by the time the sails go home.
Henry of Trastámara invades Castile to tear the crown from his half-brother — brother against brother, and the throne changing hands like dice.
Zhu Yuanzhang drives out the Mongols and proclaims the Ming — the beggar boy on the dragon throne, China for the Chinese again.
Bertrand du Guesclin takes France back castle by castle, avoiding open battle — ten years of slow, quiet winning while glory looks elsewhere.
Timur seizes Samarkand and proclaims himself ruler — the lame boy beginning the long conquest the world will learn in ruins.
Robert II takes the throne, first Stuart king of Scots — a small spring in the hills, no hint of the ocean of history waiting downstream.

t: La Rochelle: France Takes Back the Sea
x: A French-Castilian fleet smashes the English at La Rochelle — thirty years of English sea-rule ending in an afternoon of smoke.
Near death in Norwich, Julian receives the visions she'll call her Showings — the first known book in English by a woman, gentleness out of a cell.
Petrarch dies at Arquà with his head resting on a book — the laureate who tried to drag Rome back from the dead with nothing but words.

t: The Atlas Paints a Golden King
x: Abraham Cresques draws Mansa Musa on his golden throne in the Catalan Atlas — Europe learning Africa's king by name, in gold on vellum.
The Commons rise against royal corruption in the Good Parliament — impeachment forged as a tool, a ghost that will live long after.
The Mexica elect Acamapichtli, first king of Tenochtitlan — wanderers no more, a city choosing a crown to give itself weight.
Gregory XI brings the papacy home from Avignon after seventy years — Rome's bells ringing, the old city breathing again, if only for a season.
Richard II is crowned at ten, a beautiful boy with a dangerous pride — a child on the throne, and an invitation to every schemer in England.
Rival popes in Rome and Avignon excommunicate each other, splitting Christendom — the fisherman's chair sawed in half for forty years.

t: The Ciompi: Wool Workers Seize Florence
x: Florence's wool carders seize the city and rule for six wild weeks — the world turned over, then turned back, but never forgotten.
Dmitry Donskoy's Russians break the Golden Horde at Kulikovo — the Mongol yoke cracking after 140 years, the spell broken forever.
Catherine of Siena dies — the dyer's daughter who scolded popes to their faces and moved them with plain, fierce letters.
Kentish peasants march on London behind Wat Tyler, burn palaces, and demand an end to serfdom — the revolt fails, but the point stands.
Wycliffe's followers put the scriptures into plain English for common readers — the hardest contraband ever smuggled, and still winning.
Young Jadwiga is crowned king of Poland at ten — a child carrying two nations' future, and the union of Poland and Lithuania to come.
Outnumbered Portuguese troops smash Castile at Aljubarrota — the one battle a small country can't afford to lose, won for six hundred years.
Germany's oldest university opens at Heidelberg — the plague emptied the towns, and the universities are filling the minds instead.
Chaucer begins the Canterbury Tales, giving the English tongue its great voice — pilgrims telling stories in the language of plowmen.
Scots and English slaughter each other at moonlit Otterburn — a battle so bloody and pointless that only the ballads could make sense of it.
The Ottomans crush the Serbs at Kosovo; prince and sultan both die — the defeat that becomes a nation's soul for six hundred years.
Majapahit's great king Hayam Wuruk dies, and the island empire's golden age begins its slow, quiet fade.
Mobs massacre Jews across Spain in the fury of 1391 — synagogues burned, thousands fleeing or dying, a wound that never closed.
Yi Seong-gye founds the Joseon dynasty, which will rule Korea for five centuries — one general's decision, half a millennium of consequence.
Charles VI goes mad in a forest, striking down his own men — and France drifts toward civil war on the wreck of one man's mind.
Yi Seong-gye builds his new capital Hanseong — the city the world will call Seoul, its geomancers' lines holding for six hundred years.
The Ottomans annihilate the last great crusade at Nicopolis — chivalry's dream dying in the Danube mud, the crusading age's funeral.
Margaret I binds Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single crown — the whole north united not by raid but by law, under a queen.
Timur's horsemen storm Delhi and leave it in ruins and skulls — the conqueror who never stays, whose passing alone is enough to break an empire.
Henry Bolingbroke deposes Richard II and seizes the throne as Henry IV — theft in ermine, and a century of England deciding if it was right.

t: The Lion City of the Straits
x: A fleeing prince founds the harbor city that will command the spice lanes between East and West.
Owain Glyndŵr raises Wales in revolt against English rule, and the dream of a free Wales never dies.
Timur sacks Aleppo and Damascus, stacking the skulls of the fallen into towers of warning.
Timur captures the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid at Ankara, and the Ottoman Empire reels on the brink of ruin.
Timur turns his armies east, marching toward Ming China in the winter snows.
The Yongle Emperor puts Zheng He, a court eunuch, in command of the greatest fleet ever launched.
Timur dies on the march to China, and his vast empire shatters among his heirs.
Zheng He's treasure fleet leaves Nanjing with 27,000 men aboard, bound for Calicut and beyond.
The Yongle Emperor sets a million workmen to raising his great palace at Beijing.
Ibn Khaldun dies in Cairo, leaving the Muqaddimah — the first science of how empires rise and fall.
The Yongle Encyclopedia — eleven thousand hand-copied volumes holding all of China's knowledge — is completed.
The Council of Pisa elects a third pope — deepening the schism it meant to heal.
Polish and Lithuanian knights crush the Teutonic Order at Grunwald, breaking its power in the north.
Zheng He captures the king of Ceylon and carries him home to Nanjing, where the Emperor pardons him.
Joan of Arc is born at Domrémy — a farmer's daughter no one notices, yet.
Henry V takes the English throne — the tavern prince become the warrior king.
The Council of Constance opens — the whole of Christendom gathers to heal the broken church.
Portugal seizes Ceuta — the first foothold of the age of exploration.
Jan Hus burns at the stake at Constance, singing psalms in the flames — and prophesies a swan to come.
Henry V's outnumbered longbowmen shatter French chivalry in the mud of Agincourt.
Brunelleschi demonstrates linear perspective in Florence — painting learns true depth.
Martin V is elected at Constance — the Western Schism ends, and the church has one pope again.
Brunelleschi wins the contest to crown Florence's cathedral with an impossible dome.
King Sejong of Korea begins his reign — the scholar-king who will give his people an alphabet.
Henry the Navigator gathers mapmakers and sailors at Sagres — the school that will unlock the oceans.
Portuguese sailors claim Madeira — and the sugar plantations plant the seeds of the slave economy.
The Forbidden City is finished — Beijing becomes the capital of Ming China.
The Hussite Wars begin — Bohemian peasants march under the chalice banner against church and empire.
Zheng He's fleet sails its sixth voyage — to Hormuz and down Africa's Swahili coast.
Henry V and Charles VI both die — the infant Henry VI inherits the crowns of England and France.
England's archers win a second Agincourt at Verneuil, and the road to Paris lies open.
Masaccio's Brancacci Chapel frescoes show real bodies and human grief — painting grows up.
Le Loi's rebels break a decade of Chinese rule and free Vietnam.
Itzcoatl binds three cities into the Triple Alliance — the Aztec Empire is born, and the old histories burn.
Joan of Arc lifts the siege of Orléans in nine days — a seventeen-year-old girl in white armor turns the war.
Charles VII is crowned at Reims with Joan's banner beside him — her promise fulfilled.
Joan is captured at Compiègne and sold to the English — the king she crowned does nothing.

t: The First Woman of Letters Dies
x: Christine de Pizan dies — the first woman to earn her living by the pen, leaving The Book of the City of Ladies.
Joan of Arc burns at Rouen, aged nineteen — her ashes thrown in the Seine, her memory made into legend.
Portuguese sailors find the Azores far out in the Atlantic — stepping stones toward an unknown world.
Zheng He dies on the homeward voyage — and China turns its back on the ocean forever.
Gil Eanes rounds Cape Bojador, breaking the sailors' terror of sailing south.
Cosimo de' Medici takes quiet power in Florence — ruling a republic from a banker's back room.
Zara Yaqob takes Ethiopia's throne and rebuilds church and law in the highland Christian kingdom.
Brunelleschi's cupola crowns Florence's cathedral — the Renaissance gets its roof.
James I of Scotland — the poet king — is murdered at Perth.
Pachacuti becomes Sapa Inca — the Earth-Shaker — and the great Inca expansion begins.
Lorenzo Valla proves the Donation of Constantine a forgery — one essay cracks eight centuries of papal claims.
Oba Ewuare raises Benin City's great walls; its bronze casters flourish in the forest kingdom.
The first captives land at Lagos — the Atlantic slave trade's dark dawn.
Jan van Eyck dies — the master whose oil paint taught Europe to see light.
Alfonso of Aragon storms Naples and makes it his glittering humanist court.
King Sejong invents Hangul — an alphabet so simple a farmer can learn it in a day.
The last crusade dies at Varna — the young king's head on a pike, the Balkans lost to the Ottomans.
Aztec ritual Flower Wars feed captives to the gods under Moctezuma I.
Nicholas V becomes pope and founds the Vatican Library — rescuing Greek manuscripts as Byzantium falls.
Murad II crushes the crusaders at the second battle of Kosovo — no army will march to save Constantinople.
Constantine XI takes the throne of a dying Byzantium — emperor of a city, with four years left.
Machu Picchu rises in the clouds — the Inca's royal mountain estate, built stone to stone without mortar.
Trailokkanat of Ayutthaya writes laws binding princes and peasants alike.
Mehmed II, nineteen, takes the Ottoman throne — dreaming of Constantinople, building cannons.
Isabella of Castile is born — the baby who will fund a voyage to a new world and finish the Reconquista.
Leonardo da Vinci is born at Vinci — the century's most restless mind, crying in a farmhouse.
Mehmed builds Rumeli Hisarı on the Bosphorus — the Throat-Cutter — strangling Constantinople's lifeline.
Mehmed II's cannons breach the walls on May 29 — Byzantium ends, and fleeing scholars carry Greek learning west.
Castillon falls — the Hundred Years' War ends; England keeps only Calais.
The Italian states agree to the Peace of Lodi — forty years of calm, and the Renaissance at full flower.
York and Lancaster clash at St Albans — the Wars of the Roses begin, cousin against cousin.
Hunyadi hurls Mehmed's army back from Belgrade — the noon bell still rings for it.
Gutenberg's press is seized for debt — his scattered workmen carry the printing secret across Europe.
The humanist Aeneas Silvius — novelist, poet, diplomat — becomes Pope Pius II.
Fra Mauro completes his great circular world map — drawn by a monk who never traveled, from sailors' tales.
Henry the Navigator dies at Sagres — the man who never sailed far, but sent the world to sea.
Diogo Gomes claims the Cape Verde islands — the last safe harbor on the road south.
Towton — the bloodiest battle on English soil — makes Edward IV king in a snowstorm of slaughter.
Trebizond, the last Byzantine splinter, surrenders to Mehmed II — Rome's eastern story ends with a signature.
Ivan III takes Moscow's throne and begins gathering the Russian lands.
Ficino translates Plato for the Medici — antiquity walks the streets of Florence again.
Vlad the Impaler raids the Sultan's camp by night — missing Mehmed's tent, but shaking an empire.
Sunni Ali takes Gao's throne — the Lion King — and an empire rises on the Niger.
Pius II dies at Ancona, waiting on the docks for a crusade fleet that never comes.
German printers set up at Subiaco — Italy learns movable type, and soon outprints all Europe.
Erasmus of Rotterdam is born — the scholar who will mock popes and princes with laughter.
The Onin War begins — Kyoto burns, and Japan slides into a century of warring states.
Isabella and Ferdinand wed in secret — the marriage that will make Spain.
Nicolas Jenson cuts the clear roman type that books still wear today.
Young Botticelli opens his Florence workshop — the painter of Spring is coming.
Topa Inca Yupanqui carries the Inca Empire to its greatest reach — north to Quito, south past the desert.
Edward IV destroys the Lancastrian cause at Barnet and Tewkesbury — the red rose is trampled.
The Monte dei Paschi opens at Siena — the world's oldest surviving bank, open ever since.
Ivan III weds the Byzantine princess Sophia — Moscow claims the mantle of the fallen empire.
Nicolaus Copernicus is born at Toruń — the baby who will move the earth around the sun.
Caxton prints the first book in English at Bruges — the mongrel tongue gets its press.
Isabella takes Castile's throne at twenty-three — a disputed heir who seizes her crown with both hands.
Michelangelo is born at Caprese — the baby whose hands will free David from the stone.
Swiss pikemen crush Charles the Bold at Grandson and Morat — the age of the pike square begins.
Caxton sets up his press at Westminster — the first English press prints Chaucer.
Mary of Burgundy inherits at nineteen — the great duchy is carved up between France and the Habsburgs.
Ferdinand and Isabella win papal leave for the Spanish Inquisition — three centuries of terror begin.
The Pazzi stab Giuliano de' Medici at Easter Mass — murder at the altar, with Rome's blessing.
Ferdinand inherits Aragon — Spain stands united under two monarchs, and the world is about to feel it.
Portuguese caravels haul Guinea gold home — the Mina trade booms, and pays for the age of discovery.
Ivan III faces the Horde at the Ugra — it melts away, and two centuries of Mongol rule end without a battle.
Leonardo fills his notebooks with flying machines, war engines, and anatomy — the future, in mirror-writing.
Mehmed II dies — the Conqueror gone, his sons tear the court apart over the succession.
Painters cover the new Sistine Chapel's walls with the lives of Moses and Christ.

t: The Stone Castle on the Gold Coast
x: Portugal raises São Jorge da Mina at Elmina — fortress, trading post, and future slave dungeon.
Richard III takes the crown — his young nephews vanish into the Tower, never to emerge.
Martin Luther is born at Eisleben — the miner's son who will split the church in half.
Diogo Cão sails past the Congo, planting stone crosses down Africa's shore as Portugal's claim-markers.
Henry Tudor kills Richard III at Bosworth — the crown found in a hawthorn bush, the Tudors begin.
Ahuitzotl becomes the Aztecs' great conqueror-king — doubling the empire, dedicating the Great Temple in blood.
Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope — the sea road to India lies open.
The last Muslim kingdom in Iberia surrenders — Granada falls, and the 781-year Reconquista ends.

t: The Admiral of the Ocean Sea
x: Columbus reaches the Americas on October 12 — thinking it Asia, finding a whole new world.
Spain's Jews are expelled — a people scatter across the world, carrying their house keys for five centuries.
Askia Muhammad seizes Songhai and builds an empire of scholars and gold, with Timbuktu's universities at its heart.
Huayna Capac takes the throne at the Inca Empire's height — its greatest extent, with the clock already ticking.
The pope draws a line splitting the undiscovered world between Spain and Portugal — continents divided like a pie.
Tordesillas shifts the dividing line west — Brazil falls to Portugal by a pen stroke on a map.
Aldus Manutius sets up his Venetian press — inventing the pocket book, the italic, and the modern reader.
John Cabot claims North America for England — eighteen men, a small ship, and waters thick with cod.
Vasco da Gama rounds the Cape of Good Hope in November — the voyage to India is truly underway.
Da Gama reaches Calicut in May — the sea road to India is found, and the old spice roads tremble.
Savonarola burns at Florence — the bonfire of the vanities ends with the friar's own fire.
Portuguese ships land on Brazil's coast and claim the vast green land for their king, while the native people watch from the trees.
Cabral's fleet reaches India, locking in Portugal's long sea lane around Africa to the spice trade.
Under Askia the Great, Timbuktu's book markets and libraries make Songhai the pride of West Africa.
Young Shah Ismail seizes Tabriz and founds Safavid Persia, a Shi'ite empire born on the sword.
Michelangelo begins carving the seventeen-foot David in Florence — a boy carved from marble, staring down a giant.
Aldus Manutius prints the first pocket books in slanted italic type, made to be carried in saddlebags.
Columbus sails his fourth and final voyage, ending stranded for a year in Jamaica, a broken admiral in the world he found.
Leonardo begins painting Lisa del Giocondo — the portrait the world will call the Mona Lisa, and her unknowable smile.
Isabella of Castile dies, leaving her unstable daughter Juana heir to the Spanish crown.
Francisco de Almeida sails as Portugal's first viceroy of the Indies, to rule the pepper trade by cannon.
Pope Julius II lays the first stone of a new St. Peter's Basilica, meant to dwarf old Rome.
Afonso I takes the Kongo throne and writes to the pope as a Catholic king in Africa, even as the slave trade grows around him.
A small German press prints the first map to call the New World "America," after Amerigo Vespucci's letters.
Michelangelo climbs the Sistine scaffold and begins painting Genesis overhead, on his back, high above the chapel floor.
Seventeen-year-old Henry VIII takes the English throne — handsome, athletic, and hungry for glory.
Portugal smashes a Mamluk fleet off Diu and seizes mastery of the Indian Ocean in a single day of cannon fire.
Raphael paints philosophers debating in the Vatican — Plato and Aristotle at the center of the School of Athens.
Afonso de Albuquerque storms Goa and makes it Portugal's capital of the Indian Ocean.
Albuquerque seizes Malacca, the great strait port where all of Asia's trade funnels through.
Michelangelo uncovers the Sistine ceiling — nine scenes from Creation to Noah, painted in four years on his back.
Selim I seizes the Ottoman throne — cold, ruthless, and called "the Grim," clearing rivals without mercy.
Machiavelli writes The Prince in exile — cold counsel on how rulers keep power.
Balboa wades into the Pacific and claims the whole ocean for Spain.
Selim crushes Shah Ismail at Chaldiran — Ottoman guns beat Safavid holy swords, and gunpowder wins the day.
Bartolomé de las Casas gives up his own slaves and begins a lifelong fight for the native peoples of the Americas.
Twenty-year-old Francis I is crowned at Reims — Europe's most dazzling prince.
Dürer carves his famous rhinoceros in wood — a beast he never saw, built from a sketch and a letter.
Selim defeats the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq; Syria falls to the Ottomans and the old sultan dies on the field.
Thomas More publishes Utopia, dreaming of a perfect commonwealth on an imaginary island.
Martin Luther posts 95 theses against indulgences at Wittenberg and sets Europe alight.
Selim rides into Cairo; the Mamluk sultans are finished, and Mecca answers to Istanbul.
Spain licenses the first mass shipments of enslaved Africans to the Americas — the slave trade's machinery begins.
Hernán Cortés receives command of the expedition to Mexico's mainland.
Magellan sails from Seville with five ships to find the westward way to the Spice Islands.
Cortés lands at Veracruz and marches inland toward Tenochtitlan with native allies at his side.
The Mexica rise against the Spaniards; Cortés's men flee Tenochtitlan in a night of slaughter.
Luther publicly burns the pope's bull of excommunication at Wittenberg's gates — the break with Rome is final.

t: The Field of Cloth of Gold
x: Henry VIII and Francis I feast in tents of gold outside Calais — then return to scheming against each other.
Twenty-five-year-old Suleiman takes the Ottoman throne for a reign of nearly half a century.
Hauled before the emperor at Worms, Luther refuses to recant: "Here I stand."
After a brutal siege the Mexica capital falls; an empire passes into Spanish hands.
Magellan dies in a skirmish on Mactan; his expedition sails on without him.
Suleiman takes Belgrade, the white fortress guarding the road to Hungary.
The Victoria staggers into Seville — the first ship to sail around the entire Earth.
Suleiman takes Rhodes from the Knights Hospitaller after a six-month siege, and lets them sail away with honor.
Gustav Vasa drives out the Danes and is crowned king of a free Sweden.
Fired by the Reformation, German peasants take up arms against their lords.
Imperial troops crush France at Pavia and drag King Francis I off as a prisoner.
The Peasants' War is drowned in blood; Luther turns on the rebels he once inspired.
Babur's small army smashes the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat — the Mughal Empire is born.
Suleiman destroys Hungary's army in two hours at Mohács; a kingdom dies in an afternoon.
The Diet of Speyer lets each German prince choose his land's faith — for now, the wars pause.
Mutinous imperial soldiers loot Rome for days; the Renaissance's proudest city is stripped bare.
Henry VIII asks the pope to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon — the King's Great Matter begins.
Pánfilo de Narváez's expedition collapses in Florida; only four men will walk out alive.
Two royal women sign the Treaty of Cambrai — peace made by women while kings made war.
Suleiman's army reaches Vienna, but winter and high walls turn it back — the Ottoman high-water mark.
Princes who defy the emperor at Speyer earn the name Protestants — the ones who protest.
Melanchthon reads the Augsburg Confession; Lutheranism gains its founding charter.
An Indian convert reports a vision of Mary on Tepeyac hill; a new shrine rises and millions will come.
King John III brings the Inquisition to Portugal to hunt heresy and secret Jews.
Ulrich Zwingli dies sword in hand at Kappel — the first reformer killed in war.
Pizarro ambushes the Inca Atahualpa at Cajamarca; a room filled with gold is set as the ransom.
Henry secretly marries Anne Boleyn and breaks toward schism with Rome.
Atahualpa is strangled despite the ransom of gold; the Inca Empire's heart is cut out.
Anne Boleyn bears a daughter — the future Elizabeth I, unwanted by her father, destined for greatness.
Three-year-old Ivan inherits Muscovy while the boyars feast on the regency — the Terrible is being made.
Parliament declares Henry VIII supreme head of the Church of England — the break with Rome is law.
Jacques Cartier sails up the St. Lawrence and claims the land for France.
Ignatius of Loyola and six companions vow themselves to the pope in Paris — the Jesuits are born.
Anabaptists seize Münster and crown a tailor king; the siege ends in cages and torture.
Thomas More is beheaded for refusing Henry's supremacy; conscience dies with him on Tower Hill.
Anne Boleyn is executed in the Tower; Henry weds Jane Seymour days later.
John Calvin publishes his Institutes of the Christian Religion in Basel — a theology of iron logic.
Cabeza de Vaca and three companions stumble into Mexico after eight lost years crossing the continent.
William Tyndale is strangled and burned for putting the Bible into English.
Jane Seymour bears Henry a son, Edward — then dies twelve days later of childbed fever.
Titian paints the reclining Venus that teaches Europe a new way to look at a body.
Coronado marches north for the Seven Cities of Cíbola while de Soto hunts gold through Florida — both find no gold, but map a continent.
Paul III formally approves the Society of Jesus — the Jesuits become Rome's shock troops.
Almagro's partisans murder Francisco Pizarro in his Lima palace — the conqueror conquered.

t: The End of the World, Painted
x: Michelangelo unveils the Last Judgment — Christ hurling the damned down, twenty-five years after the ceiling.
Charles V issues the New Laws to protect the Indians — Las Casas's victory on paper, resisted in the colonies.
Mary Queen of Scots is born as her father dies; a six-day-old inherits a crown.
Francis Xavier reaches Goa and begins the Jesuit mission along Asia's coasts.
Cabrillo sails up the California coast — the first European to see it.
Copernicus publishes his Sun-centered cosmos — and dies as the book comes off the press.
Vesalius publishes the first true atlas of the human body, drawn from the dissecting table.
Portuguese merchants land on Tanegashima with the first muskets Japan has ever seen.
Maya nobles present jars of frothing cacao to Prince Philip — Europe tastes chocolate for the first time.
The Cerro Rico at Potosí is found — a mountain of silver that will flood the world's coinage.
The Council of Trent convenes to answer the Reformation — the Counter-Reformation begins.
Martin Luther dies in Eisleben, the town of his birth, worn out at sixty-two.

t: The Woman Who Would Not Bend
x: Anne Askew is burned for heresy — the only woman tortured in the Tower, unbroken to the end.
Francis I dies; his sickly son Henry II takes the French crown and France slides toward religious war.
Nine-year-old Edward VI inherits England; his uncles rule in his name and push the Reformation.
Sixteen-year-old Ivan IV is crowned "Tsar of All Rus" — Ivan the Terrible begins.
Charles V crushes the Protestant princes at Mühlberg — the Reformation's darkest hour.
Pedro de la Gasca defeats Gonzalo Pizarro; the age of the conquistadors ends in Peru.
Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer gives England worship in its own tongue.
Francis Xavier reaches Kagoshima — the first Christian missionary in Japan.
At Valladolid, Las Casas and Sepúlveda argue whether the Indians have souls and rights — the first great human-rights debate.
Vasari publishes his Lives — the first art history, turning painters into legends.
The Royal University of Mexico opens — the New World's first university, older than Harvard by eighty years.
Ivan the Terrible storms Kazan; the Tatar khanate falls and Russia turns east.
Francis Xavier dies on Shangchuan Island, within sight of the China he never entered.
Lady Jane Grey reigns nine days before Mary Tudor seizes the throne.
Mary I takes the throne and drags England back to Rome; the burnings follow and she becomes "Bloody Mary."
Mary marries Philip of Spain; England is yoked to the Spanish crown.
Jesuit priests found São Paulo in the Brazilian wilderness — a mission that will become a megacity.
Each German prince chooses his land's faith — cuius regio, eius religio; the wars pause for sixty years.
Bishops Latimer and Ridley burn at Oxford; Latimer's candle "shall never be put out."
Suleiman and Persia sign the Peace of Amasya — the first Ottoman-Safavid treaty.
Thirteen-year-old Akbar inherits the Mughal throne; a regent holds it for him while he grows.
Akbar's regent Bairam Khan crushes Hemu at Panipat; the boy keeps his crown.
Charles V gives up his thrones and retires to a monastery; his empire splits between Spain and Austria.
Philip II's Spain goes bankrupt — even silver mountains cannot pay for endless war.
Elizabeth I takes the throne — twenty-five, brilliant, Protestant England's hope.
France seizes Calais; England's last foothold on the continent is gone.
Charles V dies in his monastery cell at Yuste — the monk emperor's end.

t: The Joust That Killed a King
x: Henry II dies of a splintered lance in a tournament; France slides toward religious war.
John Knox returns to Scotland and preaches the Kirk into revolution.
Scotland's parliament adopts the Protestant confession; the old faith is outlawed and the Kirk is born.
Portugal drives the French from Guanabara Bay, ending France's Antarctic dream in Brazil.
Ivan buries his beloved wife Anastasia; the gentle years of his reign end and the terror begins.
Catholic troops slaughter Huguenots at prayer at Vassy; France's Wars of Religion begin.
John Hawkins sails the first English slaving voyage to the Spanish Caribbean — England joins the trade in souls.
The Council of Trent ends, having redrawn Catholic doctrine for four centuries.
Michelangelo dies in Rome at eighty-eight; the Renaissance's great hand is stilled.

t: The Swan of Avon Is Born
x: William Shakespeare is born in Stratford-upon-Avon — the glover's son who will remake the world's stage.
Ivan abandons Moscow in a staged abdication, then returns with absolute power and the Oprichnina.
Urdaneta finds the return sailing route from Asia to Mexico — the Manila galleon run is born.
Suleiman's fleet besieges Malta; the Knights hold, and the Ottoman tide turns.
Spain founds St. Augustine — the oldest lasting European city in North America.
Calvinist mobs smash church statues across the Low Countries — the Beeldenstorm, the breaking of the images.
Suleiman dies campaigning in Hungary; the Ottoman peak passes with him.
Mary Queen of Scots is forced to abdicate; her infant son James VI is crowned.
William of Orange raises the revolt; the Dutch fight for freedom begins and will last eighty years.
Philip's heir Don Carlos dies a prisoner in Madrid; the succession darkens and rumors haunt the court.
The Moriscos of Granada rise against forced conversion; Spain answers with fire and Don John crushes them.
Mercator publishes his world map with the projection that will guide sailors for centuries.
Ottoman troops take Nicosia; Venice's Cyprus begins to crumble in blood.
Humayun's tomb rises in Delhi — the first great Mughal garden-tomb, model for the Taj.
At Lepanto the Holy League smashes the Ottoman fleet — the sea's greatest galley battle.
Legazpi founds Manila, the far anchor of Spain's Pacific empire.
On St. Bartholomew's Day, Catholics massacre thousands of Huguenots in Paris — the wedding of blood.
At Molodi, Russia crushes the Crimean Tatars' last great raid toward Moscow.
Oda Nobunaga drives out the Ashikaga shogun; Japan's warring age tilts toward union.
Viceroy Toledo chains the Andes to Potosí with the mita labor draft; silver flows, villages empty.
At Nagashino, Nobunaga's musket lines shred the Takeda cavalry — the gun beats the sword.
At Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar opens the Ibadat Khana — a hall where every faith is invited to argue before the emperor himself.
Night after night at the Ibadat Khana, scholars of four faiths argue before Akbar — and the traveler listens to the world argue with itself.
Unpaid Spanish troops sack Antwerp for three days, burning its city hall — and turning the whole Netherlands against Spain for good.
On a Danish island, Tycho Brahe raises Uraniborg — the grandest observatory of the age — and maps the heavens by naked eye alone.
Francis Drake slips out of Plymouth with five small ships, bound to circle the globe through seas Spain claims as its own.
A great comet blazes over Europe for months; Tycho Brahe's measurements prove it flies far beyond the moon — and the old heavens crack.
At Alcácer Quibir, Portugal's young king and two rival sultans all die in one battle — and Portugal's throne falls vacant.
Seven northern provinces swear the Union of Utrecht against Spain — the first stone of the Dutch Republic, signed with a pen in winter.
Philip II marches into Portugal and takes its throne — the two greatest seafaring empires now wear a single crown.
The Dutch formally depose Philip II — the first modern republic is declared, and a king is unmade by paperwork.
The Cossack Yermak leads a few hundred men over the Urals into Siberia — and opens a continent-sized land for Russia.
Zhang Juzheng folds every Ming tax into a single silver payment — steadying China's economy for a generation on foreign silver.
Pope Gregory XIII cuts ten days from the calendar to fix its drift — Catholic Europe goes to sleep on October 4 and wakes on October 15.
Betrayed at Kyoto's Honnō-ji temple, Oda Nobunaga takes his own life as the flames close in — and Hideyoshi seizes his chance.
Teresa of Ávila — reformer of her order, author of the soul's Interior Castle — dies at Alba de Tormes.
Humphrey Gilbert plants the English flag at St. John's, claiming Newfoundland — England's first overseas territory — with turf and twig.
William of Orange, father of the Dutch revolt, is assassinated on his own staircase in Delft — but the cause survives him.
After twenty-one years of building, Philip II's vast Escorial — palace, monastery, and tomb of kings — is completed.
English settlers wade ashore on Roanoke Island — England's first colony in the Americas takes root in hope and bad planning.
Parma retakes Antwerp after a brutal siege — and its merchants flee north, carrying their wealth and craft to Amsterdam.
Mary Queen of Scots is caught backing the Babington plot to kill Elizabeth — her ciphered letters, all read by Walsingham, seal her fate.
After nineteen years a prisoner, Mary Queen of Scots is beheaded at Fotheringhay — in crimson, the color of martyrdom.
Drake storms into Cádiz harbor in daylight and burns the ships Spain was gathering for invasion — singeing the king's beard.
Thomas Cavendish captures the Spanish treasure galleon Santa Ana off California — the richest prize of the age.
Storms and English fireships scatter Philip II's great Armada — Spain's dream of invading England drowns in the Channel.
Sixteen-year-old Abbas takes Persia's throne amid enemies on every side — and begins the long climb to greatness.
Drake and Norris sail to strike back at Spain off Lisbon — but disease and bad luck break their fleet, and England's revenge fails.
Henry IV's siege starves Paris into submission — thirty thousand dead of hunger before politics opens the gates.
Giacomo della Porta crowns St. Peter's with its great dome, completing Michelangelo's design — the mother of all domes since.
John White returns to Roanoke to find every settler vanished — one word carved on a post: CROATOAN. America's first mystery.
Moroccan musketeers crush the mighty Songhai Empire at Tondibi in a single afternoon — West Africa's golden age ends in gunpowder smoke.
Hideyoshi's armies storm ashore at Busan — Japan's great invasion of Korea begins at dawn.
Admiral Yi Sun-sin smashes the Japanese fleet at Hansan with his armored turtle ships — cutting the invaders' lifeline in a single day.

t: Paris Is Well Worth a Mass
x: Henry IV converts to Catholicism — "Paris is well worth a Mass" — and the city opens its gates, ending thirty years of religious war.
Botanist Carolus Clusius plants the first tulips at Leiden — neighbors steal the bulbs, and a flower begins its conquest of Holland.
Christopher Marlowe — Tamburlaine, Faustus — is stabbed dead in a Deptford tavern at twenty-nine, over a reckoning no one can explain.
Jacopo Tintoretto — Il Furioso, the furious painter of light and storm — dies in Venice after a lifetime covering its walls.
Walter Raleigh sails up the Orinoco hunting El Dorado, the golden city — and finds only jungle, fever, and a story England wanted to believe.
Francis Drake dies of fever off Portobelo and is buried at sea in a lead coffin — the sea that made him takes him back.
Essex and Howard storm Cádiz and burn the Spanish fleet in its harbor — Spain scuttles its own treasure ships rather than yield them.
After twenty-seven years of work, Li Shizhen's Compendium of Materia Medica is published — nearly two thousand medicines, honestly cataloged.
Hideyoshi launches a second invasion of Korea — a hundred and forty thousand men sent by a dying man who won't admit the first one failed.
At Myeongnyang, the disgraced Admiral Yi returns with 13 ships against 133 — and wins without losing one, the current fighting beside him.
John Gerard's Herball describes the potato for English readers — a humble root that will one day feed millions, and starve them too.
Henry IV's Edict of Nantes grants French Protestants the right to worship — ending thirty years of religious war with a signature.
Hideyoshi dies at Osaka Castle, leaving a child heir and feuding regents — his generals quietly begin pulling the armies home from Korea.
Diego Velázquez is born in Seville — the boy who will paint kings as they truly are, and light as it truly falls.
Giordano Bruno — who taught of infinite worlds around infinite suns — is burned at the stake in Rome's Campo de' Fiori.
Maurice of Nassau's Dutch army beats the feared Spanish tercios on the dunes at Nieuwpoort — proving the new way of war works.
Tokugawa Ieyasu crushes his rivals in the mist at Sekigahara — one October day that decides the next two and a half centuries of Japan.
Elizabeth I charters the East India Company — two hundred merchants, a few ships, and a piece of parchment that will one day rule an empire.
The Earl of Essex, Elizabeth's fallen favorite, is beheaded on Tower Green after his foolish rebellion — charm without judgment.
England crushes the Irish and their Spanish allies at Kinsale — breaking Gaelic Ireland's last great hope in a winter morning.
The Dutch East India Company is founded — the first public stock offering, a company with its own fleets, forts, and armies.
Elizabeth I dies childless after forty-five years — and James VI of Scotland rides south to become James I of England, cheered by strangers.
Tokugawa Ieyasu takes the title of shogun — opening two and a half centuries of Tokugawa peace, built on control.
The Treaty of London ends nineteen years of Anglo-Spanish war — the privateers come home to an England that has moved on.
Guy Fawkes is caught in the cellars under Parliament with thirty-six barrels of gunpowder — and England gets its bonfire night forever.
Cervantes publishes the first part of Don Quixote — the gaunt knight and his round squire ride out of cheap paper into world literature.
Escaped enslaved Africans found Palmares in Brazil's forests — a hidden free kingdom that will defy the slavers for nearly a century.
Three English ships land on the James River — the first lasting English colony in America takes root in a swamp, on hunger and hope.
Samuel de Champlain builds a trading post where the St. Lawrence narrows — the seed of French Canada, bought with furs and frostbite.
Hans Lippershey patents the spyglass — a tube of lenses, a fairground toy that will soon be turned on the heavens.
Galileo turns his telescope to the night sky — and finds mountains on the moon, moons around Jupiter, a universe remade in one night.
Johannes Kepler publishes his first two laws of planetary motion — the planets move in ellipses, proven on eight un-fudged minutes of arc.
Spain expels the Moriscos — three hundred thousand baptized Christians of Muslim descent — cutting out its own craftsmen to purify its blood.
Gaspar Yanga — African rebel, thirty years free in the Veracruz highlands — founds the free town of San Lorenzo after forcing Spain to treat with him.
Henry IV is knifed in his carriage in Paris — the king who ended the religious wars dies, and a nine-year-old inherits the throne.
Henry Hudson sails into the vast frozen bay that will bear his name — and the next summer his mutinous crew sets him adrift to vanish.
King James's scholars publish their great English Bible — fifty-four men, seven years, and the book that will shape the language for centuries.
Jahangir marries Nur Jahan — the brilliant widow who will all but rule the Mughal Empire beside him, her name struck on the coinage.
Artemisia Gentileschi testifies against her attacker under thumbscrews in a Roman court — and goes on to paint heroines who fight back.
After English ships beat the Portuguese off Surat, the East India Company plants its first trading post on Indian soil — a shed that will grow an empire.
After the Time of Troubles, the assembly elects sixteen-year-old Michael Romanov tsar — founding a dynasty that will rule for three centuries.
A stage cannon sets the Globe Theatre's thatch alight — Shakespeare's playhouse burns to the ground in an hour, and is rebuilt within the year.
Pocahontas marries John Rolfe at Jamestown — a political marriage sealing a fragile peace that will die with her at twenty-one.
John Napier publishes his tables of logarithms — a shortcut through heavy arithmetic that astronomers and sailors will use for centuries.
Tokugawa troops storm Osaka Castle and wipe out the Toyotomi — ending the last challenge to Tokugawa rule in fire and smoke.
Anne of Austria marries Louis XIII, bringing her Spanish taste for drinking chocolate to the French court — and Paris never drinks the same again.
Shakespeare, Cervantes, and China's Tang Xianzu all die within months of each other — three masters, three worlds, one turning year.
Work begins on Madrid's great Plaza Mayor — the grand square where the city will gather, celebrate, and judge for centuries.
Protestant nobles hurl two Catholic officials from a Prague Castle window — they survive the fall, and the Thirty Years' War begins.
Walter Raleigh is beheaded at Whitehall for his failed Guiana voyage — fifteen years after his first death sentence, a king's diplomacy kills him.
The Manchu leader Nurhaci annihilates four Ming armies at Sarhu — and the Ming dynasty's doom begins in the Manchurian snow.
Jan Pieterszoon Coen seizes Jayakarta and founds Batavia — the Dutch East India Company's Asian capital, raised on a burned town's ashes.
Kepler publishes his third law of planetary motion — the harmony of the spheres, the solar system singing in mathematics.
A Dutch ship lands the first enslaved Africans at Point Comfort — twenty souls traded for food, the quiet beginning of America's wound.
A hundred Pilgrims cross the Atlantic in a leaky ship — half will die the first winter, but the Compact they sign will outlive them all.
Catholic armies crush the Bohemian rebels at White Mountain in two hours — and Bohemia's Protestant hopes die for three centuries.
Francis Bacon publishes his call for a new science built on experiment, not ancient authority — the workshop replaces the cathedral.
The surviving Pilgrims share a harvest feast with their Wampanoag neighbors — three days of food and laughter after a year of burials.
Jean-Baptiste Poquelin is born in Paris — the boy who will become Molière and teach France to laugh at itself.
Opechancanough's warriors strike the scattered settlements at dawn — a third of the colony dead in a single morning, trust dead for a century.
The Janissaries murder the young Sultan Osman II — the first Ottoman sultan killed by his own soldiers — for trying to reform them.
Shakespeare's friends publish his collected plays in the First Folio — rescuing eighteen of them, half his work, from oblivion.
The Dutch torture and execute English merchants on Amboyna for a plot that never existed — poisoning Anglo-Dutch friendship for a generation.
Nzinga takes the throne of Ndongo and begins her forty-year defiance of Portuguese slavers — sitting on her servant's back rather than sit lower than a governor.
A Dutch fleet seizes Salvador, Brazil's capital — the shock proves no empire's possessions are safe, and Holland's Brazilian dream begins.
Charles I becomes king of England — handsome, devout, and convinced kings rule by divine right; his quarrels with Parliament begin at once.
Dutch traders buy Manhattan from the Lenape for goods worth sixty guilders — a misunderstanding wrapped in a trade, on an island no one could imagine.
After 120 years of building, the new St. Peter's Basilica is consecrated — the grandest church in Christendom, an ocean of marble and song.
Richelieu's armies ring the Protestant stronghold of La Rochelle and starve it for fourteen months — the Huguenots keep their faith but lose their walls.
Parliament forces Charles I to sign the Petition of Right — no taxes without consent, no arbitrary prison; paper that will outlast the king.
William Harvey publishes his proof that the heart pumps blood around the body in an endless circuit — fourteen centuries of Galen overturned.
The Catholic emperor orders Protestants to return all seized church lands — a victor's overreach that guarantees ten more years of war.
John Winthrop's Puritan fleet lands in Massachusetts Bay — "a city upon a hill," a godly commonwealth the whole world will watch and argue over.
Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden lands in Germany with his modern army — the Lion of the North comes ashore praying, and the Thirty Years' War turns.
Catholic troops sack Magdeburg and massacre twenty thousand — the Thirty Years' War's most infamous atrocity, a city wedded to fire.
Gustavus Adolphus smashes Tilly's undefeated Catholic army at Breitenfeld — volley fire and mobile guns prove the new way of war in an afternoon.
Twenty-five-year-old Rembrandt paints Dr. Tulp's anatomy lesson — and Amsterdam learns his name overnight.
Gustavus Adolphus dies victorious in the fog at Lützen — the Lion of the North falls at thirty-seven, and Protestant Europe mourns.
Six-year-old Christina becomes queen of Sweden — the clever girl who will astonish Europe, argue with Descartes, and abdicate for Rome.
Shah Jahan commissions a marble tomb for his beloved Mumtaz, dead in childbirth — the Taj Mahal begins as stakes and trenches on the Yamuna.
Russian Cossacks found Yakutsk on the Lena River — a log fort in the permafrost from which an empire will reach the Pacific.
The Inquisition forces the old astronomer to kneel and deny that the Earth moves — but the Earth, indifferent to the verdict, keeps moving.
The Catholic armies crush the Swedes at Nördlingen — and France, watching the Habsburgs win everything, decides to enter the war itself.
Richelieu founds the Académie Française — forty immortals to guard the French language, a dictionary as a state project.
A new seclusion edict forbids Japanese to travel abroad — the island nation turns its face inward for two hundred years.
The Puritans found a college in the wilderness to train their ministers — Harvard begins as a bequest, a library, and a clearing in the woods.
Hong Taiji declares his people's new dynastic name — the Great Qing — and claims the Mandate of Heaven eight years before it will be true.
Tulip prices collapse overnight in a Haarlem tavern — the first great market bubble bursts, and Holland laughs, moralizes, and moves on.
René Descartes publishes his Discourse on Method — rebuilding philosophy from a single certain thought: I think, therefore I am.
Catholic peasants rise at Shimabara behind a boy messiah — and the shogunate answers with an army, sealing Japan's closing.
Scots sign the National Covenant in Greyfriars Kirkyard — some in blood — swearing to defend their Presbyterian church against the king.
Murad IV storms Baghdad back from Persia after a forty-day siege — restoring Ottoman power in the east at a terrible price.
The Ottomans and Safavids sign the Treaty of Zuhab — drawing a border that, near enough, still stands today.
Japan expels the Portuguese and closes its doors to nearly all Europeans — a century of contact ends in a single season.
Portuguese nobles rise and crown the Duke of Braganza — ending sixty years of Spanish rule in a single December morning.
Charles I summons the Parliament that will sit for twenty years — and destroy him; England's Parliament stops being the king's instrument.
Barbados planters switch to sugar — and the island's hunger for enslaved labor begins to reshape the Atlantic in chains.
Irish Catholics rise against English settlers in Ulster — and the bloodshed poisons English politics past saving.
King and Parliament meet in battle at Edgehill — an indecisive Sunday slaughter that means the English Civil War will go on.
Rembrandt unveils his great company portrait — the Night Watch, all motion and torchlight, Amsterdam itself marching out of the dark.
Abel Tasman sights Tasmania and New Zealand — the first European eyes on those shores, finding the future and being blamed for it.

t: The Old Man Dies, the Boy Is Born
x: Galileo dies blind at Arcetri in January; that Christmas, Isaac Newton is born in Lincolnshire — the baton passed in the dark.
The twenty-one-year-old Duke of Enghien shatters Spain's famed infantry at Rocroi — ending a century of Spanish battlefield supremacy in a day.
Four-year-old Louis XIV inherits the French throne — the child in the lace collar who will rule for seventy-two years.
Rebels take Beijing, the last Ming emperor hangs himself on Coal Hill — and the Manchu Qing ride through the opened gates.
John Milton publishes his thundering defense of a free press — Parliament ignores it, and the centuries adopt it.
Cromwell's New Model Army destroys the king's forces at Naseby — the decisive battle; the future belongs to the disciplined, not the dashing.
John Milton publishes his first book of poems at thirty-six — L'Allegro, Il Penseroso, Lycidas: the promise of the epic to come.
Charles I surrenders to the Scots — who keep him nine months, then sell him to Parliament for £400,000: a king priced and delivered.
Radical soldiers demand the Agreement of the People — votes for all men, a written constitution; Cromwell crushes it, but the words survive.
The Peace of Westphalia ends the Thirty Years' War — eight million dead, and the birth of the modern state system from the ashes.
Bohdan Khmelnytsky's Cossacks rise against Polish rule — the steppe catches fire, and Ukraine's fateful turn toward Moscow begins.
Semyon Dezhnev sails around the eastern tip of Asia — proving it is not joined to America, in a feat Europe forgets for a century.
Charles I is beheaded outside Whitehall — a king tried by his subjects and executed; England becomes a republic, and the world changes its mind about kings.
Cromwell crushes the Scottish army at Dunbar — outnumbered, sick, and trapped, then victorious by a dawn attack in the rain.
Anne Bradstreet, mother of eight on the Massachusetts frontier, publishes her poems — the first book of verse from the New World.
Dorgon, the Manchu prince-regent who put the Qing boy-emperor on China's throne, dies on a hunting trip — and power shifts behind the palace walls.
The sieges of Drogheda and Wexford in 1650, where Cromwell's campaign turned a war into a wound Ireland carried for centuries.
François Pierre de La Varenne's Le Cuisinier françois made French cooking a written art, changing how the world eats.
Parliament's trade monopoly law that choked Dutch shipping and helped ignite three Anglo-Dutch wars.
London's first coffeehouse opened the age of the "penny universities," where news, science, and revolution were argued over coffee.
England and the Dutch Republic fought the first of three naval wars over trade routes and naval pride.
The Taj Mahal was completed at Agra — a grieving emperor's monument that became the world's most famous building.
Oliver Cromwell dissolved Parliament and ruled as Lord Protector — a republic with a king in everything but name.
Queen Christina of Sweden gave up her throne, converted to Catholicism, and became Europe's most famous exile.
England seized Jamaica from Spain, turning it into the sugar-and-slavery powerhouse of the British Caribbean.
Christiaan Huygens patented the pendulum clock — the first timekeeper accurate enough for science and navigation.
Blaise Pascal's witty Provincial Letters mocked Jesuit casuistry and made theology the talk of Paris.
Fire destroyed most of Edo (Tokyo), killing tens of thousands; the shogunate rebuilt it grander and better planned.
Cromwell's death and his son Richard's collapse ended England's republican experiment within months.
Aurangzeb imprisoned Shah Jahan and seized the Mughal throne in a fratricidal war of succession.
The Treaty of the Pyrenees ended the Franco-Spanish War and made France Europe's dominant power.
Charles II's return ended the republic — theatres reopened, Christmas returned, and the monarchy was restored.

t: The Painter of the Court Dies
x: Diego Velázquez died in Madrid, leaving Las Meninas — a painting that still puzzles and delights every viewer.
Louis XIV seized personal rule after Mazarin's death, beginning the long reign of the Sun King.
Stockholm's bank issued Europe's first banknotes — money became a printed promise rather than metal.
Charles II chartered the Royal Society, and experimental science became a public, shared enterprise.
Blaise Pascal died at thirty-nine, leaving the Pensées — fragments where reason argues for faith.
Barbados's slave code declared enslaved Africans property for life — the legal blueprint for plantation slavery across the Americas.
England seized New Amsterdam bloodlessly and renamed it New York — a small port with an enormous future.
Bubonic plague ravaged London in 1665, emptying the city and killing tens of thousands.
The London Gazette's first issue began England's oldest continuously printed newspaper.
Robert Hooke's Micrographia revealed the microscopic world in stunning detail — the microscope's first bestseller.
The Great Fire of London destroyed most of the medieval city in four days; it was rebuilt in brick and stone.
Colbert founded the Paris Academy of Sciences, giving French scholars royal salaries and laboratories.
Shah Jahan died imprisoned in Agra Fort, gazing across the river at the Taj Mahal he could never visit.
Blind John Milton published Paradise Lost — his epic of Satan, Adam, and the Fall, dictated from memory.
Dutch warships sailed up the Thames, burned English ships, and towed away the flagship — the republic's boldest naval triumph.
The East India Company took Bombay — a swampy Portuguese dowry port destined to become a megacity.
John Dryden became Poet Laureate, bringing his sharp satirical tongue to the Restoration stage.
Rembrandt died poor in Amsterdam, painting self-portraits to the very end — darker, truer, and freer than ever.
After a twenty-one-year siege, Candia fell to the Ottomans and Venice's eastern empire ended.
The Hudson's Bay Company was chartered, and beaver pelts began flowing from frozen forests to London hats.
Charles II secretly promised Louis XIV he would convert to Catholicism — in exchange for French gold.
The buccaneer Henry Morgan sacked and burned Panama City, hauling away its silver — piracy at its grandest and cruelest.
Invaded on all sides, the Dutch flooded their own land to survive — while a Hague mob murdered the de Witt brothers.
Paris got its first coffeehouse, and soon the whole city was arguing philosophy over tiny cups.
Molière collapsed on stage during The Imaginary Invalid and died hours later — comedy's greatest actor exiting mid-performance.
Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad, founding the Maratha kingdom that would humble the mighty Mughals.
Greenwich Observatory was founded to map the heavens and solve the puzzle of longitude at sea.
The Wampanoag sachem Metacom led a desperate uprising that burned New England and destroyed a tenth of its towns.
Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded in Delhi for defending the right to worship — a martyrdom the Sikhs never forgot.
Vermeer died young and poor in Delft, leaving luminous interiors — milkmaids and map-rooms full of northern light.
Bacon's rebels — poor whites and enslaved blacks fighting together — burned Jamestown before the planters crushed and divided them.
Ole Rømer timed Jupiter's moons and proved light travels at a finite speed — fast, but not instantaneous.
Spinoza's Ethics, published after his death, argued God and nature are one — scandalizing every pulpit in Europe.
Antonio Vivaldi was born in Venice — the sickly boy who would make violins sing like weather.
Titus Oates invented a Catholic conspiracy, and panicked London hanged innocent men before the lie collapsed.
Imprisoned tinker John Bunyan published The Pilgrim's Progress — the allegory every English cottage would own.
Parliament's Habeas Corpus Act forbade imprisonment without charge — a leash on arbitrary power, written into law.
Denis Papin built his steam digester — a rattling pressure cooker carrying the future of engines.
Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya tax on non-Muslims, and the Mughal empire's old tolerance began to crack.
Popé led the Pueblo peoples in revolt, driving the Spanish from Santa Fe for twelve years.
Gian Lorenzo Bernini died in Rome — the sculptor who made marble breathe and stone fly.
William Penn founded Pennsylvania as a colony promising religious freedom to all comers.
The Canal du Midi opened, joining the Atlantic to the Mediterranean across southern France.
La Salle reached the Mississippi's mouth and claimed the entire vast basin for Louis XIV.
The Ottomans besieged Vienna until Polish lancers broke them at the Kahlenberg — and Europe exhaled.
Legend says Viennese bakers invented the crescent roll to mock the defeated Ottoman crescent — victory you can eat.
Qing admiral Shi Lang conquered Taiwan, completing Kangxi's China from the steppe to the sea.
Jean-Philippe Rameau was born in Dijon — the organist who would write the rulebook of Western harmony.
Antoine Watteau was born — the painter of fêtes galantes, elegant parties that never quite happened.
Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, and hundreds of thousands of Huguenots fled — carrying their skills abroad.
Bach and Handel were born weeks apart in Germany — one for the church organ, one for the world's stage.
Domenico Scarlatti was born in Naples — the keyboard acrobat who would write 555 sonatas.
James II took the throne; Monmouth's rebellion was crushed at Sedgemoor, and the Bloody Assizes hanged the rest.
Daniel Fahrenheit was born in Danzig — the man who would put numbers on hot and cold.
Lully struck his own foot with his conducting staff; the wound festered, and France's musical dictator died of gangrene.
William of Orange landed, James II fled, and Parliament remade the monarchy — the Glorious Revolution.
Aphra Behn, England's first professional woman writer, published the antislavery tale Oroonoko.
Edward Lloyd's coffeehouse became the sailors' and insurers' haunt — the seed of Lloyd's of London.
Alexander Pope was born in London — the sickly boy who would sharpen English verse to a razor's edge.
The Empress Dowager Xiaozhuang died — the steady grandmother's hand behind Kangxi's throne.
Parliament's Bill of Rights barred Catholic kings and standing armies — the contract that made monarchs answerable.
John Locke's Two Treatises argued governments exist only by the people's consent — the pamphlet that would arm two revolutions.
China and Russia signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk, drawing a Siberian border with Jesuits translating between empires.
Peter the Great seized the throne from his sister Sophia and began dragging Russia toward the sea.
Bashō set out on his long walk to Japan's deep north; the travel diary became Japan's most beloved journey.
Locke's Essay argued the mind is a blank slate — experience writes everything on it.
William III smashed James II at the Boyne — a battle Irish Protestants would commemorate for three centuries.
Job Charnock planted the East India Company's flag on the Hooghly mudflats — a trading post that became an empire's capital.
Hysteria gripped Salem Village; twenty were executed for witchcraft before the colony came to its senses.
An earthquake dropped Jamaica's pirate haven of Port Royal into the sea — half the city drowned in minutes.
A royal charter founded the College of William and Mary in Virginia — the South's first seat of learning.
The Bank of England was founded to fund a war with France — and it has never stopped funding things since.
François-Marie Arouet was born in Paris — Voltaire, the sharpest pen the Enlightenment would ever hold.
Matsuo Bashō died on the road in Osaka, leaving haiku that fit the whole world into seventeen syllables.
Henry Purcell died at thirty-six; England buried its greatest composer in Westminster Abbey.
Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, the nun-scholar of New Spain, died — her library sold off, her voice stilled by the church.
Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was born in Venice — the last great painter of ceilings full of sky.
Canaletto was born in Venice; his crisp canal scenes would hang in every English country house.
William Hogarth was born in London — the engraver who would roast the city's gin, greed, and rakes.
Charles Perrault published his fairy tales — Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots — and childhood got its classics.
Peter the Great toured Europe in disguise, working as a ship's carpenter to learn how navies are built.
The Treaty of Ryswick ended nine years of war; Louis XIV kept Strasbourg and swallowed the slight.
Thomas Savery patented a steam pump to drain mines — the first engine sold to do work with fire and water.
Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur — baptized Sikhs in steel bracelets and uncut hair, sworn to justice.
The Treaty of Karlowitz rolled back the Ottomans; Hungary returned to Christendom after a century and a half.
Charles II of Spain died heirless, and every crown in Europe reached for his empire.
Charles XII of Sweden routed Peter's army at Narva in a blizzard — the boy-king's most dazzling victory.
The Elector of Brandenburg crowned himself King in Prussia — a small title with enormous ambitions.
Osei Tutu united the Asante beneath the Golden Stool, and a gold-rich kingdom rose in the forest.
Captain Kidd was hanged at Wapping for piracy — the treasure-hunter turned into a cautionary tale.
Connecticut ministers founded a college at New Haven to keep the ministry orthodox — it became Yale.
Parliament settled the crown on Protestant heirs — the law that still chooses Britain's monarchs.
Jethro Tull invented the seed drill, sowing in neat rows instead of scattering — farming's quiet revolution.
Anne took the throne — the last Stuart, gouty, grieving seventeen lost children, and stubborn as an oak.
The Daily Courant became England's first daily newspaper — news every morning, forever after.
France and the Grand Alliance went to war over Spain's empty throne — a world war before the world knew the phrase.
Peter founded his new capital on a Baltic swamp — a window to the West built on bones.
The worst storm in British history sank fleets and flattened towns; Daniel Defoe rode out to interview the survivors.
Forty-seven rōnin avenged their murdered lord, then accepted death — loyalty's most famous arithmetic.
Marlborough and Eugène smashed the French at Blenheim, saving Vienna and shattering Louis XIV's aura of invincibility.
Jonathan Swift's savage satire on religious excess appeared — anonymous, brilliant, and never forgiven.
Maria Sibylla Merian published her great book on Suriname's insects — a woman artist-scientist alone in the tropics.
Edmond Halley predicted the great comet of 1682 would return in 1758 — staking his name on the sky's schedule.
Marlborough routed the French at Ramillies, and the Spanish Netherlands fell like dominoes.
England and Scotland united into Great Britain — one parliament, one flag, and endless argument.
Aurangzeb died at eighty-eight in the Deccan, his empire at its largest — and already cracking apart.
The San José exploded off Cartagena, carrying a king's ransom in silver down to the seabed.
Peter crushed Charles XII at Poltava; Sweden's empire ended, and Russia's began.
The coldest winter in living memory froze rivers, split trees, and starved a continent.
The bloodiest battle of the age: the Allies won the field at Malplaquet and lost their stomach for the war.
Meissen cracked the secret of hard porcelain — Europe could finally make its own china.
Wren's St Paul's Cathedral was finished, its dome rising where the Great Fire's ashes fell.
George Frideric Handel arrived in London, and would give England its anthems, oratorios, and water music.
The South Sea Company was chartered to trade with Spanish America — and mostly to gamble on it.
Addison and Steele launched The Spectator, teaching London how to be witty and polite over coffee.
Thomas Newcomen's steam engine started pumping at a Staffordshire mine — the Industrial Revolution's first breath.
The Treaty of Utrecht ended the great war; Britain took Gibraltar, Nova Scotia, and the slave-trade contract.
Arcangelo Corelli died in Rome — the violinist whose concertos taught Europe how strings should sing.
Parliament offered £20,000 to whoever could find longitude at sea — the richest puzzle in navigation.
George I of Hanover took the throne, speaking little English and trusting his ministers — Parliament's quiet gain.
Louis XIV died after seventy-two years on the throne; France was glorious, exhausted, and bankrupt.
A hurricane scattered Spain's treasure fleet off Florida; divers and pirates raced each other for the silver.
Jacobites rose for the exiled Stuarts; the rebellion fizzled, but the songs last forever.
John Law founded his bank in Paris, and paper money's grandest experiment began.
Handel's Water Music drifted down the Thames behind the king's barge — the river became a concert hall.
Four London lodges united as the first Grand Lodge — Freemasonry stepped into the open.
Lieutenant Maynard cornered Blackbeard at Ocracoke; the pirate died with five shots and twenty sword-cuts in him.
Bienville founded New Orleans on a Mississippi crescent — a French port in a swamp of mosquitoes.
Daniel Defoe published the castaway's tale — the novel England will never stop reading.
The South Sea Bubble popped; fortunes vanished in a week, and the whole mad game was outlawed.
Anne Bonny and Mary Read stood trial in Jamaica — pirates who fought as fiercely as any man, and said so in court.
The Treaty of Nystad ended the Great Northern War; Russia was an empire now, and Sweden a memory of one.
Bartholomew Roberts, the most successful pirate of the age, died in battle off Africa — the golden age of piracy died with him.
Peter the Great died at fifty-two, leaving Russia an empire, a navy, and a city raised from a swamp.
Bach in Leipzig, writing a new cantata nearly every week — music his own congregation barely noticed, though the traveler did.
Peter the Great's Academy of Sciences opens in St. Petersburg, and Russia starts studying the world in earnest.
Jonathan Swift publishes Gulliver's Travels, and London laughs at tiny emperors and giant fools without seeing itself in the mirror.
Twenty-year-old Benjamin Franklin returns from London to Philadelphia, broke but burning to make his mark.

t: The Man Who Weighed the Stars, Laid to Rest
x: Isaac Newton is buried in Westminster Abbey like a king, and the age of reason mourns the man who gave it its laws.
Eliza Smith publishes The Compleat Housewife, a book of recipes and remedies for every working kitchen in England.

t: The Sailor Who Found the Strait
x: Vitus Bering sails the icy strait between Asia and America and puts it on the map.
Franklin buys a struggling Philadelphia newspaper and turns it into the colonies' sharpest voice.

t: The Terrible Joke That Told the Truth
x: Swift's Modest Proposal suggests starving Irish families sell their children as food — a savage joke that shames England's real cruelty.

t: The Potter Who Made the World Beautiful
x: Josiah Wedgwood is born in Staffordshire, the boy who will turn common clay into art and build a fortune on it.

t: The Library That Opened Its Doors
x: Franklin and his friends pool their private books to found America's first lending library.

t: The Boy Born on the Farm
x: George Washington is born on a Virginia plantation, the first son of a modest planter — nobody dreaming what he will become.
Franklin begins publishing Poor Richard's Almanac, a yearly book of weather, jokes, and proverbs for plain country folk.
John Kay's flying shuttle doubles the weaver's speed — the machines begin to quicken, and nothing will slow them down.
Enslaved Africans seize the island of St. John and hold it for months before the planters crush them.
Jonathan Edwards' thundering sermons set New England ablaze with the Great Awakening.

t: The Man Who Named Every Living Thing
x: Carl Linnaeus publishes Systema Naturae, giving every plant and animal its two Latin names.

t: The Young Emperor Takes the Throne
x: The Qianlong Emperor takes the throne in Beijing, beginning sixty years of China's greatest wealth and power.
Franklin founds the Union Fire Company — neighbors banding together with buckets against the flames.

t: The Clock That Found the Way
x: John Harrison's sea clock survives its ocean trial, promising sailors their true position at sea at last.
Bankrupt and broken in health, Handel abandons Italian opera and turns toward the oratorio.
John Wesley's conversion at Aldersgate Chapel launches the Methodist movement.

t: The Salons Where Ideas Caught Fire
x: In candlelit Paris drawing rooms, brilliant hostesses set philosophers arguing and all Paris listening.
Enslaved men rise at Stono, South Carolina, marching for freedom in Spanish Florida before they are cut down.
Captain Coram wins his royal charter for a hospital to shelter London's abandoned babies.
