Frederick the Great takes the Prussian throne — a flute-playing warrior who will forge Prussia into a great power.

t: The Young Queen Who Would Not Bow
x: Twenty-three-year-old Maria Theresa inherits the Austrian empire, and every neighbor reaches for a piece of it — but she will not bow.

t: The Voyage That Cost the Captain His Life
x: Bering sights Alaska, then dies of scurvy on the barren island that will bear his name.
Jethro Tull dies, leaving the seed drill that taught farmers to sow in straight, thrifty rows.

t: The Hallelujah That Shook the Hall
x: Handel's Messiah premieres in Dublin, and legend says the king himself stood for the great Hallelujah chorus.
Anders Celsius proposes his hundred-degree scale, and heat learns to speak in numbers.
Thomas Jefferson is born in Virginia — the awkward boy who will write the words of a revolution.

t: The Last King to Lead His Men
x: George II charges at Dettingen — the last British monarch to lead his troops into battle.

t: The Girl Who Grew Blue Gold
x: Twenty-two-year-old Eliza Lucas perfects indigo in South Carolina, dyeing her colony's fortune blue.
Bonnie Prince Charlie lands in Scotland, and the Highlands rise for the Stuarts one last time.

t: The Seamstress Who Ruled the Court
x: Jeanne Poisson becomes Madame de Pompadour — the king's mistress and the maker of French taste.

t: The Last Battle on British Soil
x: At Culloden the Jacobite dream dies in the rain, and the Highland clans are broken forever.

t: A College Rises in the Pines
x: The College of New Jersey is founded in the wilderness — the school that will become Princeton.

t: The Cook Who Wrote It Down
x: Hannah Glasse's Art of Cookery teaches England's kitchens to roast, bake, and feast.

t: The Book That Taught Kings to Fear
x: Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws argues that liberty lives only where power is divided.

t: The Peace That Pleased No One
x: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ends a war and satisfies nobody — planting the seeds of the next one.
Henry Fielding's Tom Jones makes the novel the people's art — funny, bawdy, and full of life.
Diderot is locked in Vincennes for his daring writings, and all Paris takes his side.
Bach dies in Leipzig, blind and half-forgotten; his music will sleep for eighty years before the world wakes to it.
An unknown Rousseau wins a prize for asking whether progress has corrupted mankind.

t: The Book That Held All Knowledge
x: Diderot's Encyclopédie begins to appear volume by volume, blessing and scandalizing France.

t: The Bell That Would Ring for Freedom
x: A great bell is hung in Philadelphia's State House tower, not yet knowing the name it will one day earn.
Franklin flies his kite in a thunderstorm and proves lightning is electricity — taming the sky's fire.

t: The Year That Lost Eleven Days
x: Britain adopts the new calendar, and sleepers wake to find eleven days simply gone.
The British Museum is founded, opening its treasures to any curious visitor, free of charge.

t: The Young Officer in the Wilderness
x: Twenty-one-year-old Washington carries a warning through the winter snows to the French forts.

t: The First Shot of a World War
x: Washington's men fire on French soldiers at Jumonville Glen — the first shot of a world war.

t: A King's College in New York
x: A college chartered by the king opens in New York — the seed of what will become Columbia.

t: The Day the Earth Shook the Faith
x: An earthquake swallows Lisbon on All Saints' Day, and philosophers ask how a good God allows it.
Samuel Johnson's Dictionary fixes the English language between two covers — nine years in the making.

t: The Child Who Heard Music in Everything
x: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart is born in Salzburg, and music will never be the same again.

t: The War That Swallowed the World
x: The Seven Years' War erupts — the first war fought on nearly every continent and ocean.

t: The Battle That Bought an Empire
x: Clive wins at Plassey, and a mere trading company begins to swallow a subcontinent.

t: The Knife That Missed the King
x: Damiens scratches Louis XV with a penknife and is torn apart for it, to Voltaire's horror.

t: The Comet That Kept Its Appointment
x: Halley's comet returns on schedule — proof that the heavens run like clockwork.
The British take Louisbourg, breaking French sea power in the Atlantic.
Wolfe and Montcalm both die before Quebec, and Canada passes to Britain.

t: The Laugh That Mocked the World
x: Voltaire's Candide skewers priests, philosophers, and optimists in one merry tale.
Tacky leads enslaved rebels in Jamaica's great uprising; the planters drown it in blood.

t: The Young King Takes the Crown
x: George III ascends at twenty-two, determined to rule as well as reign.
Ahmad Shah Durrani crushes the Marathas at Panipat in one of history's bloodiest days.

t: The Day the World Watched the Sun
x: Astronomers across the globe time Venus crossing the sun to measure the size of the heavens.

t: The German Princess Who Became Russia
x: Catherine seizes the throne from her feeble husband and begins her long, brilliant reign.

t: The Book That Said Man Is Born Free
x: Rousseau's Social Contract declares that rightful rule rests on nothing but the people's will.

t: The Peace That Redrew the Map
x: The Treaty of Paris ends the world war; France loses an empire and Britain gains one.
Pontiac's warriors rise against the British forts, and the frontier burns from Detroit to the Ohio.

t: The Jenny That Spun Eight Threads
x: Hargreaves' spinning jenny lets one worker spin eight threads at once.
Beccaria's On Crimes and Punishments denounces torture and the death penalty.
The Stamp Act taxes every colonial paper and document, and America learns to say no together.

t: The First Restaurant Opens Its Doors
x: Boulanger hangs his sign in Paris, and the pleasure of dining out is born.
Henry Cavendish bottles hydrogen, the lightest stuff in the world, and names it inflammable air.

t: The Tax Repealed, the Claim Kept
x: Parliament repeals the Stamp Act but declares it may bind America in all cases whatsoever.

t: The Empress Who Wrote the Law
x: Catherine's Nakaz instructs her lawmakers in enlightenment, and all Europe reads it.

t: The Taxes on Tea and Glass
x: The Townshend Acts tax colonial imports, and boycotts spread from Boston to Charleston.

t: The Ship That Sailed for the Stars
x: Cook's Endeavour departs to watch Venus cross the sun, then to hunt the great southern continent.
Philip Astley opens his riding ring in London, and the modern circus is born.
James Watt patents his improved steam engine, and the world begins to run on steam.
Arkwright's water frame spins thread by waterpower, and the factory age dawns.

t: The Snow, the Shots, the Five Dead
x: British soldiers fire on a Boston mob; five lie dead, and the colonies have their martyrs.
Ludwig van Beethoven is born in Bonn — the boy who will make music roar like thunder.
The first Encyclopaedia Britannica is completed — three stout volumes of useful knowledge.

t: The Slave Who Sued for Freedom
x: Lord Mansfield's Somerset ruling frees an enslaved man and shakes the whole slave trade.

t: The Country Carved Like a Cake
x: Russia, Prussia, and Austria carve up Poland among themselves in the first partition.
Disguised as Mohawks, Bostonians heave British tea into the harbor.
Phillis Wheatley's poems are published in London — genius in chains that shames her masters.

t: The Library of Ten Thousand Books
x: Qianlong commands the Siku Quanshu, gathering all Chinese learning into one vast library.

t: The Congress That Dared to Meet
x: Delegates from twelve colonies gather in Philadelphia to answer Britain with a single voice.

t: The Sorrows of the Young Romantic
x: Goethe's Werther makes heartbreak fashionable, and young men weep across Europe.

t: The Shot Heard Round the World
x: At Lexington and Concord, farmers fire on redcoats, and the war for independence begins.
Pugachev's great peasant rebellion is crushed, and Catherine's age of mercy comes to an end.
In a sweltering hall, fifty-six men sign a declaration that all men are created equal.

t: The Book That Set the Market Free
x: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations argues that free hands bake more bread than commanded ones.
Cook sails on his third voyage, seeking the Northwest Passage, never to return.
Burgoyne surrenders at Saratoga, and France decides America might win after all.

t: The Winter That Forged an Army
x: At Valley Forge the Continental Army starves, freezes, and learns to be soldiers.
Voltaire and Rousseau die within weeks of each other; the Enlightenment buries its prophets.

t: The Islands in the Middle of the Sea
x: Cook names them the Sandwich Islands — paradise found at the very heart of the ocean.

t: The Captain Who Did Not Come Home
x: In a quarrel over a stolen boat, Hawaiians kill Cook on the beach at Kealakekua.
The world's first iron bridge rises over the Severn — an arch of fire-forged metal.

t: The General Who Sold His Name
x: Benedict Arnold's treason is unmasked, and his name becomes the word for traitor.

t: The Siege That Ended the War
x: Washington and the French trap Cornwallis at Yorktown, and Britain's American war is lost.

t: The Ship That Threw Men Overboard
x: The Zong's crew drowns 142 enslaved Africans for the insurance money, and England is sickened.

t: The Musician Who Found a New World
x: Organist William Herschel spots Uranus — the first new planet in recorded history.

t: The Engine That Learned to Turn
x: Watt patents the rotary steam engine, giving factories a wheel that never tires.
Rodney smashes the French fleet at the Saintes, and Britain keeps its sugar islands.
Mahadji Scindia forces the British to the peace table at Salbai, and Maratha power rises again.

t: The Peace That Made a Nation
x: The Treaty of Paris recognizes American independence; a new nation steps onto the stage.

t: The General Who Laid Down His Sword
x: Washington resigns his commission — a victorious general surrendering power of his own will.

t: The Brothers Who Taught Fire to Fly
x: The Montgolfiers' hot-air balloon rises over France, and mankind leaves the ground.

t: The Barber Who Mocked the Count
x: Beaumarchais' Marriage of Figaro laughs at aristocrats, and revolution laughs with it.
David paints three brothers swearing to die for Rome, and the coming revolution finds its favorite picture.
Cartwright's power loom weaves by steam, and the handloom weavers' doom is sealed.

t: The Necklace That Ruined a Queen
x: The diamond necklace scandal blackens Marie Antoinette's name beyond repair.

t: The Farmers Who Shut the Courts
x: Debt-crushed farmers follow Daniel Shays against the courts, frightening the nation into a stronger union.

t: The Summer That Wrote the Rules
x: Behind closed doors, the Constitutional Convention writes America's frame of government.

t: The Committee That Said No More
x: Twelve men, Quakers and Anglicans together, found the society to abolish the slave trade.
The First Fleet lands its convicts at Botany Bay, and European Australia begins.

t: The Captain Who Never Came Home
x: La Pérouse's expedition vanishes in the Pacific, and France waits decades for word.

t: The Fortress That Fell in a Day
x: The Bastille falls to the Paris mob on July 14th, and the old order trembles.

t: The Rights of Man, Written Down
x: The Declaration of the Rights of Man proclaims liberty, equality, and fraternity.

t: The First President Takes the Oath
x: Washington is sworn in on a balcony, and the great republican experiment begins.

t: The Money That Built a Nation
x: Hamilton's financial plan founds the bank, the mint, and America's credit.

t: The Book That Defended the Old Order
x: Edmund Burke's Reflections warns that revolution devours its children.
The Bill of Rights is ratified — ten amendments guarding the citizen from the state.

t: The Night the Cane Fields Burned
x: Enslaved Africans rise in Haiti, and the greatest slave revolt in history begins.
Mozart dies at thirty-five, his last mass half-written, and Vienna weeps.
Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication claims reason and rights for women as well as men.
The monarchy falls and France declares itself a republic, one and indivisible.

t: The Guillotine Falls on a King
x: Louis XVI is guillotined in the Place de la Révolution as the crowd watches in silence.
Qianlong dismisses Britain's Macartney embassy; China needs nothing from the West.

t: The Woman Who Wrote Women's Rights
x: Olympe de Gouges, author of the Rights of Woman, is guillotined by the revolution she served.
Twenty-four-year-old Napoleon retakes Toulon with his artillery, and France notices him.
Robespierre is guillotined, and the Terror ends with its architect's head in the basket.
Lavoisier, father of modern chemistry, is executed; France loses its finest mind.
Eli Whitney's cotton gin makes cotton king and chains millions more to the fields.
The Directory takes power — five directors steering a tired, bloody republic.
A country doctor scratches cowpox into a boy's arm, and smallpox begins its long defeat.
Twenty-six-year-old Napoleon outruns and outfights Austria's armies across Italy.
Britain's sailors mutiny for better pay and bread, and the mighty navy must listen.

t: The General Who Sailed for the Pyramids
x: Napoleon lands in Egypt with soldiers and scholars, wins at the Pyramids, and strands his army.
Wolfe Tone's United Irishmen rise against British rule and are crushed; Ireland's hope goes underground.

t: The Coup of the Eighteenth Brumaire
x: Napoleon overthrows the Directory at bayonet point, and the revolution ends in one man's hands.
Washington dies at Mount Vernon, and a young nation mourns the father it cannot replace.
The government moves into a half-built capital on the Potomac — all mud and marble dreams.

t: The Pile That Made Lightning Obey
x: Alessandro Volta stacks metal discs and makes the first battery, bottling electricity at last.
John Adams becomes the first president to live in the unfinished White House in 1800, blessing a half-built house that would grow into a nation's home.
In 1800, enslaved blacksmith Gabriel Prosser's planned march on Richmond collapses after betrayal and a storm; he is hanged, but the dream of freedom doesn't die with him.
At Marengo in 1800, General Desaix's last-minute evening charge snatches Napoleon victory from certain defeat, costing Desaix his life.
The Act of Union of 1800 joins Ireland to Great Britain under one parliament, a paper unity that Ireland never accepted and that fueled a century of resistance.
Britain's first census in 1801 counts over ten million people, the first time a nation counted its living population rather than its armies.
At Copenhagen in 1801, Admiral Nelson raises his telescope to his blind eye to ignore the recall signal, then destroys the Danish fleet.
Toussaint Louverture, the formerly enslaved Black general who freed Saint-Domingue, writes Haiti's 1801 constitution and names himself governor for life, openly defying Napoleon.
The Treaty of Amiens in 1802 gives war-weary Europe one brief year of peace between Britain and Napoleonic France before the fighting resumes.
Nguyen Anh defeats his last rivals in 1802, takes the name Gia Long, and unites Vietnam under a single imperial throne.
Napoleon betrays Toussaint Louverture with false peace talks in 1802, ships him to die in a French mountain prison — but Haiti's revolution fights on without him.
Napoleon's 1803 sale of the Louisiana Territory doubles the size of the United States overnight for fifteen million dollars — the greatest land bargain in history.
Lewis and Clark's Corps of Discovery sets out in 1803 to map the Louisiana Purchase from the Missouri to the Pacific, opening the American West.
Robert Emmet's 1803 Dublin rising collapses in a day, but his speech from the dock before his execution makes him Ireland's immortal rebel.
Arthur Wellesley's vastly outnumbered British army crushes the Marathas at Assaye in 1803, tightening Britain's grip on India and making his reputation.
On January 1, 1804, Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares Haiti independent — the first nation in history founded by a successful slave revolt.
In 1804 the Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio launches his jihad in Hausaland, founding the Sokoto Caliphate that will rule millions across West Africa.
In 1804 Karađorđe leads the Serbs in revolt against Ottoman rule, the first spark of the Balkan national independence movements.
Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 unifies French law under one book — and outlives every battle he ever fought, still shaping legal systems worldwide.

t: The Albanian Who Made Modern Egypt
x: Muhammad Ali seizes power in Egypt in 1805 and begins forging a modern state — schools, factories, and a European-style army.
At Trafalgar in 1805 Nelson destroys the combined French and Spanish fleets, securing British naval supremacy — and dies of a sniper's wound in the hour of victory.
Napoleon crushes the Austrian and Russian armies at Austerlitz in December 1805 — his most tactically perfect victory, fought in a single winter day.
Explorer Mungo Park drowns in the Niger rapids in 1806 on his second expedition, and Africa's interior keeps its secrets a while longer.

t: An Empire a Thousand Years Old Ends
x: In 1806 Napoleon dissolves the thousand-year-old Holy Roman Empire, and Francis II becomes simply Emperor of Austria — Germany's map is redrawn forever.
At Jena-Auerstedt in 1806 Napoleon's army destroys the famed Prussian military machine in a single day, and French troops march into Berlin.
After twenty years of William Wilberforce's campaigning, Parliament abolishes the slave trade across the British Empire in 1807.
Napoleon and Tsar Alexander I meet on a raft at Tilsit in 1807 and divide Europe's future between them.

t: The Steamboat That Beat the River
x: Robert Fulton's steamboat Clermont powers up the Hudson in 1807, proving steam can beat wind and current — the age of steam travel begins.
In 1807 Humphry Davy uses electric current to isolate potassium from potash, opening the age of electrochemistry and a flood of new elements.
The United States bans the importation of enslaved Africans in 1808 — but slavery itself continues and grows within the country.
In 1808 Sydney's military officers arrest Governor Bligh in Australia's only military coup — the Rum Rebellion, fought over the rum trade.
On May 2, 1808, the people of Madrid rise against French occupation with knives and stones, igniting the brutal Peninsular War.
In December 1808 Beethoven premieres his Fifth and Sixth Symphonies in a single freezing four-hour concert in Vienna.

t: Two Giants Born on One Day
x: On February 12, 1809, Abraham Lincoln is born in a Kentucky log cabin and Charles Darwin in an English manor — two lives that would each change the world.
Napoleon defeats Austria at Wagram in 1809 in one of the bloodiest battles yet fought, then seals the peace by marrying into the Habsburg family.
In 1809 Jean-Baptiste Lamarck publishes the first theory of evolution — wrong in its mechanism, but daring in its central idea that life changes over generations.
In May 1810 Buenos Aires throws off Spanish rule in the May Revolution, launching South America's wars of liberation.

t: The French Marshal Who Became a King
x: In 1810 Sweden elects Napoleon's marshal Bernadotte as crown prince; he founds the Bernadotte dynasty that still reigns in Sweden today.
On September 16, 1810, Father Miguel Hidalgo rings his church bell at Dolores and cries out for Mexican independence, igniting the war against Spain.
In 1811 starving English weavers begin smashing the factory machines they blame for their misery, giving the world the word "Luddite."
In 1811 Paraguay quietly breaks from Spain and becomes South America's first lasting independent republic.
William Henry Harrison's troops defeat Tecumseh's confederacy at Tippecanoe in 1811, breaking organized Native resistance in the Old Northwest.
The United States declares war on Britain in 1812 over impressment and trade, beginning three years of fighting on land and sea.
In June 1812 Napoleon invades Russia with a Grand Army of six hundred thousand men — the greatest invasion Europe had ever seen.
Napoleon captures a burning, empty Moscow in 1812, then retreats through the Russian winter that destroys his Grand Army.

t: Fairy Tales for a Dark Time
x: In 1812 the Brothers Grimm publish their first collection of folk tales, preserving Cinderella, Snow White, and the world's great fairy tales.
Jane Austen publishes Pride and Prejudice in 1813, and Elizabeth Bennet becomes one of literature's most beloved heroines.
Oliver Hazard Perry destroys the British fleet on Lake Erie in 1813, the first time a full British squadron ever surrendered to Americans.
At Leipzig in 1813 half a million men fight the Battle of the Nations, and Napoleon's empire in Germany collapses.
Defeated on all sides in 1814, Napoleon abdicates at Fontainebleau and sails into exile on the island of Elba.
Norway writes one of the world's freest constitutions at Eidsvoll in 1814, though the great powers then force it into union with Sweden.
In August 1814 British troops march into Washington and burn the White House and the Capitol — the only foreign capture of America's capital.
Europe's rulers gather at the Congress of Vienna in 1814 to redraw the map after Napoleon, waltzing while they trade nations.
Two weeks after the War of 1812's peace treaty is signed, Andrew Jackson's riflemen crush the British at New Orleans — a battle fought after the war was over.

t: The Mountain That Darkened the World
x: Mount Tambora erupts in April 1815 in the largest volcanic explosion in recorded history, and its ash will chill the entire planet.
On June 18, 1815, Wellington and Blücher crush Napoleon at Waterloo, ending twenty years of Napoleonic war.

t: Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death
x: Tambora's ash veils the sun in 1816, the Year Without a Summer — crops fail worldwide and famine stalks the globe.

t: A Monster Dreamed by a Lake
x: Trapped indoors by the cold summer of 1816, eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley dreams up Frankenstein during a ghost-story contest at Lake Geneva.
In July 1816 the congress at Tucumán declares the United Provinces of South America independent of Spain.

t: Digging the Ditch to the West
x: Ground breaks on the Erie Canal in 1817 — a 363-mile hand-dug waterway that will tie the American frontier to the sea.
In 1817 Simón Bolívar establishes Angostura on the Orinoco as his revolutionary capital and rallies the South American liberation.
In 1817 Andrew Jackson invades Spanish Florida pursuing Seminoles, seizing forts and breaking Spain's hold on the peninsula.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein is published in 1818, giving the world the modern monster — and inventing science fiction.
José de San Martín's crushing victory at Maipú in April 1818 ends Spanish rule in Chile for good.
Shaka's disciplined regiments triumph at Gqokli Hill in 1818, and the Zulu kingdom rises over southern Africa.
Illinois becomes the twenty-first American state in 1818, and settlers pour onto the tall-grass prairie.
Stamford Raffles founds Singapore as a free-trade British port in 1819 — the seed of a future great city.
In August 1819 cavalry charges a peaceful crowd demanding voting reform at St. Peter's Field, Manchester — eleven die in the Peterloo Massacre.
In 1819 young King Kamehameha II breaks the sacred kapu taboos, and Hawaii's ancient religion collapses within a season.
In 1820 sealers and explorers glimpse Antarctica's icy coast — the last continent discovered by humanity.
The Missouri Compromise of 1820 draws a line across the West — slavery permitted below it, banned above — postponing America's reckoning.
In 1820 a farmer on the Greek island of Melos digs up the armless marble Venus, now one of the Louvre's great treasures.
Florence Nightingale is born in Florence in 1820 — the girl who will one day carry a lamp through the wards of war and found modern nursing.
In 1821 the Greeks revolt against four centuries of Ottoman rule, beginning a war of independence that captures Europe's imagination.
Napoleon dies on St. Helena in May 1821, alone on his Atlantic rock, dictating the legend of himself to the very end.
After eleven years of war, Mexico wins independence in 1821 and Iturbide enters Mexico City in triumph.
In 1822 freed American slaves land on the West African coast to found the colony that will become Liberia.
Denmark Vesey's planned 1822 slave uprising in Charleston is betrayed; he is hanged, and the South tightens its slave codes in fear.
On September 7, 1822, Prince Dom Pedro shouts "Independence or death!" by the Ipiranga River, and Brazil breaks from Portugal.
In 1822 Jean-François Champollion deciphers the Rosetta Stone's hieroglyphs, and ancient Egypt begins to speak again after fourteen silent centuries.
Agustín de Iturbide's short-lived Mexican empire collapses in 1823, and Mexico becomes a republic.
In 1823 President Monroe warns Europe to stay out of the Americas — the Monroe Doctrine, backed by British sea power.
In 1824 Britain invades Burma, beginning the long carving-up of Southeast Asia by colonial powers.
Totally deaf, Beethoven conducts the 1824 premiere of his Ninth Symphony and its Ode to Joy — music's great hymn to brotherhood.
At Ayacucho in December 1824 Sucre destroys the last Spanish army in South America — three centuries of rule, finished.

t: The Prince Who Defied an Empire
x: In 1825 Prince Diponegoro launches the Java War against Dutch rule — five years of guerrilla warfare, the costliest colonial war of its age.
In 1825 Upper Peru declares independence and names itself Bolivia after Simón Bolívar — a nation named for a living liberator.
In September 1825 Stephenson's Locomotion No. 1 hauls the first public railway train on the Stockton and Darlington line — the railway age begins.
In December 1825 young Russian officers rise for a constitution in St. Petersburg; the Decembrist revolt is crushed and its leaders hanged or exiled.
Starving Missolonghi falls to the Turks in 1826, and its doomed midnight breakout becomes Greece's sacred national legend.

t: Two Founders Die on the Fourth
x: On July 4, 1826 — fifty years to the day after independence — John Adams and Thomas Jefferson die within hours of each other.
In 1826 Niépce fixes the first permanent photograph — a blurry rooftop view exposed for eight hours — and the age of captured light begins.
In 1827 Georg Ohm publishes his law of electric current — V=IR — the quiet foundation of the entire electrical age.
In the 1820s Hongi Hika's musket-armed warriors sweep New Zealand's North Island in the bloodiest of the Musket Wars.
In October 1827 the allied British, French, and Russian fleets annihilate the Ottoman navy at Navarino, sealing Greek independence.
Noah Webster publishes his American Dictionary in 1828, giving American English its own spelling and swagger.
Shaka is murdered by his half-brothers in 1828, but the Zulu kingdom he built marches on.

t: Old Hickory Takes the White House
x: Andrew Jackson wins the presidency in 1828, bringing the frontier and the common man to power in America.
The Catholic Emancipation Act of 1829 lets Catholics sit in Parliament, ending three centuries of political exclusion in Britain.
Stephenson's Rocket wins the 1829 Rainhill Trials at thirty miles an hour — the locomotive has definitively arrived.

t: Dots That Let the Blind Read
x: In 1829 blind fifteen-year-old Louis Braille publishes his raised-dot alphabet, opening books to blind readers forever.
Paris rises in the July Revolution of 1830 — three glorious days that topple Charles X and crown the "citizen king" Louis-Philippe.
The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens in 1830 — the world's first true intercity passenger railway.
Brussels revolts against Dutch rule in 1830, and Belgium declares itself an independent kingdom.
Victor Hugo publishes Notre-Dame de Paris in 1831, and his hunchbacked bell-ringer saves both a novel and a cathedral.
Nat Turner leads enslaved rebels through Southampton County, Virginia, in 1831; the revolt is crushed and the South's slave codes harden.
In 1831 Michael Faraday discovers electromagnetic induction — the principle behind every generator and motor of the electric age.
On December 27, 1831, young Charles Darwin boards HMS Beagle for the five-year voyage that will seed On the Origin of Species.
The Great Reform Act of 1832 sweeps away rotten boroughs and extends the vote to the middle class — the first great widening of British democracy.
Sauk chief Black Hawk's doomed 1832 resistance ends in slaughter on the Mississippi, opening the prairie to white settlement.

t: The Lion of the Desert Rises
x: In 1832 Abd al-Qadir begins his fifteen-year holy war against the French conquest of Algeria.

t: The Chains Fall Across an Empire
x: In 1833 Parliament abolishes slavery throughout the British Empire — eight hundred thousand enslaved people walk free.

t: Children Leave the Mills — A Little
x: Britain's 1833 Factory Act limits child labor in textile mills — the first crack in the dark satanic system.
The New York Sun sells for a penny in 1833, and news becomes something ordinary working people can afford.
Alexander Pushkin publishes Eugene Onegin in 1833, the novel in verse that made Russian literature.
Prussia's Zollverein customs union of 1834 binds most German states into a single market — the economic foundation of a united Germany.
Britain's 1834 Poor Law herds the destitute into workhouses — relief deliberately made harsher than the lowest wage.
Fire guts the Houses of Parliament in October 1834, and London watches its medieval legislature burn — only Westminster Hall survives.
In 1835 Boer families begin the Great Trek north out of British-ruled Cape Colony, seeking their own promised land.
Alexis de Tocqueville publishes Democracy in America in 1835 — the Frenchman's clear-eyed portrait of the young republic.
Texans refuse to surrender a cannon at Gonzales in October 1835, and the Texas Revolution begins.
Halley's Comet blazes across the sky in 1835, and Mark Twain is born beneath it — he would die with its return in 1910.
Santa Anna's army storms the Alamo in March 1836; every defender dies, and Texas gains its immortal battle cry.
Sam Houston routs Santa Anna at San Jacinto in April 1836 in eighteen minutes — and Texas is free.
Dickens publishes The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and all England laughs with Mr. Pickwick — a literary star is born.
Eighteen-year-old Victoria takes the British throne in 1837, beginning the sixty-three-year Victorian age.

t: The Panic That Broke the Banks
x: The Panic of 1837 collapses America's banks and brings breadlines — the young nation's first great depression.
Samuel Morse builds a working electric telegraph in 1837 — messages racing along a wire in dots and dashes.
Patriots rise in Upper and Lower Canada in 1837 for responsible government; both rebellions are crushed, but reform follows.
Working men publish the People's Charter in 1838 demanding the vote — Chartism, the first mass workers' movement, is born.
Dickens publishes Oliver Twist in 1838, and little Oliver's "Please, sir, I want some more" shames a nation into seeing its poor.
In 1838 federal troops force the Cherokee west at bayonet point; thousands die on the Trail of Tears.
Outnumbered Voortrekkers defeat the Zulu at Blood River in December 1838, and a nation-shaping Afrikaner myth is born.
Daguerre announces the daguerreotype in 1839 — sharp, silvery photographs that anyone could sit for.

t: The Opium Goes Up in Smoke
x: In 1839 Commissioner Lin Zexu seizes and destroys foreign opium at Canton, and Britain answers with warships — the Opium War begins.
In 1839 the young Ottoman sultan proclaims the Tanzimat reforms, promising equality and modern law to all his subjects.
Maori chiefs and the British Crown sign the Treaty of Waitangi in February 1840, founding New Zealand — and arguing over its meaning ever since.
The world's first adhesive postage stamp, the Penny Black, goes on sale in May 1840 — a penny to send a letter anywhere in Britain.
Britain merges Upper and Lower Canada into a single province in 1840 after the rebellions — one parliament for two peoples.
In 1840 John Draper takes the first photograph of the Moon — twenty minutes of exposure, and the heavens become capturable.
Britain seizes Hong Kong island in 1841 during the Opium War — a barren rock that will become one of the world's great harbors.
In 1841 James Clark Ross sails into the great Antarctic sea that bears his name, reaching nearer the south magnetic pole than anyone before.
Edgar Allan Poe publishes "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" in 1841 — the first detective story ever written.
In 1841 young missionary David Livingstone lands in Africa, beginning thirty years of exploration across the continent.
In January 1842 Britain's army retreats from Kabul through the Afghan snows; of sixteen thousand, one survivor rides into Jalalabad.
Britain's 1842 Mines Act bans women and young children from working underground in the coal mines.
The 1842 Treaty of Nanking ends the Opium War, cedes Hong Kong, and forces China open — the first of the "unequal treaties."
Charles Napier conquers Sindh in 1843 and sends home the famous one-word dispatch "Peccavi" — Latin for "I have sinned" (I have Sindh).
In 1843 a thousand settlers roll out for Oregon in the largest wagon train yet — the Great Migration west.
Dickens publishes A Christmas Carol in 1843, and Scrooge's redemption warms a million hearths — inventing the modern Christmas spirit.
On May 24, 1844, Morse taps "What hath God wrought" over the first American telegraph line, Washington to Baltimore.
In 1844 draper's clerk George Williams founds the YMCA in London for the city's lonely young working men.
In 1844 Ludwig Leichhardt leads an expedition across Australia's harsh interior to the northern sea, crossing the continent's burning heart.
In 1845 Alexander Cartwright writes down the first rules of baseball for his Knickerbocker club — ninety feet, nine men, three strikes.
Potato blight blackens Ireland's fields in 1845, beginning the Great Famine — a million dead, a million fled.
In 1845 the British clash with the Sikh Khalsa along the Sutlej River in the First Anglo-Sikh War — four hard-fought winter battles.
The United States annexes the Republic of Texas in 1845, and Mexico reaches for its guns.
American and Mexican troops clash on the Rio Grande in 1846, beginning the Mexican-American War.
James Smithson's bequest founds the Smithsonian Institution in 1846 — "the increase and diffusion of knowledge," the nation's attic.

t: The Stitch That Sewed the World
x: Elias Howe patents the sewing machine in 1846, making ready-made clothes possible and stitching the modern garment world.
In October 1846 a Boston dentist demonstrates ether anesthesia in surgery — and the agony of the operating table begins to end.
In July 1847 Brigham Young's Mormon pioneers reach the Salt Lake valley — "This is the place" — and build Zion in the desert.
Liberia declares itself an independent republic in 1847 — Africa's first, founded by freed American slaves.
In 1847 James Simpson discovers chloroform anesthesia, and childbirth loses its terror.
In January 1848 James Marshall spots gold flakes in Sutter's millrace in California — and the Gold Rush begins.
The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ends the Mexican-American War; Mexico cedes half its land to the United States.
Marx and Engels publish The Communist Manifesto in London in 1848 — "Workers of the world, unite!"
Barricades rise in Paris in February 1848, King Louis-Philippe flees, and the Second Republic is born.
Revolution drives Prince Metternich from Vienna in March 1848, and the old conservative order of Europe trembles.
Three hundred gather at Seneca Falls in July 1848 and demand the vote for women — the birth of the organized women's rights movement.
Elizabeth Blackwell graduates first in her class in 1849 — America's first woman medical doctor.
Britain crushes the Sikhs in 1849 and annexes the Punjab — the last free kingdom of India is gone, and the Koh-i-Noor goes to London.
Russian troops help Austria crush Hungary's 1848–49 revolution; its leaders die on the gallows at Arad.
Eighty thousand gold-hungry argonauts flood California in 1849 — the greatest gold rush the world had ever seen.
The Compromise of 1850 admits California as a free state but tightens the hunt for runaway slaves — delaying the Civil War by a decade.
In 1850 Hong Xiuquan proclaims his Heavenly Kingdom, lighting the fuse of the Taiping Rebellion — the bloodiest civil war in human history.
I was in Boston when Hawthorne's novel of sin and shame became America's first great book.
I was in gold-rush San Francisco when California became the 31st state and tipped the nation's balance.
I saw the Fugitive Slave Act read aloud in Boston, and watched the North turn cold against the South.
I heard Hong Xiuquan preach in southern China before his holy army rose and twenty million died.
I watched Singer's machine sew a shirt in an hour and saw factory speed come into the home.
I bought a remaindered copy of Moby-Dick the year it flopped and read it on the ocean crossing home.
I watched the first Channel telegraph cable pay out from the deck and link London and Paris in minutes.
I watched Stowe's novel sweep the nation, 300,000 copies in a year, and felt the country split open.
I watched Louis-Napoleon crown himself in Paris and remembered how his uncle's dream had ended.
I rode India's first train from Bombay to Thane with crowds who had never seen a locomotive.
I stood on the Tokyo Bay shore when Perry's black warships forced closed Japan to open.
I watched the allied fleets sail for the Crimea over a quarrel about church keys in Jerusalem.
I was at Kanagawa when Japan's seclusion ended with a treaty signed beneath American guns.
I walked Soho's streets with John Snow as he mapped cholera deaths to a single pump handle.

t: The Charge of the Light Brigade
x: I watched the Light Brigade ride into the wrong valley at Balaclava — magnificent and meaningless.
I was in the Scutari hospital when Nightingale arrived with her nurses and her lamp.
I watched the allies march into ruined Sevastopol after the eleven-month siege broke Russia's fortress.
I met Whitman in Brooklyn the summer he self-published the twelve poems that invented the American voice.
I watched Bessemer's converter turn cheap iron to cheap steel with a blast of air — and thought of bridges and guns.
I watched the Russians leave the Paris peace talks, defeated — and turn inward toward freeing the serfs.
I was in Canton when Britain and France attacked China again over a seized ship and forced more trade.
I read Madame Bovary in Paris the winter it scandalized France and remade the novel.
I was in Washington when the Supreme Court ruled Black people could not be citizens — and hardened the North for war.
I was in Meerut when the sepoys mutinied and all of northern India rose against British rule.
I was inside Lucknow's Residency through five months of siege, waiting for a relief that barely came.
I followed the British columns into Delhi and watched the great rebellion of 1857 die in blood and vengeance.
I was aboard when the first Atlantic cable was spliced and Victoria's greeting crawled across the ocean.
I followed Lincoln and Douglas across Illinois and watched a lanky lawyer become a national name.
I was in Calcutta when Victoria's proclamation dissolved the Company and the Raj began.
I was at Solferino the day after the battle and watched Dunant's horror become the Red Cross.
I reached Titusville within weeks of Drake's strike and watched the petroleum age begin in mud and speculation.
I was at Harpers Ferry when Brown's raid failed — and watched a hanged man become the war's marching song.
I was in London the week Darwin's Origin sold out on day one and the world started arguing.
I watched Pony Express riders tear out of Missouri on the 1,900-mile gallop to California.
I sailed with Garibaldi's thousand red shirts to Sicily and marched behind them to Naples.
I watched the Summer Palace burn for three days outside Beijing — a humiliation China would never forget.
I was in Springfield on election night when Lincoln won — and the South began to walk out.
I was in a Russian village when the Tsar's manifesto freed twenty-three million serfs.
I stood in Turin when Victor Emmanuel was proclaimed king of a nearly united Italy.
I was on a Charleston rooftop when the first shells fell on Fort Sumter and the Civil War began.
I was on the hillside with the picnickers at Bull Run when the crowd learned the war would be long.
I walked the Shiloh field after two days of slaughter and picked up a Bible nobody came back for.
I rode west with homesteaders claiming their 160 free acres while the war raged behind them.
I was at Antietam on the bloodiest day in American history — the victory that made emancipation possible.
I was in Washington when Lincoln's proclamation turned the war into a war against slavery itself.
I kept freedom's watch night in a Virginia contraband camp when emancipation became law at midnight.
I rode London's first underground railway through smoke-filled tunnels and watched the subway age begin.
I was on Cemetery Ridge for Pickett's charge and at the dedication when Lincoln spoke for two minutes.
I was at Vicksburg when it surrendered on the Fourth of July — the Mississippi became Union water.
I sat in a London tavern while eleven clubs argued out the first written laws of football.
I entered Nanjing with the Qing troops and saw the end of history's bloodiest civil war.
I watched twelve nations sign at Geneva and make mercy a law of war for the first time.
I rode behind Sherman's columns and watched them burn a sixty-mile path from Atlanta to the sea.
I walked the frozen creek bed the day after the militia massacred Black Kettle's peaceful village.
I was outside the farmhouse at Appomattox when Lee surrendered and Grant stopped the celebration guns.
I was in Washington the night Booth shot Lincoln at Ford's Theatre, five days after the war ended.
I visited Mendel in his monastery garden and held the pea notebooks the world would ignore for 35 years.
I was in the Capitol when the 13th Amendment passed and watched a freedman read it aloud in Virginia.
I was with the Prussian staff at Königgrätz when needle guns and railways broke Austria in a day.
I was aboard the Great Eastern when the permanent Atlantic cable was laid and the ocean shrank to a wire.
I was in Washington when Seward bought Alaska for two cents an acre and everyone laughed.
I was at Querétaro when Maximilian faced the firing squad and Mexico's republic returned.
I was in Ottawa on the first Dominion Day when Canada was born from a conference table, not a battlefield.
I held a stick of Nobel's new dynamite — the powder that would fund the prizes for peace.
I was in Kyoto when the shogun fell and watched Japan decide to become modern all at once.
I met Alcott in Boston the year she wrote Little Women in ten weeks and gave Jo March to a million girls.
I saw Mendeleev's table in St. Petersburg — with empty spaces predicting elements not yet found.
I was at Promontory when the golden spike joined the rails and the telegraph flashed DONE.
I sailed the Suez Canal in the opening procession — a triumph dug with forced labor that Egypt would lose.
I was in Wyoming when the territory gave women the vote — fifty years before the nation caught up.
I watched Black men vote for the first time under the 15th Amendment — and saw the South begin to steal it back.
I was in Paris when France declared war on Prussia and walked into catastrophe.
I was near Sedan when Napoleon III surrendered his army and his eighteen-year empire fell in a day.
I watched Italian troops breach Rome's walls at Porta Pia and complete the thousand-year dream of unity.
I stood in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors when Prussia's king was crowned Kaiser of a united Germany.
I was in Paris for the Commune's seventy-two days and walked Père Lachaise after the Bloody Week.
I ran with the crowds through the Great Chicago Fire and watched the city start rebuilding in the ashes.
I was with Stanley's caravan when he found the lost Livingstone deep in Africa.
I rode with the Hayden expedition through the geyser basins before Yellowstone became the world's first national park.
I voted in Britain's first secret-ballot election — a curtain, a pencil, and a revolution.
I watched HMS Challenger sail from Portsmouth to map the ocean floor and invent the science of the seas.
I was on Wall Street when Jay Cooke's bank failed and the panic began six years of depression.
I visited Maxwell at Cambridge and saw the four equations that united electricity, magnetism, and light.
I was on the Gold Coast when Britain marched inland against the Asante Empire.
I entered burning Kumasi behind Wolseley's troops and watched the Asante Empire of gold break.
I was at the first Impressionist show in Paris when a critic's sneer gave the movement its name.
I tried the first Remington typewriter in New York and watched it remake the office — and employ a generation of women.
I was in Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink for the first organized indoor hockey game.
I was at Carmen's cold Paris premiere, three months before Bizet died never knowing it would become immortal.
I was in Bell's workshop the week the spilled acid produced the first telephone call.
I rode with the burial party at Little Bighorn days after the Sioux and Cheyenne wiped out Custer's command.
I was at Bayreuth for the first complete Ring Cycle — fifteen hours of gods, gold, and twilight.
I was at the Delhi durbar when Victoria was proclaimed Empress and the Raj got its crown.
I crossed the Danube with the Russian armies and watched the Balkans begin their long road to the powder keg.
I sat on the grass bank at the first Wimbledon and watched Spencer Gore win the guinea-entry tournament.
I was in Pittsburgh when the railroad strike went national and labor showed it could stop the country cold.
I was in Menlo Park the night Edison's phonograph first played a human voice back.
I was in New Haven when the first telephone exchange connected its twenty-one subscribers by hand.
I watched the great powers carve up the Balkans in Berlin — dealing out nations like cards, scheduling Sarajevo.
I marched through the Khyber with the British column into the graveyard of empires.
I walked the Isandlwana field the day after Zulu warriors annihilated a British column.
I reached Rorke's Drift at dawn after 150 soldiers held a mission station against 4,000 Zulu.
I was in Menlo Park the night Edison's bulb burned thirteen hours and the electric age began.
I was in the theater when Nora slammed the door in A Doll's House — and on the nineteenth century.
I was at Glenrowan when Ned Kelly walked out in his ploughshare armor for his last stand.
I was in the Transvaal when Boer farmers took up rifles against the British Empire.
I was below Majuba Hill at dawn when Boer marksmen routed the British and won the Transvaal's freedom.
I was in St. Petersburg the day terrorists killed Alexander II, the Tsar who freed the serfs.
I heard the Mahdi preach in Kordofan before Sudan rose against Egypt and Britain.
I was on Allen Street in Tombstone for the thirty-second gunfight that became the West's legend.
I looked through Koch's microscope in Berlin at the tuberculosis bacterium — germ theory's great proof.
I was in San Francisco when America banned Chinese immigration — the first law aimed at a whole people.
I was in lower Manhattan when Pearl Street Station lit four hundred lamps and the grid age began.
I was with Wolseley's dawn attack at Tel el-Kebir when Britain began its seventy-year "temporary" occupation of Egypt.
I walked the Brooklyn Bridge on opening day — a mile of steel thrown across the impossible.
I was on a ship in the Sunda Strait when Krakatoa exploded — the loudest sound in recorded history.
I rode the first Orient Express from Paris toward Constantinople — Europe's imagination made into a timetable.
I was inside besieged Khartoum with Gordon, watching the desert for a relief column that never came in time.
I watched fourteen powers carve up Africa in Berlin — no African invited, no African consulted.
I read Huckleberry Finn on a Mississippi riverboat the year the libraries banned it for being vulgar.
I was on the Nile when Khartoum fell two days before relief arrived and Gordon died on the palace steps.
I was in Paris when Pasteur's rabies vaccine saved young Joseph Meister and vaccines entered the modern age.
I watched Benz's three-wheeled Motorwagen putter through Mannheim — the horse's five-thousand-year reign ending unnoticed.
I was in Bombay when seventy-two lawyers founded the Congress that would one day free India.
I was near Chicago's Haymarket Square when the bomb exploded and the fight for the eight-hour day turned bloody.
I drank one of the first glasses of Coca-Cola at an Atlanta soda fountain — five cents, nine sales a day.
I was at Skeleton Canyon when Geronimo surrendered and the Indian Wars effectively ended.
I was in New York Harbor when the Statue of Liberty was unveiled before a fleet of ships.
I was in London for Victoria's Golden Jubilee — the empire glittering at its peak, the rot already underneath.
I was in Cleveland when Michelson and Morley found no ether — the beautiful failure that cleared the road to relativity.
I was in Saigon when France proclaimed Indochina — a flag planted in a hornet's nest called a garden.
I bought Beeton's Christmas Annual the year it introduced Sherlock Holmes to the world.
I was in Rio when the Golden Law freed 700,000 — the last slaves in the Western world walked free.
I walked Whitechapel's gaslit streets during the Ripper's autumn of terror — and he was never caught.
I bought one of the first Kodaks in Rochester and took my first badly framed snapshot.
I climbed the Eiffel Tower's 1,710 steps on opening week and saw Paris spread out like a map.
I was on the starting line when 50,000 settlers raced into Oklahoma at noon and built cities by sunset.
I was in the valley when the South Fork Dam broke and twenty million tons of water took Johnstown.
I was at the Moulin Rouge on opening night — the can-can, the champagne, Lautrec sketching in the corner.
I was in Washington when the Sherman Act outlawed monopolies — a paper tiger that would grow teeth.
I stood in the Auvers wheat field after Van Gogh died broke and unknown — genius recognized one funeral too late.
I walked the frozen field at Wounded Knee the day after the massacre ended the Indian Wars.
I was at Vladivostok when Russia began the 5,700-mile Trans-Siberian across the wilderness.
I watched Naismith's first basketball game in Springfield — peach baskets, a soccer ball, thirteen rules.
I was at Ellis Island on opening day when fifteen-year-old Annie Moore became the first immigrant processed.
I was on the Monongahela when steelworkers battled Pinkertons at Homestead — labor's bloodiest fight.
I was at the Nutcracker's shrugging St. Petersburg premiere — the flop that became Christmas itself.
I was in Honolulu when American planters overthrew Queen Liliuokalani — a kingdom stolen for sugar.
I rode the first Ferris wheel at Chicago's White City fair — 27 million visitors glimpsing the future lit up at night.
I watched women queue to vote in New Zealand — the first nation on earth where women voted nationally.
I was in Chicago when the Pullman Strike stopped the nation's railroads and gave America Labor Day.
I followed the Sino-Japanese War and watched Meiji Japan dismantle Qing China in eight months.
I watched Dreyfus degraded in a Paris courtyard — the forged treason case that split France in two.
I was at Shimonoseki when China ceded Taiwan and Japan arrived as a great power.
I stood in Marconi's father's garden when his wireless signals clicked across it — and made the cable obsolete.
I held Röntgen's photographic plate of his wife's skeletal hand — the X-ray that made the invisible visible.
I was in the Grand Café basement when the Lumières screened the first paying films — a train arriving, workers leaving.
I was with Menelik's army at Adwa when Ethiopia destroyed the Italian invasion — Africa's greatest anti-colonial victory.
I sat in Athens' marble stadium for the first modern Olympics — 241 athletes, fourteen nations.
I was in Washington when the Court blessed "separate but equal" — and Jim Crow got its law for sixty years.
I watched the stampeders sail north for the Klondike — the last great gold rush on earth.
I was in a New Orleans dance hall when brass bands and ragtime fused into jazz.
I read Dracula at 2 a.m. the year it came out — and checked the locks on my doors.
I watched the Diamond Jubilee procession — the largest empire in history saluting its queen, at the edge of decline.
I was in Thomson's Cambridge lab when the electron proved the "uncuttable" atom had parts.
I was on the Havana waterfront when the Maine exploded — 266 dead, and war fever ignited by headlines.
I was in Manila Bay when Dewey fired — ten weeks that turned the American republic into an empire.
I was at Omdurman when machine guns mowed down 10,000 dervishes in a morning — courage against the Maxim.
I visited the Curies' shed laboratory and watched radium glow blue — the fire at the heart of matter.
I was at The Hague when twenty-six nations held the first world peace conference and tried to leash war.
I was in South Africa when the Boer War began — the empire's hardest fight, eighteen years after Majuba.
I watched Charlotte Cooper win tennis in Paris — the first female Olympic champion in the Games' chaotic second act.
I was in besieged Beijing during the Boxer Rebellion — fifty-five days that broke the Qing dynasty.
I was in Galveston when the hurricane drowned 8,000 — America's deadliest natural disaster.
I was in Berlin when Planck proposed energy comes in packets — the reluctant heresy that began the quantum age.
Paris's 1900 exposition shows off the wonders of a new century — moving sidewalks, talking films, the Eiffel Tower — while the traveler already knows the dark years ahead.
Anti-foreign rebels besiege Beijing's legation quarter until an eight-nation army breaks through, then loots the city — the traveler's loyalty is torn between both sides of the barricade.
Freud publishes The Interpretation of Dreams in Vienna, mapping the unconscious mind — the traveler, who has lived a hundred lifetimes, agrees the hidden country is real.
The 1900 Galveston hurricane drowns the richest port in Texas, killing thousands in America's deadliest storm — the traveler helps with the burial parties.
Women compete in the Olympics for the first time in Paris — tennis, golf, sailing — and the traveler sees a door open that will never close again.
Zeppelin's rigid airship floats over Lake Constance in 1900 — the traveler watches the crowd watch the sky grow a hull.
Paris opens its underground railway in 1900, and the traveler rides the first trains through the city's new second self beneath the boulevards.
Queen Victoria dies after a 63-year reign, and an empire mourns its grandmother — the traveler knows most of the royal mourners at her funeral will be gone within two decades.
The first Nobel Prizes honor Röntgen, Red Cross founder Dunant, and a poet — funded by dynamite money, the traveler calls it Nobel's strange atonement.
Marconi receives three faint dots across the Atlantic — the first transatlantic wireless signal, and the traveler feels the horizon dissolve.
The Spindletop gusher blows in Texas, launching the petroleum century — the traveler stands in the spray and smells the future burning.
Six Australian colonies unite peacefully as a Commonwealth on New Year's Day 1901 — the traveler notes most nations are born screaming; this one was born talking.
A grieving young Picasso paints the world in blue — beggars, blind men, mothers — and the traveler watches heartbreak become a whole period of art.
McKinley is assassinated in Buffalo and Theodore Roosevelt storms into the White House — the century's first changing of the guard by bullet, not ballot.
Mount Pelée buries Saint-Pierre in minutes in 1902, killing nearly everyone except a prisoner in a stone cell and a shoemaker — the traveler watches from a ship in the harbor.
The Boer War ends with Britain victorious — the traveler remembers the scorched farms, the camps where children died, and the Black Africans who fought and got nothing.
Willis Carrier invents modern air conditioning for a Brooklyn printing plant — the traveler shivers in the first cooled room, not knowing half the modern world will run on it.
Roosevelt spares a bear cub on a Mississippi hunt, a cartoon follows, and the teddy bear is born — the traveler calls it an empire of mercy in miniature.
Michigan crushes Stanford in the first Rose Bowl — the traveler sits in the Pasadena stands while a century-long New Year's ritual is invented by accident.
Sixty riders set off from Paris in the first Tour de France — the traveler follows the dust and punctures through villages seeing bicycle racing for the first time.
The Wright brothers' Flyer lifts off the dunes at Kitty Hawk for twelve seconds — the traveler calls it the moment humanity became a flying species.
Henry Ford founds the Ford Motor Company in Detroit — the traveler walks the early factory floor and senses the horse's four thousand years coming to an end.
Panama breaks from Colombia with American backing and the canal zone follows — the traveler notes empires dig, and small countries hold the shovel.
Boston beats Pittsburgh in the first World Series — the traveler sits in the wooden stands while October invents its own holiday.
The Great Train Robbery gives film a plot, a chase, and a gunshot fired at the camera — the traveler watches storytelling learn a new language in twelve minutes.
Japan's surprise attack on Port Arthur opens the Russo-Japanese War — the traveler watches the world learn that the European empires are not invincible.
Germany crushes the Herero uprising, driving tens of thousands into the desert to die — the traveler walks among the bones and calls it the century's first genocide, rehearsed in the sand.
Britain and France settle their colonial quarrels in the Entente Cordiale — the traveler watches old enemies shake hands and knows they are making sides, not peace.
New York opens its first subway line from City Hall to Harlem — the traveler rides opening day and feels a city deciding to never stop growing.
The 1904 St. Louis Olympics dissolve into dust and chaos — a strychnine-dosed marathon, a cheater in a car — but the traveler sees the real games survive underneath.
Troops fire on peaceful workers marching to the Tsar on Bloody Sunday — the traveler walks among the singing crowd and watches the snow turn red.
Einstein's miracle year in Bern — relativity, photons, E=mc2 — and the traveler stands outside the patent office window knowing the atom will remember that equation.
Japan annihilates the Russian Baltic Fleet at Tsushima after its 18,000-mile voyage — the traveler watches an empire's fleet sink in the mist.
Roosevelt brokers peace between Russia and Japan at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, winning the Nobel — the traveler calls peace unglamorous work: rooms, papers, patience.
Norway peacefully leaves its union with Sweden by referendum — the traveler calls it the rarest divorce in the history of nations and wishes the century would learn from it.
The first nickelodeon opens in Pittsburgh — five cents buys a dark room and an hour of elsewhere, and the traveler calls it the cheapest escape ever sold.
Las Vegas is founded as a railroad water stop in the Nevada desert — the traveler stands on the dusty lot and laughs at how beginnings never look like what they become.
The 1906 earthquake and three days of fire level San Francisco — the traveler runs through rolling streets and watches rich and poor sleep side by side in the parks.
Sinclair's novel about Chicago's meatpackers shocks America into food-safety law — the traveler honors the writer who looked where nobody wanted to look.
Europe's powers quarrel over Morocco and Germany walks out isolated — the traveler sits in the conference rooms and watches the empires learn they'd rather fight than back down.
Finland gives women the vote and the right to stand for office, first in Europe — the traveler watches them walk to the polls in the snow and calls it courage.
Fessenden broadcasts voice and violin on Christmas Eve 1906, the first radio program — played for lonely ships' operators, the traveler says the airwaves began with a gift.
Dreyfus is cleared and restored after twelve years — the traveler watched France tear itself in two over him and stood in the courtroom when the verdict came.
Picasso paints five fractured women and modern art begins — the traveler stands before the canvas and sees a painting about seeing itself.
Roosevelt sends sixteen white battleships on a 43,000-mile world cruise — the traveler calls it a parade and a threat in the same hull.
Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, is invented — the traveler holds a glossy piece and already sees it ending in every ocean on Earth.
The 1907 bank panic nearly topples Wall Street until J.P. Morgan locks the bankers in his library — the traveler thinks a civilization needing one rich man to save it is already in trouble.
Paul Cornu lifts a twin-rotor machine off the ground in France — a few shaky seconds, and the traveler calls it the helicopter's birthday.
The Model T rolls out and the automobile stops being a rich man's toy — the traveler rides one of the first down a dirt road and feels the century accelerate.
Something explodes over Tunguska, flattening 2,000 square kilometers of Siberian forest with no crater — the traveler walks the blasted taiga and admits some mysteries stay mysteries.
Dorando Pietri collapses at the 1908 Olympic marathon finish and is disqualified — the traveler was in the stands, and the measured distance becomes the marathon forever.
The Young Turks force the Sultan to restore the Ottoman constitution — the traveler parades with the hopeful crowds, knowing the dream will curdle but believing for an afternoon.

t: The Champion Who Broke the Line
x: Jack Johnson beats Tommy Burns in Sydney to become the first Black heavyweight champion — the traveler watches him smile through fourteen rounds and calls it one of the bravest things he's seen.
Blériot flies the English Channel in 37 minutes — the traveler watches from the Dover cliffs as the moat that stopped Napoleon is crossed by a Frenchman in a monoplane.
Peary claims the North Pole in 1909, a claim disputed ever since — the traveler knows the Arctic's lying distances and honors the hunger to stand where nothing stands.
Du Bois and allies found the NAACP in 1909 — the traveler sits in the early meetings and calls it an unromantic machine of minutes and dues that bent the arc of a nation.
Selfridge's opens on Oxford Street and invents the modern department store — the traveler walks the marble aisles and calls it consumerism's cathedral.
Halley's Comet returns in 1910 and crowds buy comet pills against its tail — the traveler watches from a field as Earth passes through harmlessly.
Japan formally annexes Korea in 1910 — the traveler walks the streets of Seoul and notes that swallowed nations are never digested; Korea remembered its name.
Madero calls for revolt against Diaz's 34-year rule — the traveler rides with the early rebels, knowing the revolution will eat its children for a decade.
Four colonies unite as the Union of South Africa under white rule — the traveler watches the Black majority written out of the nation at its christening.
Florence Nightingale dies at 90 — the traveler remembers her lamp in the Crimea and says every nurse who ever walked a night ward carries it still.
Revolution topples the Qing dynasty, ending 2,000 years of emperors — the traveler watches men shear off their queues in the streets and steps over history.

t: First to the Bottom of the World
x: Amundsen reaches the South Pole by dogsled, beating Scott — the traveler honors both the Norwegian's planning and the Englishman's frozen dignity.
146 garment workers die in the Triangle Shirtwaist fire — locked doors, a collapsed fire escape — and the traveler says every workplace safety rule was written in that smoke.
The Mona Lisa is stolen from the Louvre and crowds gather to stare at the empty hooks — the traveler notes the theft made her the most recognized face on Earth.
Marie Curie wins her second Nobel, the first person honored in two sciences — the traveler remembers her stirring pitchblende in a Paris shed, working toward the radiation that would kill her.
The Titanic strikes an iceberg and sinks on her maiden voyage — the traveler stands on the Carpathia's deck at dawn and calls it the century's lesson in hubris.
The Balkan states drive the Ottomans out of Europe, then turn on each other — the traveler walks the mountain battlefields knowing Sarajevo is two years away.
The Piltdown skull is unveiled as the missing link, fooling science for forty years — the traveler calls wanting to believe the oldest laboratory error.
Juliette Gordon Low founds the Girl Scouts in Savannah — the traveler watches the first meetings and says millions of women's courage traces back to a troop and a campfire.

Jim Thorpe wins the pentathlon and decathlon, then is stripped of his medals for playing semi-pro baseball — the traveler notes justice runs on its own slow schedule; they came back thirty years after his death.
The Armory Show brings modern art to New York and America argues about it for months — the traveler loves a scandal that turns out to be a birth.
Niels Bohr models the atom with electrons in orbits — the traveler calls it the first true map of the smallest country there is.
The Rite of Spring premieres in Paris and the audience nearly riots — the traveler was in the theater and says the future usually enters through a slammed door.
Ford's moving assembly line cuts car build time from hours to minutes — the traveler walks beside the first endless belt and sees the human being become a station on the line.
India's first feature film premieres in Bombay — a silent myth of King Harishchandra, and the traveler watches an audience see its own epics move for the first time.
Stainless steel is invented in Sheffield — the traveler holds a bright first knife and notes invention aims at one thing and hits the future sideways.

t: The Shot That Lit the World
x: A teenager's pistol kills Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo — the traveler was on the street and says sixteen million died because a driver took a wrong turn.
Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia and the alliance dominoes fall — the traveler watches Vienna cheer for a war that will last a month, they said.
Germany marches through neutral Belgium and Britain declares war — the traveler stands on the roads as refugees stream past and Louvain burns.
Germany encircles and destroys a Russian army at Tannenberg — the traveler walks the battlefield of lakes and forests where an empire began its long bleeding.
Paris taxicabs ferry troops to the Marne and the German advance is stopped — the traveler rides with the cabbies in the most Parisian army ever assembled.

t: The Race to the Sea Ends
x: The race to the sea ends and the trenches stretch from Switzerland to the sea — the traveler walks the first winter line and calls it a four-hundred-mile wound.
The Panama Canal opens, joining two oceans — the traveler stands on a first ship through the locks, noting Europe dug trenches while America dug a canal.
Japan besieges Germany's port at Tsingtao and takes its Pacific islands — the traveler watches Britain's efficient ally and sees it collecting debts the future will pay.
A German squadron sinks two British cruisers off Chile, avenged weeks later at the Falklands — the traveler learns again that no navy rules forever.
British and German soldiers climb out of their trenches on Christmas 1914, trading gifts and playing football — the traveler walks that strange peace the generals furiously forbade ever after.
Chaplin's Tramp shuffles onto the screen in 1914 — the traveler watches the world fall in love with a little fellow who owned nothing, and calls comedy courage in a funny hat.
Cleveland installs the first electric traffic light — the traveler stands on the corner and calls civilization traffic management, scaled up.
Benedict XV is elected and spends WWI begging for peace, calling it "useless slaughter" — the traveler honors the voice that said stop when every other said onward.
ANZAC troops storm the cliffs at Gallipoli in a campaign of courage and waste — the traveler was on the beaches and says two nations were baptized in those waters.
The Ottoman roundup of Armenian leaders begins a genocide that will kill 1.5 million — the traveler walks the deportation roads and holds the hands of the dying.

t: The Ship That Sank a Neutral
x: A U-boat sinks the Lusitania with 1,198 dead — the traveler saw her sail from New York and says some sinkings steer history; this one steered America toward war.
Germany releases chlorine gas at Ypres — the traveler watches the green-yellow cloud roll in and calls gas the coward's masterpiece: it kills the air itself.
Einstein completes general relativity in wartime Berlin — gravity as the curve of space itself, and the traveler calls it the century's most beautiful idea born in its ugliest years.
Birth of a Nation invents the feature film and glorifies the Klan — the traveler sits stunned by the craft and sickened by the lie: the blockbuster was born compromised.
Zeppelins bomb London in 1915 — the traveler stands in the dark streets and says the front line moved to the nursery; the sky was never safe again.
Edith Cavell is shot for helping Allied soldiers escape — the traveler stands outside the Brussels prison at dawn and says the Germans made a martyr and paid in enlistments.
Italy abandons the Triple Alliance and joins Britain and France — the traveler watches the army march into the Isonzo meat grinder and learns alliances are interests in friendship's uniform.
Over a thousand women meet at The Hague in 1915 to demand an end to the war — the traveler sits in the only peace conference of the year and says the idea outlived the generals.
The Battle of Verdun grinds for 300 days with 700,000 casualties — the traveler walks the ossuary hills and picks up soil that is half iron, half bone.
On July 1, 1916, Britain loses 60,000 men in a day at the Somme — the traveler was in the chalk and wire and says the poppies grow there still, red as the ledgers.
Irish rebels seize Dublin's GPO in Easter 1916; the British execute the leaders and turn Ireland — the traveler says the firing squads did what the rebels couldn't: they persuaded.
Britain and Germany's dreadnought fleets clash at Jutland — both claim victory, but the traveler notes Britain kept the sea, which was the point.
Brusilov's 1916 offensive shatters Austria — Russia's greatest victory and its last, and the traveler rides with troops whose triumph breaks the army that won it.
British tanks crawl into battle at Flers in 1916 — clumsy, slow, terrifying, and the traveler calls it the future of war arriving badly, which is how it usually arrives.
Britain and France secretly carve up the Ottoman Middle East in the Sykes-Picot agreement — the traveler has walked every border they drew and says the region is still paying the bill.
Lawrence of Arabia helps Arab riders take Aqaba from the landward side — the traveler rides with the camel columns, knowing the independence promises are already being traded away in London.
Russian nobles murder Rasputin in 1916 — poison, bullets, the Neva — and the traveler notes killing the symptom never cures the disease; the dynasty had months left.
Artists invent Dada in a Zurich cabaret in 1916 — anti-war nonsense as protest, and the traveler says you can't argue with nonsense, you can only feel it.
Margaret Sanger opens America's first birth-control clinic and is jailed within days — the traveler stands in the line of women outside and calls the right to decide the first freedom.
Bread riots topple the Tsar in February 1917 — the traveler is in Petrograd as three centuries of Romanovs dissolve like sugar in tea, arriving before the revolutionaries do.
America declares war on Germany in April 1917 after the Zimmermann Telegram and U-boat sinkings — the traveler hears Wilson's speech and watches the giant step in.
Passchendaele gains five miles for half a million casualties — men drowning in mud, and the traveler calls it the standard by which all waste is measured.
The Bolsheviks storm the Winter Palace in October 1917 — the traveler is in Petrograd that night and believes with the workers, for a night, before history does the disbelieving.
The Balfour Declaration promises a Jewish national home in Palestine in 67 words — the traveler calls it history's longest IOU, still being collected a century on.
Austro-German troops rout the Italians at Caporetto — the traveler walks the retreat roads as an army dissolves, and notes Hemingway was nearby in an ambulance.
Mata Hari faces the firing squad at Vincennes, refusing the blindfold — the traveler watches and says guilty or scapegoat, the legend outlived the trial.
The first jazz record is cut in 1917 — the traveler is in the studio and notes the irony that five white men recorded first, but the music belonged to everyone.
The first Pulitzer Prizes honor reporting, novels, and poetry — the traveler reads the first winners and says prizes tell a country what it thinks writing is for.
American women operate Army switchboards at the front in WWI — the Hello Girls under fire, called civilians for sixty years, finally recognized in 1977.
Finland declares independence from revolutionary Russia in December 1917 — the traveler celebrates in Helsinki and calls small nations the toughest things on Earth.
The Bolsheviks sign away a third of Russia's land at Brest-Litovsk to buy peace — the traveler watches the humiliated delegation and notes desperate bargains rarely age well.
The 1918 flu circles the globe from army camps, killing more than the war — the traveler walks the wards in Philadelphia, Bombay, and Cape Town and refuses to forget.
Germany's 1918 spring offensive breaks through, then outruns its supplies and stalls — the traveler watches Ludendorff's last gamble fail in the French countryside.
Foch counterattacks at the Marne and the Allies begin the Hundred Days — the traveler is there for the turning and says the tide turns slowly, then all at once.
A million Americans attack through the Argonne — the largest battle in US history, and the traveler walks the shattered woods where the Yanks grew up fast.
The Bolsheviks shoot the Tsar, his family, and their servants in a Yekaterinburg cellar — the traveler stands outside in the July night and records what he cannot forgive.
At 11 a.m. on 11/11 the guns stop — the traveler stands in the trenches as the strangest sound of all arrives: silence, and the birds singing.
Allenby smashes the Ottomans at Megiddo — the traveler rides with the last great cavalry charge in history, which charged into the twentieth century and never charged out.
The Black 369th Infantry fights 191 days straight and earns France's Croix de Guerre — the traveler watches them fight for a country that lynched their brothers at home.
Women over thirty win the vote in Britain in 1918 — the traveler remembers the marches and hunger strikes and calls it a crack, not a door, but cracks spread.
Czechoslovakia is proclaimed in Prague with Masaryk as president — the traveler stands in Wenceslas Square as the new flag goes up and sings with the crowd.
Versailles blames Germany and bills her for the war — the traveler sits in the Hall of Mirrors and says peace is not the absence of war but the presence of justice; Versailles had none.
Dyer's troops fire on unarmed Indians at Jallianwala Bagh — the traveler hears ten minutes of rifles in Amritsar and says the road to independence began in that walled garden.
Students flood Beijing on May Fourth 1919 against the Versailles betrayal — the traveler marches with them and says this awakening shook a quarter of humanity.
Alcock and Brown fly the Atlantic nonstop in sixteen harrowing hours — the traveler tracks their open-cockpit Vimy and honors the first crossing before Lindbergh made it famous.

t: The School That Redesigned the World
x: Gropius founds the Bauhaus at Weimar — the traveler walks the workshops and says the chairs you sit in and the type on this page were designed in that school.
Race riots burn across America in the Red Summer of 1919 — Black veterans home from France face lynchings, and the traveler walks the burning streets of Chicago.
Eddington photographs bent starlight during the 1919 eclipse, proving Einstein right — the traveler stands on Principe Island and calls it science's most beautiful moment.
The League of Nations is founded in Geneva — the traveler watches Wilson's dream become an institution and says dreams don't die when institutions do.
Prohibition takes effect in America — the traveler watches the last legal bars close and the speakeasies fill, calling it thirteen years proving you cannot legislate thirst.
Germany's republic is proclaimed at Weimar, born in defeat and street fighting — the traveler gives it fourteen brilliant years before the fire.
Tennessee's ratification wins American women the vote nationwide — the traveler stands outside the statehouse for the 35-49 vote switched by one young legislator's mother's letter.
KDKA broadcasts election returns from Pittsburgh in 1920 — the traveler listens on a crystal set and calls it the twentieth century's nervous system switching on.
Gandhi launches noncooperation in 1920 — the traveler walks with the crowds and calls nonviolence the century's most radical idea, wearing the simplest clothes.
Poland smashes the Red Army at Warsaw in 1920 — the traveler stands on the Vistula as history pivots, and says miracles are preparation meeting desperation.
The Red Sox sell Babe Ruth to the Yankees — the traveler is in Boston for the disbelief and calls it the worst trade in sports history, regretted for 86 years.
The IRA's guerrilla war grinds Britain toward a treaty — the traveler walks the Cork countryside and says Ireland's freedom was bought in laneways, not battlefields.
Agatha Christie's first novel introduces Hercule Poirot — the traveler reads it fresh off the press, not knowing the quiet woman from Torquay becomes history's best-selling novelist.
The Volstead Act takes hold and bootleggers become millionaires overnight — the traveler watches the rum-runners and says the law meant well; the law always means well.
The League of Nations holds its first assembly in Geneva — 41 nations, and the traveler calls it the first time humanity tried to govern its own violence.
Banting and Best isolate insulin in Toronto — the traveler visits the cramped lab and calls the rescue of dying diabetic children one of the few miracles he's seen.
A white mob destroys Tulsa's Greenwood district — Black Wall Street burned, hundreds dead, buried in silence for 70 years, and the traveler says the silence was the second crime.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty creates the Free State and partitions Ireland — the traveler is in Dublin for the anguished debates and says freedom came, but came divided.
