Thirteen men found the Chinese Communist Party in a Shanghai schoolhouse — the traveler walks past the modest brick house and says history's biggest parties start in the smallest rooms.
Einstein wins the Nobel for the photoelectric effect, not relativity — the traveler smiles at the committee's caution and notes he gave the money to his ex-wife as promised.
The World Series is broadcast on radio for the first time in 1921 — the traveler listens in a barbershop and says the imagination is the best screen.
The great powers agree to limit battleships at Washington — the traveler watches admirals surrender dreadnoughts on paper and says the idea survived even when the treaties died.

t: The Trial of Sacco and Vanzetti
x: Sacco and Vanzetti are convicted on shaky evidence in 1921 — the traveler sits in the Dedham courtroom and says justice is supposed to be blind; this time it just closed its eyes.
Carter peers into Tutankhamun's intact tomb — "wonderful things" — and the traveler stands in the 3,000-year-old air as the world goes mad for Egypt.
Mussolini's Blackshirts march on Rome and the King hands him power — the traveler watches the theater and says power rarely needs as much force as it pretends.
The USSR is proclaimed in 1922 — the traveler is in Moscow for the red banners and calls it history's largest laboratory, results still being argued.
The BBC starts broadcasting from London in 1922 — the traveler listens to the first crackling programs and says every empire of the air starts as a hobby.
Joyce's Ulysses is published in Paris — one day in Dublin, and the traveler carries a first edition through Bloom's streets, calling the ordinary inexhaustible.
Eliot publishes The Waste Land — the traveler reads it in London and says every age gets the poem it deserves; this one got ashes and a voice sifting through them.
Nosferatu brings Dracula to the screen in 1922 — the traveler sits in a Berlin cinema and notes the film survived the court-ordered destruction, like vampires do.
A dying 14-year-old gets the first insulin injection in Toronto and lives — the traveler stands outside the ward and honors the discoverers who sold the patent for a dollar.
The 1923 Great Kanto earthquake destroys Tokyo and Yokohama, killing 140,000 — the traveler walks the ruins and records the mobs' murder of Koreans as the disaster's second, human crime.
Hitler's 1923 beer-hall putsch fails and he writes Mein Kampf in prison — the traveler watches the trial and notes the republic showed him mercy; he would show it none.
Ataturk proclaims the Turkish Republic in 1923 — the traveler stands in Ankara as a general remakes a nation: fez banned, alphabet Latinized, caliphate abolished.
TIME's first issue hits newsstands in 1923 — the traveler buys a thin earnest copy and says the century learned to read itself weekly.
Yankee Stadium opens in the Bronx in 1923 — the traveler sits in the stands on opening day and calls it a temple of summer afternoons whose memories wouldn't demolish.
Walt and Roy Disney found their studio in Hollywood in 1923 — the traveler walks past the garage on Kingswell Avenue where the entertainment empire began.
Lenin dies in 1924 and Stalin seizes the levers — the traveler stands in the mourners' line in the Moscow cold and thinks the revolution died here too; it just took seventy years to bury.
The first Winter Olympics open at Chamonix in 1924 — the traveler stands at the ski jump in the cold and watches humans do beautifully what they were never designed to do.
American Army planes circle the globe in 175 days in 1924 — the first aerial circumnavigation, and the traveler tracks the Douglas World Cruisers on their 26,000-mile route.
Native Americans are granted US citizenship in 1924 — the traveler sits with elders who fought in the Great War for a country that didn't count them, and calls it justice, late and incomplete.
Breton's 1924 manifesto launches Surrealism — the traveler sits in Paris cafés with the movement and calls it the century's subconscious given a manifesto.
The 1924 Paris Games give us Liddell and Abrahams — the traveler is in the stadium and says the Olympics at their best are not nations but persons.
Macy's first Thanksgiving parade marches down Broadway in 1924 with live zoo animals — the traveler stands on the curb and says traditions are just habits that survived.
Fitzgerald publishes The Great Gatsby in 1925 — the traveler reads it fresh and calls it America's autobiography, written in advance; it flopped first, then the century caught up.
The Scopes trial puts evolution on trial in Dayton, Tennessee — the traveler sits in the courtroom-circus and says the verdict was guilty but the judgment of history was otherwise.
Baird demonstrates television in London in 1925 — a flickering dummy's face, thirty lines, and the traveler says the century's window began in a cold Soho attic.
Europe's foreign ministers promise peace at Locarno in 1925 — the traveler walks Lake Maggiore and says peace needs more than spirit; Locarno had champagne but needed teeth.
Heisenberg invents matrix mechanics in 1925 — the traveler admits he can't follow every equation but honors the young German who reimagined reality on Heligoland.
The New Yorker publishes its first issue in 1925 — the traveler buys one for fifteen cents and says it taught the country how to be funny on purpose.
Mein Kampf is published in 1925 — Hitler's blueprint, ignored by the world, and the traveler holds the turgid book and says when a man writes down his crimes in advance, believe him.
Two million British workers strike for nine days in 1926 — the traveler walks the picket lines and says the strike proved the state could outlast its workers; the workers learned harder.
Goddard launches the first liquid-fuel rocket in 1926 — forty-one feet in a Massachusetts cabbage field, mocked by newspapers, ancestor of every rocket since.
Winnie-the-Pooh is published in 1926 — the traveler reads it to children now grandparents and says the century's wisest philosophy wore a red shirt.
NBC becomes America's first radio network in 1926 — the traveler tunes in and says the nation, for the first time, had a single hearth.
Gertrude Ederle swims the English Channel faster than any man before her — the traveler watches from a boat as the 19-year-old beats every male record.
Hirohito becomes emperor in 1926, beginning the Showa era — the traveler stands in Tokyo knowing the "enlightened peace" will hold war, ruin, and then miracle; names promise, history decides.
Lindbergh flies New York to Paris solo in 33 hours — the traveler is at Le Bourget when he lands and says for one night the whole world agreed on a hero.
The Jazz Singer brings synchronized speech to film in 1927 — the traveler hears Jolson's voice come out of the screen and says the silent era ended in that sentence.
Babe Ruth hits 60 home runs in 1927 — the traveler is at the Stadium for number sixty and says every slugger for a generation chased that number.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle in 1927 — the traveler sits with the arguing physicists in Copenhagen and says the universe keeps secrets by making them unaskable.
Chiang Kai-shek purges the Communists in Shanghai in 1927 — the traveler walks the bloody streets and notes the purge drove communism into the countryside, where it grew.
Belgian priest Lemaître proposes the universe began in a primeval atom in 1927 — the traveler sits in Louvain and says the priest was right: the universe has a birthday.
Sacco and Vanzetti are executed in 1927 as the world protests — the traveler stands outside Charlestown Prison and says the truth came fifty years late, but came.
Fleming notices mold killing bacteria in 1928 — the traveler looks at the petri dish and calls it the most important accident in medical history.
Steamboat Willie premieres in 1928 — Mickey Mouse whistles at the ship's wheel, and the traveler says the entertainment empire started with a whistle.
Britain gives all women over 21 the vote in 1928 — the traveler stands outside Parliament; Pankhurst died weeks before, missing the victory by days.
62 nations sign the Kellogg-Briand Pact outlawing war in 1928 — the traveler watches the signatures and says Nuremberg would hang men on the strength of that paper.
Women compete in Olympic track and field for the first time at Amsterdam 1928 — the traveler sits in the stadium as the old men's predictions collapse and the women just run.
Amelia Earhart becomes the first woman to fly the Atlantic in 1928, as a passenger — the traveler meets her beforehand and says the passenger was just the beginning.
Sliced bread goes on sale in 1928 — the traveler buys a loaf in Chillicothe, Missouri, and says civilization advances one convenience at a time.
Stalin launches the first Five-Year Plan in 1928 — the traveler walks the Magnitogorsk construction sites and calls it progress by force, modernity by murder, its cost still being counted.
The stock market crashes on Black Thursday 1929 — the traveler stands on Wall Street as the ticker falls behind and the Jazz Age ends at the closing bell.
The first Academy Awards honor Wings and Sunrise in 1929 — the traveler sits in the Roosevelt Hotel's Blossom Room when it was just a fifteen-minute dinner.
Hubble discovers the galaxies fleeing in 1929 — the universe is expanding, and the traveler stands at Mount Wilson watching the redshifts pile up.
The Lateran Treaty makes Vatican City a state in 1929 — the traveler watches Mussolini and the Pope sign and calls it diplomacy: both used the other.
Capone's men machine-gun seven rivals in a Chicago garage on Valentine's Day 1929 — the traveler walks past the brick wall and says the massacre doomed Capone by demanding action.
The Museum of Modern Art opens in New York in 1929 — the traveler walks the first rented galleries and says the rebels got a museum and the museum got the rebels.
The Graf Zeppelin circles the globe in 21 days in 1929 — the traveler watches the silver giant rise and calls it the most graceful travel ever invented, before the fire.
Arab riots kill 67 Jews in Hebron in 1929 — the traveler walks the alleys after and says the land's long agony found its modern rhythm.
Gandhi walks 240 miles to the sea and makes illegal salt at Dandi — the traveler marches the last miles and says the empire's monopoly was broken by a handful of seawater.
Clyde Tombaugh finds Pluto in 1930 — a speck at the edge of the solar system, and the traveler says it's still out there, cold and faithful, whatever we call it.
Uruguay hosts and wins the first World Cup in 1930 — the traveler sits in the Centenario Stadium as football becomes the planet's great ritual.
The Nazis win 107 Reichstag seats in 1930 — the traveler watches the returns and says respectable Germans still called Hitler a clown; the clown had a private army.
Birdseye's frozen foods hit the shelves in 1930 — the traveler buys peas in Springfield and says winter came in a box, learned from Inuit flash-freezing in Labrador.
Getulio Vargas seizes power in Brazil in 1930 — the traveler is in Rio and says strongmen promise order and deliver it, with interest.
Japan stages the Mukden explosion and seizes Manchuria in 1931 — the traveler stands by the railway tracks and says the road to Pearl Harbor began there.
The Empire State Building opens in 1931 — 102 stories into the Depression sky, and the traveler rides to the observation deck and calls it hope in limestone and steel.
Spain proclaims its Second Republic in 1931 — the traveler celebrates in Madrid and says the attempt was glorious and the failure catastrophic.
Capone goes to prison for tax evasion in 1931 — the traveler sits in the Chicago courtroom and says you can dodge the bullets but you can't dodge the books.
Nine Black teenagers are railroaded in Scottsboro, Alabama, in 1931 — the traveler sits in the courtroom and says American justice learned its conscience there, slowly.
The Star-Spangled Banner becomes America's official anthem in 1931 — the traveler stands for it at ballparks and says some anthems are chosen; this one was survived into.
Roosevelt defeats Hoover in 1932 promising a New Deal — the traveler is at the convention and says the words were vague but the hope was specific.
Earhart flies the Atlantic solo in 1932 — the traveler tracks her Vega through ice and leaking fuel to an Irish pasture, and says the world finally stopped calling her a passenger.
The Lindbergh baby is kidnapped in 1932 — the traveler stands outside the Hopewell house and says the hero learned what fame costs; the grief is still fresh.
Los Angeles hosts the 1932 Olympics on a shoestring — the first Olympic Village, and the traveler says Hollywood hosted the Games and the Games learned Hollywood.
Chadwick discovers the neutron in 1932 — the atom's hidden heart, and the traveler stands in the Cavendish Lab knowing the atomic age needed that missing piece.
Lake Placid hosts the 1932 Winter Games — the traveler stands by the bobsled run and says winter came to America and America learned to love it.
Germany burns through chancellors in 1932 while Hitler waits — the traveler watches the backroom deals and calls Papen's bargain the most catastrophic miscalculation in modern history.
Hitler becomes Chancellor on January 30, 1933 — the traveler watches the torchlight parade through the Brandenburg Gate and notes the twelve-year night began with a legal appointment.
The Reichstag burns in February 1933 — the traveler stands in the Berlin night and says the fire burned the building but the decrees burned the republic.

Roosevelt's first hundred days flood America with new agencies in 1933 — the traveler walks Washington and calls it the presidency as rescue operation; it ended the despair, and that was the emergency.
The 21st Amendment ends Prohibition in 1933 — the traveler is in a bar that December night and says the drinks were on the Constitution.
Students burn books in Berlin in May 1933 — the traveler stands in the Opernplatz and picks up a half-burned page he says he still has.
The first drive-in opens in Camden, New Jersey, in 1933 — the traveler parks on the gravel lot and says the movies went outside and never quite came back in.
A monster is sighted in Loch Ness in 1933 — the traveler stands on the misty shore and says the legend didn't need the truth; every loch needs its mystery.
The Red Army's Long March covers 6,000 miles in 1934 — the traveler walks parts of the route and calls it defeat transfigured into destiny, Mao's road to power.
Hitler murders his SA leaders in the Night of the Long Knives in 1934 — the traveler is in Berlin and says it taught Germany no one was safe, not even the loyal.

t: The End of Bonnie and Clyde
x: Texas Rangers ambush Bonnie and Clyde in Louisiana in 1934 — the traveler drives the road later and says the Depression made them folk heroes and the posse made them dead.
The first Masters is played at Augusta in 1934 — the traveler walks the azaleas and says it started with a retired champion's dream and a Georgia nursery full of flowers.
Black blizzards bury the Plains in the Dust Bowl — the traveler drives roads dark as night at noon and says the land died but the people didn't.
The Nuremberg Laws strip Jews of citizenship in 1935 — the traveler reads the bureaucratic forms and calls it genocide's paperwork phase; the cold would get colder.
Mussolini invades Ethiopia in 1935 — the traveler hears Haile Selassie's plea in Geneva ("it will be you tomorrow") and watches the League do nothing.
Roosevelt signs Social Security in 1935 — the traveler stands outside the White House and calls it the New Deal's most enduring promise: the government as guarantor.
The first canned beer goes on sale in 1935 — the traveler buys one in Richmond and calls the can the package that conquered the world.
Monopoly hits stores in 1935 — the traveler plays it in parlors across America and notes the real inventor's warning against monopolies became the celebration of them.
Two alcoholics meet in Akron in 1935 and Alcoholics Anonymous is born — the traveler sits in the first church-basement meetings and calls it the most successful therapy ever invented.
Franco's generals rise against the Spanish Republic in 1936 — the traveler is in Barcelona and calls the civil war the dress rehearsal for world war.
Jesse Owens wins four golds in Hitler's 1936 stadium — the traveler sits under the swastikas and says Owens beat the master-race myth but came home to segregation.

t: The King Gives Up the Crown
x: Edward VIII abdicates for Wallis Simpson in 1936 — the traveler hears the radio broadcast and says he got the woman and lost the world; the voice shaking was real.
Stalin's show trials open the Great Purge in 1936 — the traveler sits in the Hall of Columns as Old Bolsheviks confess to scripted crimes; the revolution eats its children.

t: The Dam That Tamed a River
x: Hoover Dam is completed in 1936 — the traveler stands on the curved wall and calls it the New Deal in concrete: a dam built like a cathedral, still holding.
Chiang Kai-shek is kidnapped at Xian in 1936 and forced into a united front with the Communists — the traveler calls it the kidnapping that changed history.
The BBC begins regular television broadcasts from Alexandra Palace in 1936 — the traveler watches the flickering images and calls it the century's hearth being lit.
German bombers flatten Guernica in 1937 — the traveler walks the Basque town after and says Picasso painted the scream from a town most couldn't find on a map.

America's election hung on Florida recounts and the Court decided; the traveler stood in Tallahassee as paper scraps chose a president and the century ended contested.

t: The Night the Computers Didn't Break
x: The Y2K panic spent billions fixing two-digit dates, then the millennium arrived without a glitch — humanity's most expensive scare that never happened.
The Human Genome Project's working draft printed humanity's three billion DNA letters — the instruction book of a species, read for the first time.
The dot-com bubble burst and wiped out trillions — the internet's first gold rush collapsed into empty offices and abandoned whiteboards.
Sydney's 2000 Olympics crowned Cathy Freeman's 400m gold — a moment of national healing watched by a whole continent holding its breath.
The 2000 US election came down to Florida's recount and a Supreme Court ruling — a presidency decided by judges, leaving half the nation unconvinced.
The Nokia 3310 sold over a hundred million units and became legend for surviving anything — the toughest phone ever made, still unmatched.
Napster let millions of teenagers trade songs freely before the lawsuits shut it down — but the window it opened could never be closed again.

t: A Thousand Songs in Your Pocket
x: The iPod's launch began the end of the album — a thousand songs in a pocket dissolved the record store and the long-player forever.

t: The Giant That Cooked Its Books
x: Enron's accounting fraud produced the largest US bankruptcy ever — workers' pensions vanished and a giant fell on cooked books.
Anthrax-laced letters killed five and terrorized America in late 2001 — fear arrived in the mailbox in the shadow of the September attacks.
Camera phones spread and the world began photographing everything — memory itself changed as nothing was lost and nothing stayed private.

t: The Ogre Who Mocked Fairy Tales
x: Shrek mocked every fairy tale convention and won the first-ever animated-feature Oscar — animation learned to laugh at itself.

t: A City of Vice to Steal
x: Grand Theft Auto III invented the open-world game — players got a living city instead of a level, and games were never the same.
Euro notes and coins replaced twelve national currencies in a single morning — a continent woke up sharing one money for the first time.
Mars Odyssey's instruments found vast ice fields beneath the Martian soil — water enough for a future, waiting under the red dust.
Brazil won its fifth World Cup across Japan and Korea — the samba kings reclaimed football's crown and Rio poured into the streets.

t: A Court for the World's Worst Crimes
x: The International Criminal Court opened in The Hague — a courtroom for genocide and war crimes with no country on its door.
SARS emerged in southern China and rode airplanes around the world — eight thousand cases, a rehearsal for a pandemic nobody knew was coming.

t: Forty Hours in a Moscow Theater
x: Chechen fighters seized a Moscow theater; the rescue gas killed 130 hostages along with the captors — a rescue that killed the rescued.
The 2002 Bali bombings killed 202 people, mostly young tourists — fire in paradise, on the island of the gods.
The Iraq invasion toppled Baghdad in weeks on live TV — then came the long insurgency, the missing weapons, and a war with no end.
The Human Genome Project declared the full human DNA code complete — the reading done, the understanding still barely begun.
Columbia disintegrated over Texas during re-entry, killing seven astronauts — a wounded wing, superheated air, and space's unforgiving physics.
Spirit and Opportunity launched for Mars on a 90-day mission — two small rovers carrying humanity's curiosity across two hundred million kilometers.
The WHO declared SARS contained after 8,000 cases — the masks came off, the playbook was filed away, and seventeen years later we'd need it again.
A tree branch in Ohio triggered the great Northeast blackout — fifty million people dark, and Manhattan walked home across the bridges.
MySpace launched social media's first great boom — profiles, Top 8s, glitter backgrounds, and bands discovered in bedrooms.
Facebook began as a Harvard dorm directory and grew into the social graph — billions eventually living half their social lives inside it.

t: The Wave That Crossed an Ocean
x: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed 230,000 people across fourteen countries — the sea pulled back, then returned as a wall.
Spirit and Opportunity bounced down on Mars in airbags and opened their petals — six wheels in red dust, on a 90-day warranty that lasted years.
Ukraine's Orange Revolution filled Kyiv's snowy squares with protesters until a rigged election was annulled and rerun — the people refused to go home.
Cassini orbited Saturn for thirteen years — geysers, methane rain, shepherd moons — then burned up in the clouds to protect the moons it revealed.
The 2004 Olympics returned to Athens, their ancient birthplace — the torch lit by sunlight at Olympia, the games home after 108 years.
Coordinated bombs killed 193 on Madrid's commuter trains — Spain answered terror with candles, dignity, and votes three days later.
YouTube launched with "broadcast yourself" — anyone with a camera became television, and the gatekeepers were walked around, not toppled.
Hurricane Katrina's broken levees drowned New Orleans — the world watched America fail its poorest on live television.
Ten simultaneous Live 8 concerts demanded an end to Africa's debt — billions watched as the planet sang one chorus at the summits.
The Kyoto Protocol became international law — the first climate treaty with binding targets, a thin beginning wearing victory's clothes.
Google Earth put every rooftop on every screen — the whole planet became a thing you could hold, spin, and zoom into.
Deep Impact slammed a copper projectile into Comet Tempel 1 to read its insides — the debris held water and clay, the ingredients of oceans.
Four suicide bombers killed 52 on London's Tube and a bus — and the city answered with full pubs, running buses, and refusal to be scared.
Twitter launched with 140-character updates and became the world's wire service — news by the sentence, revolutions in real time.
Astronomers voted Pluto out of the planet club in Prague — the universe didn't attend, but the schoolchildren protested anyway.
Saddam Hussein was executed in Baghdad and the hanging leaked on phone video — justice to some, revenge to others, and a fire that burned for a decade.
The Wii got grandparents swinging controllers at televisions — games stopped chasing graphics and started chasing joy, for everybody.
Google bought the money-losing, 18-month-old YouTube for $1.65 billion — the bargain of the century, the future of television for a rounding error.
Muhammad Yunus won the Nobel for banking for the poor — tiny loans to Bangladeshi basket weavers that were paid back, with interest.
New Horizons launched for Pluto on a nine-year journey — carrying Clyde Tombaugh's ashes to the world he discovered, demoted before the mail arrived.

t: The Phone That Ate the World
x: The iPhone launched with no keyboard, just glass — and swallowed the camera, the map, and the music player whole, then the whole industry.
The Kindle made a library weightless — readers resisted, then surrendered, and the strangest thing happened: people started reading more.
The subprime mortgage crisis began — houses bought with unpayable loans, foreclosure signs blooming like weeds, the great boom rotting from inside.
Hackers hammered wired Estonia offline — banks, government, everything — the first cyber siege in history, with no soldiers and no shots fired.
Burmese monks marched in saffron robes against the junta — prayer against rifles — until the guns came and the world watched on shaky phone video.
In 2007 humanity became majority-urban for the first time since farming began — no ceremony, just the slow drift from village to megacity.
Benazir Bhutto was assassinated at a campaign rally in Rawalpindi — the bravest woman in South Asian politics, gone in the dust of a December blast.
Lehman Brothers collapsed and the world economy seized up — governments wrote unsayable checks while ordinary people lost houses for tower sins.
Beijing's Olympics opened with the greatest ceremony ever staged — two thousand drummers as one body, five thousand years painted in light.
Barack Obama's election drew a quarter million to Grant Park — "Yes we can," three syllables carrying four hundred years of waiting.

t: The Machine That Sees the Beginning
x: The Large Hadron Collider fired up beneath the Swiss-French border — seventeen miles of tunnel built to rewind the universe to its first trillionth of a second.
A mysterious Satoshi Nakamoto published the nine-page Bitcoin paper — money without a bank, without a king, without anyone in charge.
Terrorists held Mumbai for sixty hours of fire — the Taj burning on live TV — and the city that never stops refused to stop.

t: A Million Pockets, A Million Apps
x: The App Store opened with 500 apps and turned the smartphone from a phone into a universe — a store in every pocket for everything imaginable.
The Bitcoin network went live with its genesis block — carrying a bank-bailout headline in its code, money honest about being made of trust.
H1N1 swept the globe as the first pandemic of the internet age — milder than feared, a rehearsal with real bodies that we should have studied harder.
Nearly two million packed the National Mall for Obama's inauguration — the largest crowd Washington ever held, there to witness a door opening.
NASA's Kepler telescope stared at 150,000 stars to count their planets — and found thousands, proving the galaxy is crowded with worlds.
The Copenhagen climate summit collapsed without a binding deal — a hundred leaders, two weeks, and the hollow feeling of firefighters leaving a burning house.
Millions protested Iran's disputed election in a peaceful green wave — and the regime crushed it with batons, jails, and motorcycles.
Usain Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.58 seconds in Berlin — smiling mid-race while history chased his shadow, a record still untouched.
The iPad turned the computer into a sheet of glass — toddlers swiped before they could read, and the machine dissolved into something held like a magazine.
Instagram launched with a dog photo and quietly rewrote beauty, fame, and self-image — a mirror that taught the world to pose.
A Tunisian fruit vendor's self-immolation set the region ablaze — one man's refusal of humiliation lit the Arab Spring.
A 35-second earthquake leveled Port-au-Prince — palace, cathedral, hospitals — and the world promised everything Haiti is still waiting for.
Deepwater Horizon exploded and bled crude into the Gulf for 87 days on live feed — the marshes black, the pelicans dying, our reach exceeding our grip.
South Africa hosted the first World Cup on African soil — vuvuzelas droning, fan parks dancing, a continent's pride on full display.
WikiLeaks dumped a quarter-million secret diplomatic cables — every embassy's unfiltered gossip, read by the whole planet at once.
Tahrir Square's eighteen days toppled Mubarak — millions refusing to go home, and the Arab Spring blazed outward from that recipe.
Japan's earthquake and tsunami melted down Fukushima's reactors — the wave killed 20,000, the atoms scattered a fear that closed reactors worldwide.
US Navy SEALs killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad — a decade of hunting ended in forty minutes, and ten years of grief found release.
Steve Jobs died and the world mourned a salesman like a saint — shrines of flowers and half-eaten apples outside stores worldwide.
A car-sized nuclear rover launched for Mars — the most ambitious machine ever aimed at another world, riding fire toward its seven minutes of terror.
South Sudan voted itself into existence — dancing in Juba's dust on independence day, the world's youngest nation born in joy.
Occupy protesters camped in Zuccotti Park with no leaders and one phrase — "we are the 99%" — and changed the conversation even after the tents were cleared.
The Higgs boson turned up at the Large Hadron Collider — fifty years of hunting ended with a bump in the data and tears in the auditorium.
Curiosity survived its seven minutes of terror — heat shield, parachute, then a sky crane lowering the rover to Mars on cables.
London's Olympics opened with the Queen apparently parachuting in with Bond — wit, rain held off, and Bolt defending his crowns.
Superstorm Sandy drowned New York's subways and shore towns — the city improvised kindness in the dark, and started listening to the warning.
Psy's horse dance became the first billion-view video — a joke with a beat that gave the world one shared dance floor.

t: The Schoolgirl Who Would Not Stop
x: Malala was shot for going to school and survived to shame the world — the Taliban tried to silence a schoolgirl and created its loudest voice.

t: A Man Falls from the Edge of Space
x: Felix Baumgartner skydived from 39 kilometers up — stepping off the edge of space, falling faster than sound, and living to tell it.

t: A Pope Named for the Poor
x: Francis became the first Latin American pope — asking the crowd's prayers before his blessing, riding in a Ford Focus, washing prisoners' feet.

t: The Man Who Carried the Secrets
x: Edward Snowden revealed the NSA was watching everyone — every call, every email — and fled to Moscow as the debate split the world.
Nelson Mandela died at 95 — twenty-seven years in prison, one walk to a free presidency, and a world that bowed to proof hatred can be outlived.
China's Chang'e-3 landed the Jade Rabbit rover on the Moon — the first soft landing in 37 years, and a message: the Moon has new visitors.
Super Typhoon Haiyan devastated the Philippines at record strength — Tacloban flattened, a preview of stronger storms where the poorest pay first.

t: Three Words on a Facebook Post
x: "Black lives matter" was written online for the first time — three words that traveled from a post to a worldwide reckoning.
The Boston Marathon bombing killed three at the finish line — and a year later a million lined the route: Boston Strong, a city that runs toward.
Ebola ravaged West Africa — 11,000 dead — and health workers in moonsuits became the bravest people on Earth, beating it with courage and tracing.
The Ice Bucket Challenge flooded ALS research with $200 million — the silliest, most successful medical fundraiser in history.
The Philae lander touched down on a tumbling comet after ten years of travel — bounced twice, landed anyway, and rode it around the Sun.
MH370 disappeared with 239 aboard and was never found — the transponder dark, the ocean keeping its secrets, aviation's greatest mystery.
Russia seized Crimea with unmarked soldiers and a gunpoint referendum — the old map tore, the West frowned, and nobody acted like it was a rehearsal.
ISIS proclaimed its brutal caliphate across Iraq and Syria — black flags spreading like a stain, ancient temples falling, evil gone viral.
Hong Kong students held the streets for 79 days under a sea of yellow umbrellas — the most polite occupation in history, asking only for a real vote.
196 nations adopted the Paris climate accord — every country on Earth promising to hold the warming line, the gavel falling to tears and cheers.
SpaceX landed an orbital booster upright for the first time — rockets had never come back standing up, and spaceflight got cheap overnight.
New Horizons revealed Pluto's great icy heart — Tombaugh Regio, bigger than Texas — and the demoted planet had the most beautiful last laugh.
The Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage across America 5-4 — couples who waited forty years lined up for licenses as the arc bent.
Terrorists murdered Paris cartoonists, and millions marched in reply — "Je suis Charlie," four million pencils held up to the sky.
A million refugees crossed the Mediterranean in a year — the largest movement since WWII — as Europe argued with itself about its own soul.
A 7.8 earthquake killed 9,000 in Nepal and toppled ancient temples — centuries of carved wood became dust, and the survivors rebuilt by hand.

t: The Dress That Broke the Internet
x: One blurry dress photo split the planet — blue-black or white-gold — the first truly global argument about nothing, proving we see different worlds.
The Brexit referendum shocked the world 52-48 — the pound fell, the PM resigned by lunch, and the arguing never stopped.
Donald Trump won the presidency against every poll — the map turned red state by state, and American politics broke in new ways.
The Zika virus spread through the Americas — a mosquito bite casting a shadow over every pregnancy, leaving fear and unanswerable questions.
Pokémon Go turned parks into monster-hunting grounds — millions chasing digital creatures, augmented reality's first irresistible proof.
AlphaGo defeated Go champion Lee Sedol 4-1 — move 37 made the master smile at a beauty no human had ever seen.
Juno slipped into orbit around Jupiter — first pictures of blue storm-tossed poles, cyclones the size of continents waltzing.
The Olympics went to South America for the first time — Bolt's triple-triple, the refugee team's march, Brazil's football gold in the Maracanã.
Native-led protesters faced down a pipeline at Standing Rock — tipis in snow, prayer fires, water cannons — teaching America "water is life."
"Me too" became a roar — millions of women speaking at once, powerful men falling one by one, and the end of the silence abuse hid behind.
Harvey, Irma, and Maria battered the Americas in one season — Houston drowned, the Caribbean flattened, Puerto Rico left in the dark.
The Moon's shadow raced coast to coast — twelve million in its path, the corona's white fire, and a whole country looking up at once.
Myanmar's army drove 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh — the fastest exodus of the century, a million people in bamboo and plastic at Cox's Bazar.
Bitcoin hit $20,000 and everyone suddenly knew crypto — taxi drivers day-trading, a mania that crashed but left the idea standing.
The interstellar rock Oumuamua streaked through our solar system — cigar-shaped, speeding up mysteriously, gone before we reached the door.
Cassini burned up in Saturn's clouds after thirteen years — its signal fading in mission control, a funeral and love letter sent at once.
Saudi Arabia lifted its ban on women drivers — the first morning brought laughter, tears, and a freedom that had been illegal the day before.
A Chinese scientist announced the first gene-edited babies — the world recoiled, he went to prison, and humanity hadn't decided if it wanted them.

t: A Robot Listens to Mars's Heartbeat
x: InSight landed on Mars to feel its quakes — four years of listening to a cooling world's heartbeat, slower and older than ours.
France won the World Cup in Russia — Mbappé a blur at 19, the Champs-Élysées a river of joy, a team that was France in miniature.
Twelve Thai boys and their coach were rescued from a flooded cave after 18 days — sedated, swum out one by one, all alive: a happy ending on live TV.
Apple became the first trillion-dollar company — the bitten apple worth more than most countries, built on the phones in all our pockets.
Jamal Khashoggi was killed inside a Saudi consulate in Istanbul — a columnist lured and murdered for writing, the lies collapsing one by one.
The Kepler telescope retired after finding 2,600 planets — out of fuel, drifting silent, having answered: yes, the galaxy is full of worlds.
Parkland survivors led a million people to Washington — teenagers refusing the script, turning grief into the most eloquent lobbying Congress ever feared.

t: The Shadow of a Black Hole
x: Eight telescopes became one planet-sized eye and photographed a black hole — an orange ring of fire around darkness, 55 million light-years away.
Fire gutted Notre-Dame and the spire fell on live TV — crowds sang hymns to the burning church as Paris decided she would rise again.
Greta Thunberg scolded the UN — "how dare you" — a 16-year-old's fury indicting a generation, millions of kids walking out behind her.
Hong Kong rose against Beijing's grip — two million in the streets, the bill withdrawn, the grip tightening anyway, one summer of unafraid.
Doctors noticed a strange pneumonia in Wuhan and the alarm was silenced — whistleblowers scolded, but the virus didn't read memos.
NASA named its Moon-return program Artemis — Apollo's twin sister — promising not flags and footprints this time, but a base, and a woman walking first.
Australia's Black Summer burned an area the size of England — red skies over Sydney, three billion animals lost, a preview of the century's fire.
India's Vikram lander crashed into the lunar surface on live TV — a stumble at the Moon that was still a reach, rehearsal for the landing to come.
The WHO declared a pandemic and the world stopped — empty highways, silent cities, chalk rainbows in windows, humanity holding its breath together.
mRNA vaccines were approved in eleven months — sequence to shot, the fastest vaccine in history, science running faster than fear.
George Floyd's murder set off the largest protests in American history — "I can't breathe" filmed on a sidewalk, the world marching in masks.
SpaceX flew astronauts to the space station — America launching its own crews again, on a commercial spaceship with a touchscreen cockpit.
A port warehouse of ammonium nitrate exploded in Beirut — the century's biggest non-nuclear blast, half the city leveled by six years of negligence.
Lockdown's strangest shared obsession — a tiger breeder, a murder plot, and the whole planet bingeing the same fever dream in two weeks.
The UAE's Hope probe launched for Mars — the Arab world's first interplanetary mission, a region deciding its future is in the stars.
Perseverance launched carrying Ingenuity — a four-pound helicopter bound for Mars, aiming for the Wright brothers' second flight on another world.

t: The Eye That Sees First Light
x: The James Webb telescope launched on Christmas Day — a gold origami mirror unfolding a million miles out, built to see the first light.
Billions were vaccinated in the race against the variants — stadiums turned clinics, the largest medical campaign in history, hope in a syringe.
A mob stormed the US Capitol — the first breach since 1814 — while Congress hid and the world watched American democracy shake.
COP26 in Glasgow pleaded for the planet's future — coal phasedown, methane pledges, island nations begging, time bought but not enough.

t: The First Flight on Another World
x: Ingenuity's helicopter lifted off on Mars — twelve seconds, the first powered flight on another world, the Wright brothers' dream repeated.
The Taliban retook Kabul in eleven days as America left — chaos on the runway, babies over the wire, twenty years ending in grief.
The Ever Given wedged sideways in the Suez Canal for six days — twelve percent of world trade stopped by one gust of wind and a tiny excavator.
Zuckerberg renamed Facebook to Meta, betting the whole company on the metaverse — billions burning on the wager that we'll live inside the screen.
Webb's first images stunned the world — star-birth cliffs, thousands of galaxies in a speck of sky, thirteen billion years of light in a frame.
Russia invaded Ukraine — the largest European invasion since 1945 — and millions fled west as Kyiv held and the world relearned war's return.
An uncrewed Orion looped the Moon and came safely home — Artemis I, fifty years after Apollo, the way back remembered.
DART slammed into the asteroid Dimorphos and shoved it off course — humanity's first rehearsal for the day a rock comes for Earth.
A California lab achieved fusion ignition — 192 lasers, more energy out than in, the stars' fire finally paying for itself.
Qatar hosted a winter World Cup amid fierce controversy — Messi lifting it, Mbappé's hat trick, glory on screen and ghosts underneath.
Elizabeth II died after seventy years on the throne — a five-mile queue of mourners, an era measured in a single lifetime of duty.

t: The Town Square Gets a New Owner
x: Elon Musk bought Twitter for $44 billion and renamed it X — walked in carrying a sink, fired half the staff, and the town square argued about it.

t: The Year Everybody Talked to AI
x: ChatGPT went mainstream — a hundred million users in two months, the world discovering the machine could write, code, and talk back.
Hamas attacked Israel on October 7 — 1,200 dead, hostages taken — and war engulfed Gaza, the old wound torn open and bleeding still.

t: India Touches the Moon's South Pole
x: Chandrayaan-3 landed where no craft ever had — the Moon's south pole — four years after the crash, the rehearsal become the performance.
Barbie and Oppenheimer dueled at the box office on the same day — memes, pink suits, a billion in pink and an Oscar sweep, and both won.
Twin earthquakes killed 50,000 in Turkey and Syria — cities folded in the night, rescuers digging side by side across borders.
The Titan submersible imploded diving toward the Titanic — five lives, a game-controller sub, and the sea's indifference to hubris.
Apple's Vision Pro put a $3,500 computer an inch from the eyes — floating windows, typing on air, the future pressing its face to the glass.

t: A New King Crowned at Last
x: Charles III was crowned at Westminster after a 70-year wait — the longest apprenticeship in history, the ancient ritual, the open question.
The Paris Olympics opened on the Seine — 85 boats floating past 300,000 spectators, the whole city as the arena, rain and all.
A total solar eclipse crossed Mexico, the US, and Canada — forty million in its path, the diamond ring, strangers hugging in noon-darkness.
SpaceX caught a returning 20-story booster with the launch tower's arms — like chopsticks picking up a falling tree, the sky itself caught.
Trump won a second, non-consecutive term — only the second in US history — the pendulum swinging hard back to the original.
Notre-Dame reopened five years after the fire — spire rebuilt, stone glowing clean, proof that some burned things come back.
India voted with 968 million eligible — six weeks, a million polling stations, inked fingers held high, the mighty humbled by the count.
New malaria vaccines reached African children at unprecedented scale — mothers queuing with babies, humanity's oldest enemy met with a needle.
Polaris Dawn astronauts stepped outside their capsule — the first private spacewalk, no government, no agency, just a depressurized cabin and nerve.
The Sun's peak brought auroras over Texas and Spain — green and red ripples, neighbors in pajamas, the star reminding us it's still there.
Humanoid robots began trial shifts in warehouses — careful as new employees on day one, the temp workers of the machine age clocking in.
AI assistants started booking, coding, and shopping on their own — the chatbots grew hands, and the tool became the employee.
Lab-grown chicken reached supermarket shelves — it tasted like chicken because it was chicken, minus the farm, the feathers, the beak.
Starship's test flights quickened toward full reusability — the explosions becoming rhythm, the biggest rocket ever learning to come home.
Power grids strained as the AI boom's electricity hunger collided with them — the cloud has a body, and the body needs feeding.
Cheap smartphones crossed 80% of sub-Saharan Africa — mobile money, market prices, school lessons, a century of wires leapfrogged.
Milan and Cortina host the Winter Olympics — speed skaters, downhillers through the Tofane pines, winter's party in the beautiful mountains.
The United States celebrates 250 years — the declaration's argument still running, the experiment still arguing about its founding sentence.
Forty-eight teams play across the US, Mexico, and Canada — 104 matches, sixteen cities, the biggest World Cup ever staged.

t: The Year of the Talking Machines
x: Conversational AI becomes ordinary household help worldwide — grandparents adapting fastest, children never knowing the silence before.
Artemis II carries four astronauts around the Moon — the farthest humans since 1972, Earthrise again for a new generation.
Vaccines and gene-drive mosquitoes push malaria deaths to historic lows — the red zones fading, humanity's oldest killer losing millennial ground.
Record numbers turn 100 as longevity gains spread — the centenarian club's membership exploding, a hundred years becoming a plan, not a miracle.
The first commercial fusion plant breaks ground — from ignition to concrete, the thirty-years-away joke finally retiring.
AI begins spotting diseases years before symptoms — medicine's oldest dream, from treating the sick to warning the well.

t: The First Woman Walks the Moon
x: Artemis III lands and a woman's boot prints join Armstrong's in the lunar dust — half the human race finally seeing itself in the footprints.
A quantum computer solves a useful chemistry problem no supercomputer could — the strange physics finally earning its keep, smelling like new medicine.
Vaccine plants across Africa make routine shots close to home — sovereignty in a vial; next pandemic, Africa supplies instead of waiting.
Electric cars pass half of new sales in China and Europe — the combustion century ending not with a ban but with a better deal and a test drive.

t: The Mind Held a Little Longer
x: New Alzheimer's drugs slow the disease enough to matter — one more Christmas of remembered names, one more good year; sometimes the gift is just more time.
India's digital rails make welfare fully paperless for a billion people — the farmer paid instantly, the middleman's cut gone, dignity at scale.
Air taxis ferry fans across the LA Olympics — quiet, electric, the Jetsons at last running on schedule above the crawling 405.
The Moon-orbiting Gateway station welcomes its first crew — modules from four continents, a porch light on for the long trip down.
A fusion company feeds steady power into a real grid — seawater for fuel, the star in a bottle finally paying the electric bill.
The global plastics treaty takes effect — single-use begins to die, beaches cleaner, the disposable century unwinding one refill at a time.
The world installs a terawatt of solar in a single year — blue-black fields to the horizon, humanity finally building at the scale of its hunger.
A sample-return mission lands Martian rocks on Earth — sealed tubes, four billion years old, holding the answer to whether anything ever lived there.
The great asteroid Apophis passes closer than the satellites — a cosmic near-miss turned global festival, three billion people watching one rock go by.
Floating barriers clear the core of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch — the plastic coming home by the shipload, the sea forgiving but remembering.
Rapamycin-class drugs enter large human lifespan trials — not immortality, just more good years; humanity negotiating with aging at last.
The world checks its 2030 pledges — emissions bending, barely, the first time in history the curve bowed down; not an ace, not a failure.
A permanent crewed lunar base endures its first full year — greenhouses glowing through fourteen-day nights, humanity's first airless address.
Coal falls below a fifth of world electricity — the black rock's three-century reign ending in a decade's cliff, cooling towers going silent.
Every type of human cell is mapped and named — 37 trillion cells catalogued, the body's complete parts list, medicine's new foundation.
Africa's working-age population passes one billion — the youngest continent's energy becoming the world's workforce, markets, and momentum.

t: The Year of the Robot Nurse
x: Care robots ease the global nursing shortage — lifting, fetching, monitoring, freeing human nurses for the human work of holding hands.
The Europa Clipper flies through the moon's geysers and tastes the spray — water, salts, organics; not life found, but the kitchen where it could cook.
CRISPR cures reach low-income countries at low cost — children in Nigeria and India cured of the pain their grandparents bore for life.
The Arctic Ocean opens blue in September for the first time in memory — milestone and mourning, the Northwest Passage simply open at last.
Brisbane hosts a carbon-neutral Olympics — solar stadiums, a timber village, the biggest party on Earth leaving no footprint but memories.
The first crewed Mars mission departs Earth — six months of falling toward the red, the species that left Africa leaving Earth itself.
A great telescope finds water vapor on a rocky world — not life, but air and water: a place where life wouldn't be crazy to try.
Real-time earbuds erase the language barrier — five thousand years of Babel dissolved; we finally hear each other, in a hundred tongues.
Human feet touch Mars for the first time — the dust puffing in thin air, the species becoming two-planet in footprints, not theory.
Rich nations finally fund climate adaptation at scale — sea walls, drought crops, raised streets; the invoice paid, costing less than the wars.
Nations share Himalayan glacier data to manage Asia's rivers — old rivals cooperating; water proving stronger than borders.
Saudi Arabia hosts the World Cup — stadiums from sand, brilliant football, fierce scrutiny; the ball rolls and the questions roll with it.
The first Mars crew returns to Earth as heroes — two years on red dust, blinking in blue air; they left as astronauts, returned as ancestors.
Cultured meat undercuts factory farming on price — dinner without slaughter, ten thousand years of husbandry ending with a price tag.

t: The Last New Gasoline Car in Europe
x: The EU combustion-engine ban takes effect — the last new gasoline car, the twentieth century's greatest machine retired by law, replaced by silence.
Solar becomes the cheapest power in history, everywhere — the decade the Sun won; we spent a century digging old sunlight, now we look up.
Lunar greenhouses yield their first harvest — lettuce and tomatoes in regolith, the oldest human art practiced where nothing was supposed to grow.
New therapies put type 2 diabetes into routine remission — half a billion people getting their lives back; the body wasn't failing, it was asking for help.
The planet crosses 1.5 degrees of warming — not the end but the assignment; grief, then work, the adaptation age in full swing.
A second crew lands and the Mars foothold grows — the first were visitors, these are residents; one plants a flag, the other plants a garden.
Brain implants restore lost memories in early trials — the Alzheimer's father recognizing his daughter; forgetting becoming optional.
A new vaccine ends TB's reign as the top infectious killer — history's deadliest infection beaten with a shot, persistence, and the decision that every life counts.
The Dragonfly rotorcraft lands on Titan — hopping between dunes under orange skies, a nuclear dragonfly sampling prebiotic chemistry.
Heat-proof corals are replanted across dying reefs — the white dead blooming color again; not the same, but alive, and that's enough.
Demographers call the top of the human wave — the peak nearing, the exponential age ending not with disaster but with diplomas.
Airships sail Venus's clouds hunting life's chemistry — hell below, haven above, floating labs seeking the one thing that changes everything.
New therapies end age-related farsightedness — the 60-year-old reading fine print unaided; a small miracle celebrated like a holiday.
The final recorded malaria death; eradication certified — millennia of fever ended not with war but with nets, shots, and patience.

t: The United Nations at One Hundred
x: The UN's centenary arrives — reformed or relic? It fed millions and gave small nations a microphone; still arguing, still there.
Ten thousand people live on the Moon — domes, tunnels, low-gravity sports, children who never felt full Earth weight; a city, lighter.
Brain-computer interfaces restore speech and movement routinely — not mind-reading but mind-restoring; the difference between a cage and a key.
AI tutors revive a hundred dying languages — grandmothers' tongues on grandchildren's lips; a hundred worlds brought back from the edge.
Ocean settlements house climate refugees — platforms, gardens, children swimming to school; the sea took their homes, so they built on the sea.

t: The Water Wars That Didn't Happen
x: Desalination treaties defuse the coming water conflicts — the dog that didn't bark; peace, it turns out, is plumbing.

t: The People's Republic at One Hundred
x: China marks its centenary — from poverty to power in a century, the fastest rise in history; the fact stands, the questions remain.

t: The Interstellar Probe Crosses the Heliopause
x: Humanity's farthest craft tastes interstellar space beyond the Sun's bubble — faint, fading, still talking; we've left the Sun's house.

t: Lakes of Methane, Streets of Ice
x: A research town rises on Titan — methane lakes, ice streets, orange skies; the outer system's first hometown on the strangest shore.

Robots mine Mercury's metals — heat-shielded miners, mass drivers launching ore; the closest planet, once useless, now a treasure.
Lab-grown staples end caloric hunger — the oldest curse lifted not with charity but with vats and the decision that no child goes unfed.

t: The Year Nobody Died of the Flu
x: A universal flu vaccine ends seasonal flu — no more winter waves, no more annual gamble; the old killer retired, winter got kinder.
A craft touches a world beyond Neptune — landing gently on ice older than Earth; the solar system's attic, finally under our feet.
A century after Sputnik's beep, a million satellites orbit — the night sky busy with metal; the question now is whose sky it is.
Elephant populations recover to pre-1900 levels — matriarchs leading, calves playing; the largest land animal back from the brink, Earth remembering how to heal.
Moon settlers ratify self-rule — the first new nation not on Earth writing its own constitution; they didn't rebel, they just grew up.
Humanity's farthest orbiter settles around Neptune — every planet now orbited, the map complete, the exploring not.
Waste becomes a forgotten word — everything reused, materials looping forever; "waste" marked archaic in the dictionary, Earth unburdened.
Telescopes begin mapping the Oort Cloud — trillions of comets, the last unmapped region; we live in a snow globe a light-year wide, now counting flakes.
The human population peaks near ten billion — the wave cresting, the crowded planet asking can we; the peak is the test, the plateau the grade.
Mars's population passes fifty thousand — neighborhoods, schools, the Martian-born outnumbering the Earth-born; an outpost become a civilization.
Vaccines end nearly all childhood killers — mothers calm, children thriving; the old fears become history, and the children just live.
Forest cover passes its year-2000 extent — the green coming back, carbon buried in wood; the lungs of Earth breathing deep again.
The famous comet swings by the Sun again — on schedule, as always; the old friend returning, and we're still here watching.
The verified oldest humans pass 140 — living history, a century and a half of life; the question not how but what for, answered: for all of it.
Silent-speech devices become as common as phones — think and it's written; the keyboard retired, the world quieter and louder than ever.

t: The Grand Tour of the Outer Moons
x: Crewed flybys reach Uranus and Neptune — the ice giants filling windows; a century of robots, now we go ourselves; the system next door.
The rainforest's dieback reverses — canopy whole, rivers clear; we nearly lost the lungs of the world, then chose to stop cutting.
Ancient microbial fossils are found in Martian rock — proof of past life; the question answered yes, the next question: are we its echo?
A world referendum weighs shared AI dividends — humanity's first planet-wide money decision; the machines make plenty, the answer being counted.

t: The Ear on the Far Side
x: A giant radio telescope opens on the Moon's far side — shielded from Earth's noise, listening to the first stars; the universe talking, us listening properly.
Early detection ends most cancer deaths — the emperor dethroned not by cure but by catching it first; a century of fear become a footnote.
A probe intercepts an interstellar object — last time we watched it go; this time we chase it, touching another star's rock.
Vertical farms feed half the cities — stacked greens under LED suns, water recycled; agriculture leaves the field, the city feeding itself floor by floor.
Regenerative farming restores the world's topsoil — the dark rich earth alive again; we treated dirt like dirt, now like the foundation of everything.
An orbiter settles around Pluto — the 2015 flyby's glimpse become a stay; the little world with the big heart, waited for and returned to.
Free elections reach their widest extent in history — more humans choosing rulers than ever; the wave high and still rising, imperfect and real.
A probe melts through Europa's ice into the ocean — kilometers down to dark ancient water; we're in an alien sea, and we'll know soon.
Companion AIs end the epidemic of isolation — not replacing people but accompanying them; the cure not a drug but someone to talk to.
A telescope photographs an Earth twin — the pale blue dot doubled; another blue pixel out there, and the universe less lonely.

Family-based care replaces institutions worldwide — the last orphanage closes, every child with a family; it took long enough, we got there.
Warming stabilizes below two degrees — the ceiling holds; not the dream but the line, held barely and together; the planet warmer but ours.
Mars passes one hundred thousand residents — domes, streets, the Martian-born majority; a people, a culture, a world calling itself home.
Extinction rates fall to pre-industrial levels — the bleeding stopped, the red list shrinking; the sixth extinction halted, Earth keeping its children.
The first verified 150th birthday — a century and a half of mornings; the frontier moving, the question changing from how long to how deep.
Whale populations exceed pre-whaling numbers — blues and humpbacks everywhere; hunted to the edge, then stopped, now the ocean sings again.
A city rides Mercury's twilight line — on rails, always in cool dusk; too hot one side, too cold the other, so we live in between.
Biometrics and keys end the password era — the last "Fluffy123!" typed; decades of sticky notes and resets over, security made invisible.
Ten thousand people live among the asteroids — spun habitats, miners, markets; home a hollowed rock with a view of everything.
Chronic pain becomes treatable at its source — decades of agony switched off, not dulled; the body's circuits learned, suffering's oldest form answered.
Laser links give Mars broadband — video not just text, four minutes late; the web leaves Earth, the species staying connected across the void.
Restored lands welcome climate refugees back — the great displacement reversing; they left because the land died, return because it lived again.
Fusion drives cut the Earth-Mars trip to weeks — the torchship's constant thrust; distance stops mattering, the system shrinks to a neighborhood.
Africa holds a third of humanity's youth and its fastest economies — the engine become the driver; the century has an address, and it's African.
Starshot's sails phone home from Alpha Centauri — faint four-year-old signals, the first pictures of another star's planets; "wish you were here."
Every book ever printed is digitized and free — Alexandria rebuilt and fireproof; every human with a screen holding every book ever written.
The United States marks its tricentennial — three hundred years, the experiment still running, the bell cracked and the promise still powerful.
A craft rides a comet for a full orbit — landed, hitched to the ice, studying all the way around the Sun; the oldest travelers with passengers.
Games become humanity's largest art form and classroom — the classroom, concert hall, and novel all playable; we thought games were for kids.
Orbiters map Uranus and Neptune completely — the last planets' close-up; the family album complete, every world known, exploring continuing.
Four living generations become the norm — great-grandmother to child all at the table; longevity's gift not years but overlap.
A million people call the Moon home — cities, districts, the Moon-born majority; not an outpost but a world, born under Earthlight.
The first generation treated for aging itself reaches 120 healthy — aging managed like a disease; the verdict: it works, the future got longer.
Mars's population passes one million — cities, culture, the Martian-born thinking of Earth as the old country; a world, fully.
Climate engineering steadies the storms — the managed skies, hurricanes softened; we spent centuries at the sky's mercy, now we negotiate, carefully.
Saturn's moons host fuel depots — tankers, ice mines, the outer system's gas stations; the rings become history's most beautiful truck stop.
Global literacy reaches one hundred percent — the last illiterate taught, the oldest divide closed; the word finally everyone's.
A century without great-power war is tallied — the near-misses, treaties, luck, and work; the balance sheet in lives saved: uncountable.
Robots do most physical labor, humans do the caring — the machines lifting, the people loving; the caring economy finally valued.
A telescope at the Sun's gravitational lens sees continents on exoplanets — the Sun used as a lens; pixels become places, alien shores resolved.
Desalination makes water abundant on every coast — the oldest scarcity solved; the sea full, and now so are we; the wars that didn't happen, this is why.
A hundred thousand people live in Venus's skies — habitats, districts, a people of the air; the hell-planet's sky colonized, the ground never missed.
A complete human life's archive fits in a locket — a century of moments kept; we used to lose everything, now the question is what to do with forever.
A settlement rises on Pluto's moon Charon — habitats under a Pluto-filled sky; the farthest town ever built, the edge become home.
Humanity votes limits on the all-seeing cameras — safety yes, privacy too; we built the eyes, then blinked and chose who masters them.
The first multi-generation starship departs — thousands aboard, centuries ahead; the bravest journey in history just began, watched by crowds who'll never see it again.
The global immune shield stops outbreaks in days — the age of plagues ended not by luck but by design; the microbes still try, they don't succeed.

t: The Second Wave to the Stars
x: Bigger light-sails chase the first toward the stars — the whisper become a voice; we're not visiting the stars anymore, we're moving in.

Longevity's frontier keeps moving — the verified 175-year-old; the question no longer how long but how deep, how kind, how much.
A submersible swims Europa's alien sea — descent into dark water, lights on; we're swimming on another world, and the moment is everything.
Self-contained green cities house a billion people — towers with farms inside, closed loops; the city as ecosystem, the future vertical and green.
Mars passes two million residents — cities, de facto nations; the Earth-born a minority now, the Martians just people, the world fully itself.
Ten thousand languages are archived and living — the tower rebuilt not to reach heaven but to keep every way of saying human; all alive.
The ocean moon Europa is declared a protected wilderness — the first world we chose not to take; we visit, we don't stay, the ocean stays wild.
Most humans work because they want to — the machines do the necessary, we do the meaningful; the question changed from "what do you do" to "what do you love."
A crewed outpost stands at the Sun's edge — the farthest human address; the Sun behind, the stars ahead, people on the porch of the Sun's house.
Carbon dioxide falls back toward 350 ppm — the restored sky; we filled it, then emptied it; the number comes down, the planet exhales.

The first bicentenarian — two hundred years of mornings; the frontier moving, the question what for, answered: for this, for all of it.
A hundred thousand people live under Titan's orange sky — domes, streets, methane rain on roofs; the outer system's great city, home.
Fish stocks exceed all recorded history — the teeming waters back; we emptied the ocean, then let it refill; the sea forgives when we let it.
Power stations orbit close to the Sun — great collectors drinking starlight at the source; we went to the fire for power, collecting at scale.
Billions link minds for one night of celebration — the planet as one mind; separate for all of history, for one night we're not.
A depot rises at the solar system's edge — fuel, supplies, the last stop before the dark; the edge has an address, ships resting before the silence.
The World Bank retires the "developing nation" category — the old divide closed, every nation arrived; the category is history, the work continues.
Venus settlers vote on terraforming — green it or keep it wild; the cloud cities deciding their world's fate, the vote close, the future theirs.
AI tutors give every child a personal genius — the patient teacher always there; not replacing teachers but multiplying them, every mind taught like it matters.
Light-sails depart for Barnard's Star — after Alpha Centauri, the next; the stars getting closer one sail at a time.
The healing of soil, sea, and sky is declared complete — not pristine but whole; the work of a century done, the keeping begins.
The first planet-wide referendum — ten billion voices, one question; not nations voting but humanity, deciding together for the first time.
The first third-generation Martian is born — grandparents Mars-born; Mars not the new world but the old world to them, Earth just the story.
Every willing human's story is archived — the species' memory; no one forgotten who wanted remembering; the archive complete, the story continuing.
The generation ship phones home from deep space — faint signal, we're here, we're well; the bravest journey reporting in from out there.
Carbon dioxide returns near pre-industrial levels — the air our ancestors breathed; we broke the sky, we fixed it, the planet what it can be.
A million humans live beyond Mars — belt, moons, stations; the frontier populated, the dark with addresses, living everywhere the Sun reaches.
Humanity prepares to close its wildest century — from the internet to the stars in a hundred years; we did that, and the next century is waiting.
The bigger sails report from Proxima's planets — the whisper become a letter; worlds described, maybe life, the stars talking back.
Ten billion souls counted, on Earth and beyond — Earth, Moon, Mars, beyond; the peak, the plateau; everyone matters, everyone is counted.
The digital century closes — connected, crowded, still arguing, still alive; we connected the world and crowded the planet; the verdict: human.
Mars holds three million people — from footprints to millions in seventy years; the red planet a world, the second world, ours.
The verse history ends where the reader begins — the traveler hands over the pen; the future isn't written yet, and now it's yours.
